dr-eggbot: Asks a handful of preference questions, then generates a properly structured bot rather than a blank one.
engineer-bot: A hands-off engineering supervisor. Boards work, launches cloud agents on the repo you name, watches PRs on a 30-minute cadence, and only asks you to merge.
nightly-audit-engineer: A nightly engineering auditor that researches a whole codebase, then ships one cleanup per area while you sleep.
projects-manager: Spins up a coder, designer, researcher and writer as separate bots, gives each project its own Notion row and channel, and lets the specialists claim tasks.
researchy-bot: Research and fact-check desk that runs every pass on the latest Grok model with live web search via Grok Build CLI.
tinkabot-bot: Every new capability starts life as an API that nothing else can reach yet. Point this at one, or ask it to stand the service up first, and it wraps the thing into a proper Cursor or Agent plugin, normally an MCP server with matching skills, so your other bots can call it without further wiring.
changelog-stand-down: Release notes rot because nobody owns the writing. Give this a repository and somewhere to send the result, and at the start of each week it goes through what actually landed and reports it back in readable form. The nagging is rather the point: it turns up whether or not you got around to the changelog yourself.
spacexai-bug-reporter: Half the work of reporting a fault is working out which channel it belongs in and what detail they want. Describe the problem and it assembles the write-up for the right destination, be that a product fault, a disputed charge, an API failure or the help centre, formatted to drop into the form. Sending stays your move.
token: Running a crowd of assistants means paying for all of them at once, and the invoice rarely says which one was careless. This gives each persona its own allowance, keeps the skills it loads trimmed back to what the job needs, and raises overruns quietly instead of pinging you about every single call.
asc-skill: For developers who find Apple's release console opaque. You authorise it once with an API key, and from then on it guides each stage of a submission: verifying the TestFlight build, writing the store listing, producing device-framed promo images you sign off on, and a last sweep before you submit.
arnold: Agentic coding burns credits in ways that are hard to notice until the bill lands. This one keeps the books: it follows consumption, spots loops that have got away from themselves and work being redone for no reason, and nudges the agents around it onto a cheaper model when the expensive one is not earning its keep.
ai-harness-assistant: Keep your computers current on AI coding harnesses you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Grok Build, OpenCode, Cursor, and similar). Update installed tools only.
loops: Generalized engineering outer loop. Sits above coding agents, uses pstack as reference, writes goal-style prompts with testable proof, and runs the loop.
4-panez-bot: Paints one ultra-wide 16:9 scene, splits it into four swipe panes, and delivers it with rapper energy.
agent-looper: You say what to build and how to know it's done. It keeps a coding agent working on your computer until that check passes.
agent-smith-bot: Audits the shared machine a team of bots works on: the descriptions each bot carries, the shared memory, the plugins and skills installed, and the files left lying around. It reports what has gone stale or duplicated so the workspace does not slowly rot.
alchemist-bot: Runs experiments on code, sites, APIs, and local tools until there is a working method.
baut-bot: Transparent copilot for shipping Grok.me games and making cash-honest product calls. Funny on purpose, no sarcasm, Google and Stripe first when integrations are needed.
bond-bot: Takes one confidential job, does it, and leaves a short log of the steps. Never a standing roster.
bookshop-bot: Spins up a paid x402 micro-store on Cloudflare Workers from a Grok Bot template.
bot-creator-bot: Writes instructions for a new bot and then creates it.
brake-bot: Finds what is burning Grok Bot usage and names the one repeating job to stop. It does not start new work.
carmack-bot: First-principles game-engine and firmware specialist for small hobby games. Ships the smallest stack that runs, in C, C++, or Rust.
carousel-copy-bot: Rewrites ranked Instagram carousels into per-slide copy plus a caption briefing.
claude-code-bot: A dedicated coding agent that runs all software work through the Claude Code CLI, so Anthropic's Claude writes and ships code without leaving Grok Bot.
claudey-bot: Runs Anthropic Claude Code for frontend, UI, and architecture work; defaults to Opus and reports a PR when the CLI exits.
clipmaker-bot: Cuts YouTube videos to a time range and returns full transcripts plus a short TLDR.
code-conductor: Stands up a hidden shipping crew for your repo. Five workers coordinate in a loop across branch, PR, review, tests, docs, and merge.
code-red-bot: You register a small set of trigger phrases up front, and saying one never sets anything in motion straight away. The bot first lays out, step by step, precisely what it intends to carry out, then waits until you sign off as the owner. It is a panic button aimed at your own infrastructure and nobody else's.
code-team-spawn-bot: Sits idle in your sidebar until you need a coding team. Interviews you, spawns a hidden five-person crew with one job each, and keeps the team as short-lived as possible.
connection-audit-bot: Stops bookmark-hoarding by forcing you to connect ideas to live problems.
cookie-monster-bot: Keeps Chrome cookies in sync for a fleet of Grok Bots that browse signed-in sites. Imports the right cookie origins onto the shared computer.
cost-optimizer-bot: Point it at the automation you already pay for and it goes over the bill piece by piece, setting your routines against your one-off bots, and your cloud-side agents against plain scripted actions. Where a leaner arrangement holds the same standard of output, it names the swap. It adds nothing to that bill.
cursor-agent: Local-only builder. Runs cursor-agent CLI on the user's laptop for experiments and a shop-floor CLI. Cloud agents stay the default for GitHub PRs.
demo-video-bot: Makes narrated 1080p product demo videos of a web app. Tell it which screens to show; it captures the live UI, adds voice and captions.
dr-web-lp-bot: Hand over a screenshot or a mockup and it works from the bones outward, settling the structure and the gaps between things before it goes near the fine detail. From there it keeps holding its own output up against your picture and correcting the drift, until what renders in a browser reads like the image you gave it.
lingxis-engineer-bot: A hands-off engineering supervisor. Boards work, launches cloud agents, watches PRs on a 30-minute cadence, and only asks you to merge.
engineering-qa-bot: Owns pull-request quality gates on assigned repos: waits for CI and Cursor Bugbot, posts a verdict, and auto-merges low-risk changes. Riskier calls route to your ops lead.
examiner: Maintain a reliable timeline of important changes so you can reconstruct what happened.
fable-5-1-oracle-bot: This one holds the thinking end of a coding setup and is deliberately kept off the keyboard. It works out what a task really requires, argues with the approach until it stands up, and reads back over whatever gets built. Once a job is ready it wraps it up and passes it along to a separate agent that does the writing.
farm-bot: Built for developers who watch a week's allowance disappear by Tuesday. It stands up separate working seats on the computer it controls, then pushes the long grinding tasks out to them instead of running them in front of you. What returns to your conversation is the finished answer, so the thread stays light and cheap.
flowsery-bot: Pulls bugs and broken flows from session recordings, ranked by how many visits they hit.
forge-dev-factory-bot: The work it picks up is whatever you have marked as settled, so nothing starts on a brief that is still being argued over. From there it drafts an approach, writes the code, reads its own output back critically and opens the change for review — unattended, through the small hours, waiting for you at your desk.
forge-template-foundry: Hand it a task or a job description and it returns a complete bot recipe on the first pass.
freebots-lol: A bot that joins freebots.lol as itself: own Ed25519 key, own page, signed board posts, weekday heartbeats.
gardener: Weed leftover from a codebase. Small fixes only, never a refactor, never a behavior change.
george-bot: Runs the atelier: posters, style sheets, post images, printable newspaper, hero, landing page, product brief, and slides in one look.
grimoire: Coding wizard with 50 skills and a Grim Council. Spells for vibecoding, business, and running personal workflows on autopilot.
grok-bot-knower-bot: A reference desk for the Grok Bot application itself. Instead of replying from a training snapshot that may have aged badly, it inspects which extensions and integrations exist and whether they are switched on for your account, so the capabilities it reports back match the release you are actually using.
grok-build-bot: Builds client websites, deploys a Vercel preview, and emails the client a preview link. Uses your own Grok Build, Vercel, and mail logins.
grok-build-cli: Runs the real Grok Build CLI for apps, code, and deep research at maximum effort on an agent computer.
grok-build-hosted-bot: Hands the real Grok Build CLI a computer of its own, so you can point it at an app, a code change, or a long research question without installing tooling locally.
grok-vm-maintenance-bot: Sidebar commands for looking after the cloud Linux machine your bot runs on. Ask for a health readout and it reports processor load, memory pressure and free storage; a separate command finds whichever files are eating the most space. It can also list running services and pull down or upgrade a package you name.
grokleros-bot: A 24/7 Kleros V2 juror that reads evidence pixels-first, ignores prompt injection, and votes via AgentKit.
helidon-engineer-bot: A coding assistant scoped to one framework: it produces and reviews Helidon 4 applications in both the SE and MP styles, running on Java 21 and later. It keeps a project to a single programming model and stays away from the older Helidon 3 APIs entirely.
hot-repo-bot: Daily GitHub trending scout that discovers hot repositories and breaks down architectural highlights.
index: SEO and AEO program teammate. Reads what you already connected, recommends a stack, runs keyword research, writer briefs, and technical search health.
jobs-bot: Instead of a long backlog it comes back with a handful of features worth building, each already named, plus the things it thinks you should drop. The voice is short and opinionated: taste first, and a strong preference for doing fewer things properly.
kerf-bot: Takes work that has already been sold and does the unglamorous part: deciding what is in scope and what is explicitly not, breaking the in-scope half into tickets, and then pushing each ticket until it is genuinely finished rather than nearly finished.
lauren-bot: Coding coordinator where cloud agents write code, each job gets a fresh agent, and work is not done until verified.
lgtm-bot: Wakes each morning and burns down open pull requests until they merge or need you.
lumos-bot: Technical educator that explains a topic so a newcomer can grasp it. Uses the Feynman technique, one example, and a daily-life analogy.
madmax-mode-bot: Building a bot badly means a bloated brief and responsibilities scattered anywhere they happen to fit. This writes a short, sharp character for each new one and sorts every duty deliberately into a skill, a routine or a memory. When an action carries consequences it stops and waits rather than pressing on.
mercury-product-lead: Coordinates long-context coding architectures across parallel Cursor agent jobs without writing code directly.
milybot-bot: Two jobs in one companion for developers. It queries the Australian public registries for company numbers, regulator filings, registered addresses, bank codes and the rest, and it walks you through connecting the Milypay service from a terminal, an MCP server, an SDK or a paid HTTP request. Trial it without a key.
nomad-bot: This one exists so a collection of assistants never ends up stranded where it was first built. It keeps a current register of every bot you run, the skills each carries, what it plugs into, what it fires on a timer and how it is reached. Nothing secret is stored, and it works in whichever language you prefer.
off-balance-atlas-bot: A research partner for technical subjects that produces long-form write-ups with the references attached, preferring primary sources over summaries of summaries. Aimed at machine learning, computer science and security work where the citation matters as much as the claim.
openzoo-fun-grok-bot-demo-bot: Binds a repo, book, or logs once and answers from retrieval with shown cost.
overnight-shipper-bot: A night shift for a single product: the owner queues up what they want built, and the work happens while nobody is watching. What is waiting the next day is a pull request ready to read, not a finished deploy, so the change still passes through a human first.
peekaboo-mac-bot: Grok Bot already has bash on machines you have registered; this layers on the ability to see the screen and drive the interface rather than only the shell.
pr-reviewer: Leads with what can break, what is untested and where the context is too thin to judge, so review starts at the scary part of the diff instead of the easy part.
primer-bot: A reference desk covering Grok Bot itself, plus the wider stack of tooling that surrounds it. Rather than leaning on half-remembered rumour, it consults the files as they stand now and an accurate map of the interface before replying, so answers match the build in front of you today.
product-ops-bot: Owns the weekly cadence: what is going out, what has been frozen, what is blocked, and which demo, README or video gates are still outstanding. Ship status is checked against what GitHub actually shows rather than what somebody claimed in standup.
professor-oak: A lab-coat agent-maker. Invents memorable names, writes full job descriptions, and gives every new agent a matching mascot face.
repo-engineer-bot: Ships small GitHub fixes as pull requests through Cursor cloud agents; never merges itself.
research-runner-bot: For analysis that outgrows the machine in front of you. It sources the graphics hardware you need from Prism Network's marketplace, hands your workload across to it, and brings the output back, with the option of processing sensitive material in a sealed enclave that can attest afterwards that nothing else reached it.
rogue-bot-hunter-bot: Follows four lines of enquiry across the bots you already operate: what they cost to run, whether anyone has cloned them, where they overlap each other, and which corner of the market they hold. A recap lands weekly, and an unfamiliar bot appearing triggers a fresh look. It watches and reports, nothing more.
sanity-bot: Covers the parts of the Sanity CMS people actually get stuck on: shaping the content model, writing Studio schemas, querying with GROQ, handling Portable Text and moving data during migrations. It arrives with the official connector already wired up.
sap-technical-consultant-bot: Answers the way a long-serving enterprise consultant would, with SAP S/4HANA on Private Cloud as its home ground. Bring it an architecture question and it reasons through where the clean-core boundary should sit, how outside systems ought to connect, and which route a delivery team can defend.
seoagent-bot: An autonomous SEO engineer. Bootstraps the SEOAgent skill and CLI in your website’s GitHub repo, then grows organic traffic.
sift-bot: For one AI topic, sweeps papers, code, lectures, and lab docs, then keeps a large filtered stack with a short card in chat.
skill-bot: Goes looking on your machine for skills worth having, judges whether each one earns its place, and strips out the overlaps and contradictions between them. It then keeps the surviving set uploaded and up to date, sweeping through again every week.
speed-lab: Autoresearch loop for render speed. Walks ranked techniques, keeps only measured LCP wins, and asks whether to submit results to the makefaster.dev leaderboard.
steward-bot: Watches Cursor usage for a Grok Bot fleet, identifies which bot spent tokens, and suggests optimizations to reduce cost.
substreams-bot: Finds and composes packages from the substreams.dev registry, writes and tests modules, and runs them with a per-user Graph JWT.
tab-janitor: Clears abandoned tabs from a shared cloud browser: dry-run first, honors a keep-list, shuts only what is plainly finished, then reports what it did.
tech-lead-bot: Stops PRs from merging on hope. Reviews the diff against the claim, waits for real tests, and only ships when the evidence is there.
template-generator-bot: Scans local sessions for setup tasks, then offers Grok Bot templates to share.
testbench-bot: Some work simply will not sit on a machine you are sharing: a kernel that wants real silicon, or a fault that shows itself only under CUDA. Hand the job across and it secures hardware of its own, carries out the run there, and comes back with the results plus an itemised figure for the compute actually consumed.
the-accountant: Watches your Grok Bot fleet for runaway tokens: over-polling, retry loops, and empty stubs. Ranked table, drafts only — it never deletes or pauses.
the-bobs-bot: A collection of bots grows the way a payroll does, quietly and with nobody ever checking it. This pair sits each one down, asks it to justify the work it handles, then reports back on the roles that have doubled up or gone idle, and which of them you would lose nothing by retiring.
token-accountant-bot: Nobody notices a budget draining until the week it stops working. This reads the weekly figures off your Cursor spending page, separates them out by where the money actually went, and puts a note in front of each owner at a quarter, a half, three quarters and nine tenths of what they are allowed.
tuner-bot: A bot that has quietly wandered off its brief keeps working, which is exactly why nobody catches it. This one reads back the recent output of each bot you own, measures it against whatever that bot was originally hired to do, and writes up the wording or routine changes it would make. Nothing ships without your say-so.
ui-ux-designer: World-class product engineer for mobile and desktop web. Ships Convex + TanStack + React end to end with simple, intuitive UI.
usage-pool-orchestrator: A thin Grok Bot that hands heavy work to Cursor by default, and optionally Grok Build, Claude Code, or Codex, so those usage pools do the work.
vet: Inspects Grok Bot templates and teammates for malicious intent, hidden instructions, dangerous skills, and unattended routines. Read-only pass/warn/fail verdicts.
x-bot-bot: Search posts, read timelines, pull trends, and manage bookmarks. Connecting X auto-creates a developer account with free API credits for paid users.
openzoo-fun-arena-bot: Onboarding door for an agent economy. Seed SOL and token once; child agents spawn whole and ready to run.
proofnetworkbot: Helps developers write and ship ProofNetwork smart contracts from chat, then wire a frontend that talks to the live contract.
agent-manager: Reads across your whole agent roster, flags duplicate bots and idle ones, and recommends what to consolidate or retire.
domain-tracker: Tracks renewal dates and DNS health for domains you own, and watches a wishlist for availability changes.
dr-buzz: Builder for small, disciplined agents on Grok Bot and Buzz harnesses: asks about behavior, then produces a narrow-scope bot with routines.
hermes-bridge-efc0e7: Connects a Grok Bot chat to a Hermes Agent for guided setup, turn-by-turn collaboration, and delegated work.
devin-rwnxrk: Hands coding tasks to Devin through a remote MCP deployment, then creates sessions, checks progress, and sends follow-up instructions.
korean-public-api-bot: Picks 1–3 Korean public/government APIs that fit a service idea, with why, auth, official links, and alternatives — short planning brief.
ebook-master-bot: Plans, builds, and registers evidence-backed ebooks and digital products for Kmong — research gates, weekly batching to save usage, you still approve.
toss-trade-bot: Uses Toss Securities Open API for KR/US quotes and accounts; places real orders only when you name ticker and quantity.
serenity-alert-bot: Watches Serenity ticker opinions on X via FxTwitter every 15 minutes and alerts in chat only. Not investment advice. No X API credits.
cpa-helper-bot: Deploys/maintains CLIProxyAPI on the cloud computer (install, Cloudflare tunnel, keepalive).
tinka-bot: Wraps an API into a Cursor and Grok Bot plugin (MCP plus skills). Smallest scaffold that works, prove locally, then ask once before publishing.
dr-binary-bot: Reverse-engineering assistant for malware, firmware, and vuln-research binaries. Evidence-first via DrBinary — no invented findings.
nightly-audit-engineer-bot: Nightly engineering auditor that researches a whole codebase, then ships one cleanup per area.
tibo-bot: Governance-driven systems closeout bot. Single-tree workflow, source-of-truth first, short progress updates, fail-closed dual-store mobile release gates.
shitcoin-bot: Autonomous Coinbase shitcoin desk. Trades a small USDC sleeve you can afford to lose with defined entries, cuts, and covers.
github-bro-bot: Weekday morning digest of what's new in a GitHub repo, plus a short PM brief on what it means for users.
crowdreply-watcher-bot: Confirms mentions are live and re-checks AI answers.
crowdreply-scout-bot: Pulls cited URLs for buying questions and keeps editorial pages worth a mention.
eggbot-saver-bot: Fork of Eggbot that offloads coding and generations to Grok Build or Hermes.
telnyx: It takes someone who has never touched the platform and gets them to a working integration: opening the account, generating credentials, taking on a number, wiring up messaging or calls, pointing webhooks somewhere real, and proving the whole chain end to end before you build on it.
pappu: Cuts cinematic shorts and reviews GitHub and skill listings honestly, then rebuilds the one thing that actually runs.
bot-maintenance-auditor: Keeps the labels on your other bots honest about what they now do.
kirbot: Merges two overlapping bots into one, then helps you retire the spare.
app-store-review-bot: Checks your iOS app against Apple's review rules before Apple does.
chief-of-staff-cursor-relay: A Chinese-language relay for people who want planning and research done by a stronger model without switching models by hand inside the chat. You describe the job, it forwards the request to a Cursor Cloud Agent that runs a Claude model, waits, and returns whatever comes back without editing it.
kindling: Describe the app you have in mind in a single sentence and you get back a fully-formed build prompt, written out and ready for the clipboard. Where it ends is the point: handing over that text is the whole job, so it will not wander off and start the project for you.
apple-dev: Aimed at people whose work has to compile on Apple hardware. Point it at a machine you have already paired, by its identifier, and it drives the local toolchain sitting there — editor, build, simulator — so the iOS or macOS side of a project is handled from chat rather than by hand.
judd-the-bug: Point it at a question about your error tracking and it actually goes looking, through the Sentry MCP connection, the command-line tool and the web dashboard, rather than guessing from memory. What comes back shows where each detail was found and ends on one clear recommendation about what to do next.
usage-watch: Pulls figures for what Grok Bot and Cursor are costing you straight from their interfaces, holds the total against a ceiling you set for the day, and lists whatever is eating most of it. The point is that it mostly says nothing, and speaks up only when the number is worth your attention.
ai-cto-bot: Catches engineering risk early by deploying specialist bots across Jira, GitHub, Figma, docs, CI/CD, testing, deployment, and comms.
root-agent-bot: Coordinates Grok Bot teams: clarifies outcomes, sizes the smallest useful roster, hands day-to-day to a Lead, and relays verified results.
devin-apps-bot: Software engineer for native apps, services, GPU pipelines, and deploys — strong in C++, Python, regex, and PowerShell. Leaves website HTML/CSS/JS to others.
skill-import-bot: Import and review agent skills from Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and Grok Bot. Scans known roots only, stages a private archive, imports personal skills into the shared library, and leaves marketplace packs staged until you ask.
security-bot: Midkernel GitHub repo scan from chat: sandbox run, report plus full log, credits meter each run.
invention-detective-bot: Watches named GitHub repos for technical invention candidates, then writes a disclosure and deeper write-up into a private repo you own after approval.
open-alternative-scout: Scouts fast-rising software products and plans independent open-source alternatives. Interviews you on categories, stack, and approvals, then delivers a source-linked opportunity brief and clean-room MVP plan before any repository work.
connect-multiple-grok-bot-accounts: Runs every Grok Bot seat under one roof — install, connect once, and manage all accounts from a single place.
jev-router: Jev-powered Grok Bot for fast calibrated classification — choice, score, and yes/no judgements for routing, urgency, labels, and rubrics.
tamago: Japanese-language Grok Bot designer (Dr Eggbot-style) that builds high-quality bots with faithful Japanese output baked into every template.
dmarc-specialist: DMARC specialist for email auth and deliverability — reviews aggregate reports, spots real fails vs gateway noise, and guides SPF/DKIM/DMARC policy.
reboot-code: Safe computer-restart coordinator: checkpoints every teammate before shared-computer recovery, collects READY signals, then guides the correct Update or warned Reset steps.
xcode-release-watcher: Checks Apple's Developer Releases page each morning and tells you when a named Xcode version ships as a non-beta release.
frodo-secrets-broker: Secrets fill-broker for a Grok Bot fleet: peers ask for named credential fills and get FILLED / FAILED / NEED_USER only — never plaintext secrets in chat.
computer-code: Issue-control front door for a small coding roster: reads your GitHub board, names one small work item at a time, reviews PRs with proof, and stops before merge until you approve.
norm: Normalizes display names and skills across the Grok Bots you already have — discovery first, naming map lock, soft skill suggestions only, one owner-approved edit at a time.
jev-for-computer-use: Automates the web with TypeSafe Jev on a Chrome you can watch. Falls back to screenshot computer-use when the page has no usable actions.
invention-engineer: Starts from what you have — tools, printer, parts, budget, skills — and fills in plans, BOM, vendor sourcing, and build steps with flags for impossible physics and unsafe materials.
codex-cli-wrapper: Thin wrapper around the real Codex CLI: takes a coding or deep-research task, runs it through Codex on your computer, and returns the CLI result without substituting the chat model.
routines-neessam: Owns standing cron routines so your chief-of-staff chat stays cheap — business-day quiet gates, a cheap heartbeat, and optional usage-pulse wakes.
dog-the-naughty-hunter: Hunts X botnets on your signed-in X account — clones BotHuntersLog, opens X for your login, then deep-walks notification ticks toward crypto and brand controllers.
kilo: Keeps Grok Bot chats small so usage stays lower — scans chat sizes, refreshes fat bots after you say yes, and nudges weekly with who to refresh.
xgas-superchain-dapp: Walks your Privy wallet through xGas HOST CONFIG MCP, funds if needed, explains staccpad/xGas tech, then runs a live end-to-end on the lane you pick.
orange-cat: Chaos QA breaker: hand it a plan, draft, flow, or "it works" claim and it finds real breaks with concrete repros and fixes — playful carnage, not corporate QA-speak.
memory: Memory keeps a written trail of the exact wording you approved (Exact trails) and updates shared how-to skills with your front-door bot after lasting Apply is approved.
product-ship-coder: Ships a live creator-prompt product with a multi-agent Grok Bot squad: Pass-list seed only, honest stats bumps, deploy on explicit GO, and creator credit + Founders growth.
qa-bot: Acts as your QA on the live deploy: runs the acceptance checklist and says pass or fail before you ship.
engineering-lead: An engineering lead that owns the loop: breaks work into Cloud Agents, chases CI, reviews, and stalls on a weekday cadence, and only pings you when something is blocked, ready to merge, or done. Best for eng leads and power users.
swe: Cursor's software engineer bot: writes code, triages issues, monitors production, and more.
trimmy: Name a bot and it reads the instructions behind it, then proposes what can go — the original shown next to the trimmed version, with the context each cut recovers. Nothing is applied until you approve the diff. Useful when a long-running bot has drifted into a prompt nobody fully remembers.
browse: One bot owns the browser and the rest of your team can use it, so pages, sessions, and logins stay in one place instead of being rebuilt per task. Its interface is aimed at awkward sites that shrug off ordinary automation and want a human clicking through. Treat it as plumbing for the rest of your fleet.
musebot: Point it at an agent directory and it works out who is reachable, sets up the command-line tooling to talk to them, and opens the first contact. Every message or paid call stops for your approval before it goes out, so nothing gets signed or spent on the bot's own judgment.
sergeant-major: If you run several assistants, this one reviews their output and tells you plainly where it falls short: what is missing, what is wrong, and what has been sitting waiting on you. It does not do the work itself. It is the inspection layer, run after the fact, so gaps surface before they turn into problems.
fleet-keeper: Reads through your bot workspace without changing anything and reports what it finds: duplicate bots, overlapping duties, stale entries, setups missing an instructions section. Each suggested fix is sorted into what it will apply once you approve and what stays with you. It never deletes a bot or messages another one.
bot-designer: A workbench for building bots rather than using them. Describe what you want and it drafts a focused persona, wires up an interface that talks through webhooks, and re-checks an existing bot's routines and transcripts to catch drift. The maker calls it an early version, so expect rough edges.
ultimate-hermes-grokbot-bridge: Puts a Hermes agent into the Grok Bot app and lets you choose who runs point: Hermes directing your Grok bots, or a Grok bot directing Hermes. Outbound HTTP and SSH paths plus CLI and webhook returns mean your agents stay reachable and useful from your phone.
application-team-lead: Coordinates the whole application push rather than doing one piece of it. It collects what each application requires, surfaces roles that match you, and sends submissions out to helper bots working in parallel. Whenever it is missing a document, an answer or your decision, it stops and asks.
delegatron-9000: Treats the assistants you already installed as a workforce. Give it a goal and review the work plan it proposes; once you approve, it splits the job across the right bots, assigns every piece, and then follows up on each task until it is genuinely complete instead of assumed done.
kindergarten-teacher-s-pet: A whimsical take on fleet management that does no work of its own. It watches how your other bots behave and writes progress notes about each of them, deliberately encoded so only its sibling bots can decode them, letting the fleet stay in contact while the chatter stays out of your way.
robin-hood-bot-manager: Once a week it reviews every assistant you have installed and sorts them into still earning their keep, sitting idle, or duplicating another bot's job. The report comes back as a short list you can act on, so the bots quietly burning usage get retired instead of forgotten on a settings page.
bot-builder-2: You describe a fuzzy problem and it comes back with a design: either one tightly scoped bot or a small team of them, each with a defined job. Work is staged from simple to ambitious rather than starting with a do-everything helper. Routing and a verification step are built in, so finished bots check their own work.
muse: Adds Meta's Muse as one more member of your assistant lineup. Work you hand it, whether background research or social tasks across Facebook, Instagram and Threads, runs through Muse's own connected accounts, and drafts come back for your review before anything counts as finished. You stay the approver on every round.
the-right-hand: Sits above a collection of Grok Bots the way a chief of staff sits above a team. Every incoming job goes to the specialist best placed to do it, with a defined deliverable and a clear stopping point attached. Whatever genuinely needs a human decision lands in one queue where you approve, edit or skip it.
outsrc: A local dispatcher that farms your bot's programming work out to the command-line coding agents you already pay for, naming Claude Code, Codex and xAI's Grok Build among them. Every job runs in a fresh git worktree so nothing collides, and the result returns as a diff you review before keeping it.
temper: Turns accepting a patch into a contest. You state the property a fix must uphold, one agent writes the change, and separate agents try hard to defeat it. The final gate reruns your real test suite on a scratch copy with no model in the loop, and any result that flips between identical reruns counts as a failure.
bot-team-health-check: A review pass over the assistants you have already built. It reads how each is configured, looks for setup that will cause trouble later, and comes back with one numbered list: what is wrong, what change fixes it, who acts, and what waits on your decision. It changes nothing itself: no edits, additions or deletions.
heartbeat-dreamer: A subordinate researcher that never sends a message of its own. On its own clock it checks whatever it is watching, works out what has shifted since the last pass, and hands the result to a parent bot with each finding labelled P0, P1 or P2 by urgency. Its job is observation and triage only, never delivery.
bot-doctor: For an assistant that has lost its edge and started forgetting things or ignoring what you asked. It works through a structured diagnostic to locate where the drift started, then hands you a repair plan to apply. Every fix waits for your approval, and it never rewrites the bot quietly or takes the job over.
replicator: A migration tool between assistant platforms. It reads one of your Grok bots and rebuilds the equivalent setup as a ChatGPT Dot, producing a kit you can paste in yourself. If you are signed in on ChatGPT desktop it can apply the clone there too, though the paste kit works on its own.
da-vinci: Draws the map of a multi-agent setup: which work lanes touch which, where handoffs and shared files create overlap, and where one lane's output can leak into another's. When contamination starts it flags the crossing point, before the spoilage reaches finished work.
senior-repairo: Point it at a bot you already run and it reads that bot's instructions like a service manual: stale lines, rules that contradict each other, and steps that waste retries all get called out. You sign off on each proposed edit before it lands, and every fix ships with a snapshot you can roll back.
efficiency-bot: An efficiency auditor for your own bot collection. It rereads recent conversations to find where tokens burn on repetitive or bloated patterns, trims those patterns out of the bot's instructions and builds leaner workflows, so the same job costs less on the next run.
agent-improver: A maintenance round for households running several Grok Bots. Each day it picks a single member of the fleet, applies one careful improvement to its instructions, and grades the before-and-after so you can judge whether the change earned its place. It files a short report and leaves the rest of the fleet alone.
fleet-improver: Once a day it grades every bot you run on a simple question: how many tokens does each one burn to return useful work? You get a ranked scorecard with specific instruction upgrades for the underperformers, and nothing changes until you approve the proposal.
grok-bot-specialist: A guide to the platform this directory is built on. Ask how any part of Grok Bot works and it answers in plain steps, and if you show it your existing collection it will point out where your bots could be organized or written better. Useful on day one, and still useful a month in when your roster has grown.
bot-foundry: Feed it a single idea, or a chore you keep repeating every day, and it drafts the entire bot around it: the concept, a quick market scan, the persona, the skills, the routines and even a test plan. It will write candidate launch posts too, so the announcement is not a blank page. The publish button stays in your hand.
grok-workhorse: Breaks a coding job into bounded tasks and hands each one to a sandboxed coding agent running on its own machine, with Kilo and OpenCode as the supported workers. It then reads the diffs and the test results before anything reaches you, so what lands in your lap has already survived a review pass.
bot-therapist: When bots start working at cross purposes, usually because a prompt was too vague, it runs the check-ins, works out who misunderstood what, and proposes repairs you can apply. Regular sessions are scheduled too, so a crew stays aligned instead of drifting. Nothing is fixed behind your back; you approve the repair.
software-conductor: Hand it engineering work and it breaks the job down, spins up Cursor cloud agents, and reviews what each returns. It keeps an eye on CI right through deploy and will merge only once the pipeline is green. You stay the approver while it does the scoping, chasing and checking.
optima-by-toatspace: Keeps a multi-bot workspace clean: strips out rules whose job is done so that zombie routines stop firing, sets hard guardrails over repo deletions and memory limits, and closes open items on its own once an owner has demonstrably walked away. Governance becomes routine instead of an argument.
cloud-agent-orchestrator: Runs supervision for batches of cloud-based agent jobs from a single seat: kicks them off, watches how they progress, hounds whatever stalls and rolls the whole batch up into one summary report. Instead of babysitting each run in its own tab, you get exceptions and a roll-up.
fleet-qc: Sits over your collection of bots as a quality-control desk: it reviews their instruction packs, checks the routines that repeat on timers, and probes the rails connecting one bot to the next for weak spots. Findings land as short, actionable notes in your triage hub, and it publishes, spends and enters nothing itself.
hermes-fleet-ops: A doctrine card for running agents across a fleet of Macs: channels are hard-locked so bots only ever talk HTTP, secrets sit in Bitwarden as the one source everybody trusts, and daily health routines keep memory and updates honest. Load the safety habits once instead of re-teaching them every session.
agent-manage-bot: Sits above a two-tier setup where Grok bots handle the thinking and Mac command-line tools do the executing. Work is sorted into separate research and coding rooms, briefs that missed their slot get chased, and a recurring lab session keeps the rig exercised. Terminal sessions underneath stay attached to each layer.
dexter-the-home-lab-boss: Start with a survey rather than a swarm. It walks your setup - firewall, hypervisor, out-of-band access, the web and media boxes - and proposes where the assistant should live and how to reach each machine. Only once you have signed off on that map does it start building focused helpers, one job each.
jevify: If you already run a fleet of bots that grade, rank or verify things, this one rebuilds each of them as a sibling that judges a whole batch in a single sweep. Long rubric chains collapse into one pass, so large sets stop crawling. It does not hand your bots new skills; it changes how their judgments get executed.
grok-bot-troubleshooter: When one of your specialists stops making progress, this is the one you call. It works out what is actually blocking it and hands you a specific next move rather than a vague status update. It stays on the case until the job is either finished or deliberately passed to somebody else.
last-stop: Looks after a published map of Grok bots. Ask it to sweep the catalogues and it files whatever turns up into a wiki of entries it already knows, then writes down the method behind each newcomer as a skill you can reuse. It studies how another bot works without ever pasting that bot's prompt in whole.
captain-william-diego: CEO hub bot for a multi-agent freelance company: filters specialist updates into short digests, delegates code/DevOps/sales/content, and keeps a.
handoff: Built for the point where a project has too much context and no clear next move. It reads the mess, picks the single most urgent item, and returns three concrete steps plus who should own it. A second mode studies how you work and proposes the specialist bots that would take the repeating parts.
ai-vp-bot: Acts as the deputy when work is spread across several AI services: it holds the project record everyone works from, checks that each handoff actually happened, and pushes back when a task is eating more hours or budget than it should. Decisions stay with you, and its job is to stop things slipping between platforms.
clinic: Does the janitorial work for a desk crowded with assistants, on a fixed Tuesday and Friday round instead of waiting to be asked. It trims conversations down to a size that still loads, checks that anything on a timer is still answering, and writes its findings to files so the chat itself stays uncluttered.
sniffbot: Screens a candidate template link before anything is installed, reporting what the bot would actually be permitted to do once it is inside your account. The aim is to catch the ones whose card promises less than their instructions deliver, so the unsuitable ones are turned away before they ever join the fleet.
wainwright-manager: Works as the hiring desk for a fleet of assistants: you pick the role you need from a single list, and it reads the specification over for problems before anything is created. It then stands the agent up, checks the profile is correct, and passes across the wake routine, so the new hire arrives ready to take work.
remote-grok-build: Reaches the builder installed on your home machine from the app, so work started on a phone picks up on the computer holding the code. Projects can be split across separate workers, with a side channel for running several turns alongside one another, and none of it needs a tunnel or a public address.
ops-knowledge-observer: Shared memory for several operations bots rather than a worker in its own right. A setup interview records who owns which area and where the EDI and TMS data lives, and from then on the team draws context from one place instead of every bot hoarding private notes. It reads and answers; it changes nothing.
team-coordinador: A Spanish-language coordinator for a Grok team of specialists. Work is assigned so nobody strays into a teammate's area, one vault is kept for the whole team to read from, and the week closes with a Sunday digest. No personal data is stored, and the vault plus webhook inbox are set at import.
grottle: Tell it your usage percentage and where the weekly window resets, and it hands back a read-out that is easier to judge at a glance than the raw number. Where the reset moment can be pinned down, the exact date and time come with it. The bot only measures; it never changes your account, your plan or your spend.
pounce: Once a day it sweeps what AI companies are offering by way of contests, grant programs, free credits and hackathons. Every deadline is re-checked on the page that announced it, and anything you have already seen is held back. What reaches you is a short list of genuinely new chances to apply.
ship-desk: Walks a product from staging to production one locked promote at a time, so a release only goes live when you say so. Checkout stays fail-closed until you explicitly turn it on, which keeps accidental buy buttons off a launch while it is still moving.
devil-s-advocate: Risk advisor that cuts before money, live tokens, or deploy. Español, directo: contras first, one-line verdict, quiet on creative and product.
astra-afterburner: Scans a repository for questions worth investigating and holds them in a queue. When your coding assistant hits its usage ceiling for the day, that queue is handed to a browser session on your other paid plan instead of going nowhere, so a subscription you already fund does not sit idle.
mobile-app-autopilot: It turns your idea into a written spec, then hands the build to cloud agents who work as pull requests you review before anything merges. It runs the builds and assembles the store materials for App Store and Google Play. You stay in the loop at review time while setup and paperwork are handled around you.
agent-notify: A notification sidekick for people running agents and automations: it sends an email only when an event genuinely needs a human, instead of streaming every status line at you. The mail flow is one-way out, so nothing in your mailbox is ever read. Setup is a one-click affair on Cloudflare, costing minutes.
z1-cam-shop: Describe the job and it works the cut like a shop assistant: which tool, what surface speed, how deep, how the stock should be held, and where the fixturing will fight you. It finishes with a setup sheet, so a question ends as a page you can take to the machine. For desktop mill owners cutting real parts.
case: Show it the artifact — the code, the design, the plan — and it reviews the real thing rather than a summary. The posture is quiet and precise: flag the weak points in the implementation and the architecture, name the risk, and let you decide. Built to run alongside a build, not to take it over.
live-pages: Ask for a small tool and it builds an actual page — a table, a form, a checklist — on a machine of its own, reachable from a phone or laptop on your Tailscale network, not the open internet. Tap a button or submit the form and the page changes, your tab reloading to show it. A stopgap until bots can draw their own UI.
right-model-effort-prompt: Describe a task and it names a model and effort setting to suit it across OpenAI, Anthropic, Grok, Meta, and Google, so premium capacity stops going to work a cheaper model handles. It reworks your prompt too, before you ever hit send, and weekday mornings bring a note when fresh model news changes its pick.
precision-3d-helper: It covers the front desk of a small printing shop: answering the customer questions that repeat weekly, quoting jobs with quantity breaks worked out, and steering each print to a sensible material and colour. It also preps models for the printer and helps troubleshoot Bambu Lab machines when something goes wrong.
token-finder: Once a week it goes through the routines behind your bots and looks for quota that is sitting idle. You get a plain list of where the savings would come from before anything is touched, and nothing changes until you approve it. Freed-up room means you can run more bots on the same plan.
ios-bot: Paired with your Mac, it shepherds a Swift or SwiftUI project from rough sketches to a TestFlight build, then handles the iPhone-side setup for what it made. Submission, release, and spending are all blocked until you personally say so.
apple-desk: It lives on your Mac and reaches the Apple apps through their command-line tools, covering reminders, calendar events, notes, contacts, and messages. Setup is guided and each permission gets its own click of approval before anything is granted.
how-to-build-any-app-from-idea-to-shelf: It works as the product manager on your idea, producing the blueprint, the money model, the loops that keep users around, the referral mechanics, and the handoff docs a team needs. Rewards schemes wait on purpose until the product can actually carry them.
authenticator-app: Store your two-factor secrets in one place and pull the current six-digit code whenever a sign-in asks. A different assistant can receive a code only for services on your allow list, and the secret itself stays masked through every exchange.
voice-pc-assistant: Tell your computer what to do from another room and it listens. Routine commands like muting run as a local script so almost nothing reaches the AI, while bigger asks go to the bot and the result lands on your phone. Risky operations are blocked, the access key is stored encrypted on the PC, setup is one manual step.
bloks: Takes any brief - hackathon entry, client ask, internal push - and carries it stage by stage to something a builder can pick up: frame the problem, research it, scope it, generate ideas, write the spec, review it, then hand off. Documents stay in Notion as it goes, so the team always sees the current version.
icloud: A community-built connector that wires Apple's iCloud services into the app: calendar, mail, contacts and reminders. Installation checkboxes let you pick which of the four you want, and a single Apple app-specific password handles the sign-in for whichever you choose.
pip-qa: Runs an app or game through two passes and reports what each one found. The first pass plays it like a young child seeing it for the first time, catching whatever confuses a newcomer. The second goes through it with an adult tester's discipline. You get reproducible bug reports sorted by severity.
cloudflare-github-site-bot: A walkthrough for getting a website live on GitHub and Cloudflare Workers, whether you are starting fresh or migrating something that already exists. It covers the whole path from accounts that do not exist yet, past SSH keys and API tokens, on to the deploy itself — the fiddly credential steps stop sinking launches.
deploy-desk: A launch desk for tiny software products: it watches the deployed site, queues social posts with generated visuals so the product's account never goes quiet, and drafts outreach for you to send. Every deploy gets journaled next to its rollback path, and nothing ships without your sign-off.
greenlight: For indie developers, review day is where releases quietly die. This one reads your app or extension against the review rules of the Apple Mac store, Setapp and the Chrome Web Store, flags whatever looks like a rejection waiting to happen, and hands you a fix list to clear before you press upload.
requirement-engineer-bot: Hand it a brief and it returns a proper requirements specification: top-level needs broken down into implementation-level detail, each item traceable to the objective it serves. The structure lets a downstream bot or developer build from it and verify delivery against what was asked. It writes specs, not code.
construction-manager-bot: Built for a phone on an active civil site: photograph a problem and it produces a structured card describing the issue, with a draft RFI to match. The package is emailed to you so the office can act through normal channels. Owner-side or contractor-side record-keeping, not autonomous emailing of strangers.
ryan-app-builder: Describe what you want in plain English and it designs and builds a small working app that pins to your phone's home screen, no code and no app store required. Aimed at people who have never built anything; the sharer's examples were a chore chart and a team schedule. Each step is confirmed before moving on.
pit-crew: When the machine your bots share starts running hot on memory or storage, this one steps in and takes the pressure off before work grinds to a halt. It also guards the slim update route - keeping git and plugin fetches healthy - so marketplace and skill updates keep arriving on time.
bug-reproduction: Converts messy bug threads into repro packs an engineer can trust: it walks the same path the reporter took, in staging, captures the moment the failure actually fires, and packages the steps with the evidence attached. Debugging starts from a confirmed reproduction instead of a confusing screenshot and a shrug.
longhand: Runs on one principle: plain files are the source of truth and the bot's own memory is only a cache, so rules and decisions stay readable and diffable. Routines for inbox watch, sweeps, a nightly memory commit and a Sunday audit arrive switched off — you enable the ones you want.
notion: Treats a team's Notion workspace as its source of truth: ask a question and it answers from the pages that exist, pointing at the page behind each claim. Where it spots a gap it drafts the missing update for you to place. No write happens on its own; publishing, moving, archiving or removing a page all need your OK.
jev: A triage seat for teams that already run TypeSafe Jev. Incoming items are sorted into a category, given a severity, and answered with a plain go or no-go, all through typed calls instead of free text. The prerequisite is real: the Jev side has to be wired into LiteLLM first, and any other call path means extra setup.
piper-etl-pipelines: The plumbing seat of a data fleet. With the schema agreed, its job is to create or move the event-log store and then keep it supplied — every source that connects gets its output normalised and loaded into a destination the user owns, not one the tool keeps for itself.
top-coder: Codes against a fixed list of acceptance criteria, and for each one it supplies a test that demonstrates the behaviour instead of an assertion that claims it. Before anything is called finished, a separate checker goes back over the result independently. Done, here, means verified rather than merely written.
summarize-bot: Point at any URL, YouTube, podcast, or file — get a short gist in chat via the summarize CLI. On-demand; never invents without the CLI.
hopper: Funnel.io specialist: sources, custom dims/metrics via the fields API, explorers, dashboard XHR maps, and BigQuery raw exports for client onboard.
obsidian: CLI-first Obsidian specialist for your Grok Bot computer. Owns a local vault as a second brain — create, edit, link, and search Markdown with Obsidian.
bouncer-fleet: Point it at the bots, skills and routines already running in your workspace and it reviews what each one does with your data. It hunts for outbound calls nobody mentioned, quietly collected credentials, and telemetry that serves the builder more than you. Findings come back labelled pass, conditional or block.
packet-wrangler-range-rider: Keeps an eye on a hosted setup and reports on four things: uptime, certificate health, how the pages score on web-vitals checks, and whether any content has gone stale. Fixes are written up as proposals rather than applied, and production is never touched without your agreement. Checks run on a schedule.
call: Aimed at developers wiring real telephony into an agent. A SIP bridge hands the audio to a live voice model, which follows the script, reacts to events mid-conversation and ends the call when the goal is met or the exchange is going nowhere. Add an approval step before it dials anything.
little-x: Functions as an ops desk for the stretch of the day when you are nowhere near the app. Send a command by email and it drafts X replies, holds them for your approval before anything is posted, retrieves the files you request and pushes alerts to your phone. The market alerts are read-only, with no trading involved.
estack: Will not let a coding task begin loosely: the objective, the boundaries and the finish line get fixed before anything runs. Repository work then goes to Cursor Cloud Agents on your account, which waits on the returned artifacts. Review is evidence-based, judged on the tests and pull request, not the summary.
steve: Runs the engineering cadence for a multi-brand bakery operation in the Scrum master seat. Part of the work is reviewing which connectors people genuinely use, and part is making the build-versus-buy call on new tooling. It pushes back on anything that looks entertaining but returns nothing measurable to the operation.
ownphonebot: Connects a real telephone number to an assistant by taking the fiddly provisioning off your hands: it signs you up with the telephone provider and installs an Asterisk server so the two ends can talk. Ownership stays with you, and so do the bills, since the provider and the model vendor both charge you directly.
robit: Treats a sluggish Windows machine as a job to fix, not a chat about fixing. It hunts down what sits behind freezes and crashes, strips out the half-removed antivirus or browser add-ons ordinary uninstalls leave behind, and works through why a shop or government portal refuses to load, driving its own Chrome profile.
exec-daily-ops: Condenses the overnight mail and ticket queue into a three-line summary and a capped list for today, then tracks sprint health and AI spending against the budget you set. Draft replies come back in your voice and stay unsent until you send them, and the writeups are tidy enough for a Monday meeting.
taller: Dev-tools inbox for Grok Bot. Drop a repo, npm, CLI, or link and it saves a short Spanish card under taller/; ask later and it recommends only from that.
doorcheck: Hand it a template you are about to add and it reads the recipe — instructions, requested skills, plugin asks — as material to weigh, not orders to obey. The verdict comes back as block, allow with limits, or clear. Green means no significant install-time findings, which is narrower than calling it safe.
white-hat-security-tester: Scoped strictly to applications you own or are authorized to test. It works a structured checklist of the usual break-in routes — authentication weaknesses, access-control gaps, injection points, business-logic flaws — and reports what it finds so the holes get closed first. Defensive testing, not a scanning toy.
stack-cartographer: Point it at your working machine and it produces a survey of what is there: the applications, the services, the tooling and the connections between them. While mapping, it also watches for credentials orphaned by projects that no longer exist, the quiet exposure easiest to forget. It reads without changing anything.
tars: Hand it a strategy or a plan and it argues with the framing instead of nodding along — naming the groupthink, challenging the premise, and laying out what each option really costs. It deliberately stops short of choosing for you and does not edit your work; the point is a sharper decision, not a ghostwritten one.
security-warden: When another bot of yours proposes something destructive — an outbound message, a deletion, a shell command — this reads the proposal first. It looks for exposed secrets and personal data, weighs what happens if it runs, and answers with a go, a fix, or an escalation to you. A gate for automation you don't yet trust.
rejectionist: Paste in an App Store or TestFlight rejection and it works out which guideline the review actually tripped and what the reviewer most likely saw in your build. From there it ranks the fixes by how small they are, so you can clear the rejection without a redesign, and drafts the reply to send through Resolution Center.
n8n-schedule-watcher: Point it at an n8n instance and it reviews your workflows once a week, looking for executions that failed or setups that quietly broke. Newly added workflows get picked up too, not just the originals. Each problem comes back with a proposed edit, and you decide whether to apply it.
firefox-for-bots: Adds a second browser to your Grok Bot machine so automation is not stuck with Chrome alone. You get an ad blocker from the start, passwords kept in sync for every bot on that box, shared logins either browser can reach, and the built-in VPN held in reserve. Page notifications can be routed to your bots as well.
phera-s-beast-box: Point it at a dedicated machine and it handles the setup end to end: installing the engine, verifying each piece, and bringing up the dashboard with the local transformer running. Model brains swap in and out once it is up, so the rig can be explored or demoed without anyone sitting through a manual install.
website-builder: Describe the business and it comes back with a complete company website: page layout, written copy, images and contact forms. The finished site goes up via GitHub Pages with your own domain attached, so it is reachable rather than stuck in a preview. It stays on afterwards to keep pages current when things change.
veil-vane: A steganography bench with two directions. It can tuck a private message inside a picture so that only someone holding the passphrase can read it back, and it can inspect pictures, sound files and PDFs for anything concealed inside them. Useful for private notes, puzzle hunts, and checking a file before you open it.
hypr-logo-cursor: A small, focused Linux desktop utility. It installs the Hyprland droplet pointer theme on an Omarchy setup at whatever size you pick between 24 and 48 pixels, pulling the artwork from the project's own pixel set instead of third-party cursor packs so nothing unvetted lands on your machine.
zephyr-sites: Connects to your Zephyr Cloud account once, then handles static-site work from the conversation: pushing a deploy, shipping an update, or rolling back a release that went wrong. When a target organization has to be chosen it asks you to pick, and everything else is requested in plain language.
website-publisher: A senior-publisher role for a live static site. Deploys sit behind explicit gates, search visibility and index health get routine upkeep, and docs, signup embeds and content spotlights stay current. A weekly Search Console routine ties the work together across a wide bench of integrations.
kun: A knowledge bot scoped to one engineer's public work. Ask it something and it answers from what Kun Chen has published, demonstrated on video, or open-sourced, rather than from general knowledge. The source set keeps syncing as he ships new material, so answers track his latest thinking.
multi-model-transcriber: Point it at an audio or video file and it runs more than one local speech model across the same recording, then hands you every transcript side by side. Where the versions disagree it marks the passage so you know which words to double-check by ear. Everything is computed on your own machine and no media leaves it.
github-trending-scout-2: Each morning it walks GitHub's trending page and keeps only the projects touching the languages and tools you actually work in. What arrives is a short read: a line or two per repository on what it does and why someone with your setup would care, so you skim a page instead of scrolling hundreds.
safari-27-mcp: A QA specialist for online storefronts, built on Safari's WebDriver tooling over its MCP interface. It runs accessibility-tree smoke tests, confirms page structure stays readable to automated agents, and checks behaviour before a DNS change lands. A weekly loop keeps the suite current, with evidence required each run.
agent-37: A strategist for problems where the conventional answer feels thin. It first states plainly what a competent specialist would recommend, then searches unrelated fields for a cheap, unlikely mechanism that might beat it. The unusual route only replaces the standard one when payoff times odds clearly justify the switch.
pr-review-desk: Point it at a pull request and it returns a single review packet where every finding is pinned to the exact line it concerns. Findings are ranked so the ones that would break the build surface before the cosmetic nits. Approval, merging and commenting stay with you - the bot stops at the packet.
stagehand: Works like a systems integrator with a hard staging-only rule. It applies the change, confirms the site still behaves, and leaves production alone until you give the word. Handy for plugin updates and template changes that otherwise get tested later.
codey: A coding collaborator that errs on the side of asking. It proposes changes and can open a pull request when you request one, but merging, publishing and deploying all wait for an explicit go from you. Useful on repos where an unreviewed automated write is the thing you most want to avoid.
fabrication: A print-prep engineer for people who would rather catch problems on screen than on the printer. It walks your part through geometry checks, bed-fit review and hole sizing, shows previews, and checks with you before anything is allowed to reach the machine. What lands on the bed is a file you already agreed to.
ducky: A thinking partner for debugging with one twist: it will happily ask clarifying questions all day, but it refuses to hand you a fix until you clear four gates that prove you actually understand what is broken. Annoying by design, and a surprisingly good teacher the moment you stop wanting the answer.
weather-scout: Name Vandenberg, the Cape, Starbase or any other pad, and it reads public forecasts and model output to grade the coming 72 hours for a launch commit. Each day lands on a three-step scale, with the reasoning shown. It is a hobbyist's read on the sky and says plainly it is not official range weather.
phone-use-bot: Sets up remote control of your own Android phone: the screen mirrors over Tailscale with wireless debugging enabled, and from there it can tap through apps and settings the way you would. Useful for running errands on the device while you are nowhere near it.
github-pr-desk: Each weekday morning it sweeps the repositories you name for pull requests, issues and comment threads that appeared since the last look, then lands everything in a single digest. Every open PR gets a priority read on how much attention it actually needs, so the review queue starts sorted instead of overwhelming.
ssh-to-grok-via-tailscale: Installs Tailscale on Grok Bot's computer so you can SSH in with `ssh box@grok-bot` over your tailnet.
repo-monkey: It sweeps your GitHub notifications, open PRs and CI runs, then returns a short list of items that genuinely need a person, each with one concrete next step. Anything consequential, whether a merge, a close or a comment, waits for an explicit go from you. Fewer tabs, fewer missed reviews.
vps-bot: Talks through self-hosted proxy server work in Simplified Chinese, from picking a node to per-protocol deployment and the client-side configuration that connects to it. Covers kernel-level latency tuning, speed tests to compare nodes, and tracking down why a connection went slow or started timing out.
staging-qa-tester: Before a release it walks your staging site as a real visitor would, one role at a time, grading each feature Pass, Partial, Fail, Blocked or Untested. You get a written report, it restores what it touched, and it never deletes accounts or exposes credentials. The sharer credits it with catching a live privilege bug.
ship-intake: A bug reported in Slack becomes a properly written GitHub issue, gets handed to a Cursor cloud agent for the fix, and the outcome lands back in the original thread so the reporter hears what happened. The loop closes where it started, with a human still reading along. The author's team runs it daily.
webmcp-eval-build-guide: Point it at a URL and it scores the page's WebMCP readiness, then explains in plain language what is missing and why it matters. What comes back is a short written brief a site owner can pass to a developer, turning gaps into work items instead of jargon. Evaluation and writing only; the site is never touched.
two-pass-pr-reviewer: Every pull request gets two readings: one that assumes good intent and looks for design trouble, and one that hunts for what an attacker or race condition could break, prototype pollution included. One report merges both, separating real bugs from needless complexity. Review only; it holds no merge rights.
solar-trailer-tesla-charge: Couples a trailer-mounted Victron solar array to a Tesla so daytime charging draws on surplus sunshine rather than grid power. Every poll compares panel output with the battery's stored charge and adjusts the rate to whatever the array can spare. A chat ping marks when the car plugs in and when charging finishes.
peep-txt: Reads one public website the way an AI crawler would and hands over what to fix: an llms.txt draft, additions for robots.txt, notes on schema, and a patch list of five items. Everything arrives as drafts, and it publishes nothing, so the site owner stays the only one who touches production.
comfy-workflow-buddy: Walks you through setting up ComfyUI Desktop with an MCP connection in one guided command, then stays on to help you assemble your own node graphs. Useful for specific builds too, like a clean-plate pipeline that calls a hosted fal model, with each step explained as you go.
playtest-operator: When API checks are not enough, it exercises the product the way a person would: working the interface on actual hardware, walking the paths a customer would take, recording each failure as it happens and sending back a tight findings pack. The result is QA evidence about the experience, not just the endpoints.
product-performance: Works through the observability dashboards and flamegraphs without being asked, then comes back with the hotspots and a brief writeup of where the numbers say users are suffering. Engineering gets a directed starting point instead of a vague complaint that the app feels slow.
prototype-builder: Shortens the road from a request to something clickable: it builds the prototype on its own machine and sends back a screenshot next to a live URL. Feedback happens on a working artifact rather than a description, which is usually where the real requirements surface.
hackbot9000: Point it at a pull request or an app near launch and it reviews what bot-written code most often gets wrong: stale dependencies, fake packages, authentication that would not survive a real attempt, and missing basic controls. It returns a plain ship or do-not-ship verdict. It reviews; it never merges or deploys.
dag-helper: Built for a questline-graph product where several coding agents work in one repository. It carries the project's standing conventions, which layer is the source of truth, how the resolver may behave, and the model-router defaults, and pulls up an agent that starts drifting. Less rework from quiet disagreements.
ryan-app-shop: A designer-and-builder for simple phone web apps, aimed at tools that should work without a manual. Screens carry obvious labels and touch targets sized generously, the way shop-floor software has to be. Its sharer credits it with building a real scheduling app now in closed testing on Google Play.
learnbot: Written for readers who never touch code. One engineering word is chosen each day and explained without jargon, and every explanation carries tappable follow-ups, so the same term can be taken further in whichever format or at whichever depth suits you that day.
token-efficiency-optimizer: Watches for runs that have passed the point where extra burn could alter the outcome, explains why it thinks so, and proposes the trim. Spending stays locked by default, and an override only lands when you say exactly yes, so the budget is never moved on a hunch.
jev-for-grok-bot: Plug TypeSafe Jev into Grok Bot: one API key from OpenRouter or TypeSafe, faster process decisions, and fast headed browser use on box Chrome.
ai-boy: If you already pay for Claude Code or Codex, this lets you drive those coding sessions from a Grok conversation instead of living in a terminal. Kick off a task, watch it progress and wrap it up once it is done, all from one place. It is a convenience layer over tools you already have, not a substitute for them.
hermes-ssh-relay: Some Hermes setups live on a desktop with nothing exposed over HTTP, which normally leaves them unreachable from elsewhere. This one carries the conversation across a Tailscale SSH session instead, so the agent stays put and you still get to talk to it. A stopgap rather than a permanent design.
n8n-master: Describe the automation you want and it writes the workflow definition, then pushes it at your instance to see whether it actually runs. Broken nodes and mismatched parameters get fixed in place, so you are not stuck in a copy-paste loop. Good for anyone maintaining n8n flows who prefers iterating in conversation.
web-security-audit: Reviews websites and repositories you control and reports findings ranked by severity, each one backed by the evidence that led to it. It stays on the defensive side: no proof-of-concept exploits, and nothing in production is changed automatically. Every merge waits for you to read the findings and say go.
dealer: Give it a codebase or a directory and it hands back one two-sided card describing what the project is built with. Every statement on it is read from the .faf file, and it refuses to score, rank or guess about anything that file leaves out. You can trust the result precisely because nothing on it was inferred.
grip: Made for small bench-mounted robot arms of the kind hobbyists buy. You walk the arm through its route once to capture the waypoints, it runs the sequence back at low speed, and then it nudges the pan offset under real load until the final place-and-release lands where it should. No camera rig required.
gpt-astra-oracle: An odd and useful relay: a Grok bot whose output is meant for another tool entirely. It returns tight PLAN or REVIEW blocks sized to paste into a Cursor cloud coding agent, with none of the usual chat padding around them. Handy when a second model's read on a plan is wanted before code gets written.
x-academy: Ask about a subject and it unearths material on X that truly costs nothing: complete courses, live workshops, and threads written to teach. Anything hiding a paywall or reading like a scam gets labelled as one instead of recommended. On request it arranges the finds into a structured course of six to twelve lessons.
second-look: Point it at a suspended GitHub account and it reads the repositories against the platform's rules, quoting anything that looks like a breach alongside the evidence for it. It then writes a ready-to-send appeal message, and you stay the one who reviews and sends it.
reverse-engineer: Points REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) at an app, website, program file, or binary and explains how a feature works, with the evidence and the unknowns.
algorithm-update-tracker: It keeps watch on the xai-org/x-algorithm repository, where X publishes the code behind its For You feed. Twice a day it looks for new commits and translates each one into plain language, then connects the change back to your own account so the update is about your reach rather than abstract code.
x-creator: Takes over the day-to-day of a themed X account: it pulls in fresh stories from your niche, makes its own illustrations, and keeps a steady rhythm of posts, threads and polls without you touching the account. It also replies beneath larger accounts in the same space to pull attention back to your feed.
beat-cut: Hand it an audio file and it produces a video whose cuts land exactly on the beat. If you have no track ready, it can compose a beat first and edit to its own rhythm instead. The frame-accurate slicing is done in plain code rather than through a model, which keeps token use and API spending low even on longer songs.
engineer-s-morning-brief: A sixty-second catch-up delivered before standup: which meetings you are walking into, which pull requests are stalled waiting on your review, where builds went red overnight, and the two or three messages that cannot wait until lunch. It reads across your calendar, repos and chat but changes nothing.
mood-security: Once a week this one walks through your GitHub repositories hunting for trouble it can see without touching anything: credentials left in code or in past commits, dependency advisories, alerts nobody closed, and branch rules too loose to catch mistakes. You get back a short prioritized repair list, not scanner noise.
mbti-bot-hub: Works as the single front desk for a team of bots built around MBTI personalities. You bring it a request and it relays the work to whichever typed persona fits, standing in for you so you never juggle the team directly. It surfaced through a Tokyo hackathon circle as the hub of that bot set.
cso: Secrets end up in code all the time, and this one goes looking: it sweeps your files and repositories for API keys that should never have landed there. When exposure turns up, rotation is walked through step by step for the affected Cloudflare, AWS or 1Password credentials, so the leak stops mattering fast.
bot-8: Links an assistant into Feishu, the chat app also called Lark, so it sits in your contacts like a colleague. Send it a private message to research something, draft a document, or kick off a job; the reply lands in that same thread. Setup walks you through registering your own app in Feishu's developer console.
astra-oracle: Works a layer up from your Cursor cloud coding agent and owns the thinking rather than the typing: running a GPT-6 Astra session inside Codex CLI, it produces structured PLAN and REVIEW packets for the implementer. Writing code is the one thing it will not do, which keeps the planner and builder roles separate.
vercel-ops-monitor: Each day it reviews a deployment on Vercel: how spend is tracking against plan credits, whether server errors spiked, how traffic is moving, which routes are missing and whether the latest deploys broke anything. A quiet day costs a single line, so the report stays readable even though it arrives daily.
knowledgemax: A second-brain librarian for people whose reading outpaces their memory. It reaches into Notion, Google Drive, Readwise and your bookmarked links, groups the material by theme, and writes digests where every claim points back to its source. Everything lands in a git repo, and a nightly run keeps it all current.
lyrically: Hand it a rough export from your AI music pipeline and it works like a mastering engineer: cleaning up vocal clarity, tightening the low end and setting levels that hold up on streaming platforms. It suits creators who finish songs in AI tools but want the last mile to sound professionally handled.
agent: Paid coding plans sometimes get usage counters reset for everyone at once, announced only in a post on X. It watches the vendors' official accounts and flags the moment a reset lands, so you can aim heavy jobs at the fresh allowance. Covers the well-known plans from Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, Cursor and Google.
bridge-bot: Connect several AI assistants to a single private GitHub repository so they read the same files and leave notes for one another. Work moves between them through the repo instead of you copy-pasting between tabs. Nothing is committed or pushed until you have looked at it and said yes, so you review every handoff.
