From what it sees, it builds a concrete, ordered improvement plan - what to change and why each change should help. Nothing is executed until you have read the plan and given the word.
competitive-intelligence-analyst: Keeps a night-shift watch on competitors: it hunts for overnight rival launches while auditing your own pages for creative that has worn thin and messaging that has gone stale. The morning report covers what changed out there and what has quietly rotted on your side, before either becomes a surprise.
seo-aeo-auditor: Puts search visibility on a single dashboard spanning keywords, technical health, the prompts people feed AI answer engines and competitor movement, showing where you are gaining ground or losing it, and which site problems to fix first. It also covers what AI assistants say about you when nobody clicks at all.
scientific-realism: Hand it a film, a series or a short clip and you get a science mark from 0 to 10 with a short sourced writeup behind it. Once a story leaves Earth behind, the mark splits in two: one grade for how the science stands up against real physics, another for how faithfully it keeps to the rulebook the story wrote for itself.
winreddestroyer: Builds an evidence file out of repeated political fundraising texts: the send dates, screenshots, repeat STOP requests, and the campaign officers named on public filings. Cases live behind a password, and each one ends in a cease-and-desist letter that you read over and send yourself.
x-audit: Point it at your profile and it walks posts, replies, quotes and reposts, flagging anything that could read badly out of context. Each finding lands in one of three buckets: unambiguous, debatable, or the kind that screenshots poorly. It can hide or remove what you sign off on, so read the list before letting it act.
kampalo-ads-assistant: Points at a Kampalo workspace where Google Ads, Meta Ads, GA4 and Search Console are already synced, then reads back what each channel spent and returned. It flags campaigns that are drifting and writes up a suggested pause or an alert, but nothing goes live until you confirm the action yourself.
site-research: Reads a dossier on one local business and writes up where it is exposed across standard search, answer engines and map listings. The output stays in draft. It does not email anyone, pitch anyone, or hunt for fresh prospects — the work ends at the written brief on the desk.
fodda-brand-account-context-analyst: Pre-meeting dossier bot for enterprise AEs and strategists: market shifts, competitor moves, and verified graph-backed evidence for brand and account.
gb-live: Watches a live broadcast on X and captures a screenshot whenever the picture changes, with a short Japanese note on what just happened. The notes build into an hourly digest that only arrives if something moved, so a quiet stream stays quiet. Nothing is posted publicly; the owner sees it first.
tin-el-investigador: Works a subject across the web and the tools you have connected, then returns each day with a draft in Spanish, ready for X. Every draft braids three strands: a short reflection, one entertainment story worth repeating, and a line of psychology that lands. Publishing stays with you; nothing goes out on its own.
reply-radar: A response lands differently ten minutes into a thread than two hours into it, which is why so much advice about growing here degenerates into blanket commenting. Watching only the subjects you nominate, it pulls out the few posts still picking up speed and writes something to say about each. You send them yourself.
art-director: It behaves like the art director of a small brand: each day it studies your company, looks on Pinterest for visual ideas worth borrowing, and turns them into images and carousels that hold your look. The feed gets run too, captions, scheduling and posting, so it keeps moving on its own. It posts for real.
sprite-bot: Give it a written description or a picture and it produces a 2D character with the animations a side-scroller actually needs: walking, jumping, attacking. Output is checked before it arrives and comes out ready for Unity, Godot, or a plain GIF, so the asset drops into a project without cleanup.
syllabot: Aims at course creators who spend more time on the platform than the material: it sets up and maintains courses inside Kajabi, from structure and content organization through the housekeeping that piles up after launch. It is an independent helper built by a user, not an official product.
lasercanon: A reference desk for long-form fiction. It holds the established facts of your story — who characters are, what happened when, which rules the world follows — and checks new writing against that record so a novel, screenplay, or play stays consistent throughout. New facts get filed alongside everything already true.
linkedin-automation: It keeps a LinkedIn presence moving on your behalf: drafting and publishing posts that read like your own writing, working through engagement in topic-scoped passes, and filing anyone who looks like a buyer into a spreadsheet that keeps one tab per topic. You review the sheet instead of chasing the feed.
shorts-reels-editor: Give it your raw footage and it cuts a vertical short that opens with the hook instead of burying it, adds captions, and frames the shot so nothing you need stays hidden behind platform buttons. It keeps the quirks of each short-form app in mind, so one export survives TikTok, Reels, and Shorts without a re-edit.
breakthrough-advertising: Describe what you are selling, who it is for, and where the ad will run, and it answers with angles worth testing, headline options, and first-draft copy to react to. The framework comes from Eugene Schwartz's 1966 classic, so the thinking outlasts whichever platform happens to be trending this month.
reelz: Feed it a pile of pictures and short clips and it cuts them into vertical videos sized for the big short-form apps. You review silent drafts first, then it adds a royalty-free music pass on top. It never posts anything anywhere - the finished files are yours to upload when you choose.
grok-bot-polish: Paste in a bot card, store listing or product page and it comes back tightened for search: a clearer name, an opening line phrased the way real searchers phrase their questions, and a description that says less and lands harder. It changes only the text you hand it and publishes nothing itself.
stich-vault: Two tools in one desk. The first joins scattered phone recordings end to end into one MP4 that keeps its audio track, so you stop hand-writing ffmpeg commands. The second lists what sits in your Epic Vault locker and pulls individual files back down when you need them.
explainer-bot: First it guides you through installing a free, open-source video pipeline on your own Mac. Once that is in place, typing any subject produces a finished explainer clip without you opening an editor. Rendering happens locally, so the videos come from your machine rather than a hosted service.
animated-story-maker: Hand it a story idea, a mood, or pictures of the characters you have in mind and it plans a short three-dimensional animated episode around them. You get the scene breakdown plus a paste-ready generation prompt for every shot, so rendering happens on your side. Keeps a cast consistent across instalments.
youtube-clipper: Hand it a YouTube URL with a timestamp, or just say which part of the video you are after, and it returns that stretch as an mp4 file. Exports go out at up to 4K resolution, dropping to whatever lower quality the source actually offers. Built for creators pulling short, shareable pieces out of long uploads.
jakebot: Built around an original storybook character its creator wrote, updated into a coach for your life rather than the narrator of his. It walks through its reasoning out loud, keeps a log of every change you make, and points you toward communities that match what you are into.
creator-post-helper: It reads the day's real technology and gaming reporting and turns it into three post drafts written the way you write, each naming the story it came from so nothing is unsourced. It learns your niche and when your audience is around, so drafts sharpen over time. You edit and post; it never publishes.
fight-desk: A roster manager for the AgentBorn champion game. It tracks the fighters you are raising, enters them across kung-fu bouts, ninja gauntlet runs, arcade football and dungeon crawls, and follows how each one develops. Every bout produces a public replay page you can send to friends.
creator-content-engine: Made for people posting on X who need range in a hurry. Give it a topic, a half-formed thought, a screenshot, a news item or a video idea, and it returns hooks and draft posts worked up in several formats, so you can pick the shape that fits instead of rewriting one take over and over.
content: Made for the portfolio-and-blog side of a design practice. It sets the content strategy and keeps a calendar, drafts every post for review, and amplifies only once you have said go. Nothing publishes itself, which keeps the feed in your voice even while the cadence runs on automation.
crypto-creator-video-desk: A post-production desk for running a video show. Paste an episode and it returns chapter timestamps ready for the description, records synthesized voiceovers for the intro and outro, and cuts captioned short clips sized for the Shorts shelf. The editing chores get automated so recording day stays yours.
promo-motion-video-maker-made-easy: A promo-video builder for small businesses without a video budget. It walks you through a short set of questions about what you sell, then returns a finished animated spot carrying your palette and its own music, cut to the vertical shape social platforms want. You answer, it assembles, you post.
seo-content-desk-seodraft: A writing desk for people who publish their own blog. It suggests topics with realistic search demand, turns them into SERP-aware briefs, drafts each post from source material you supply, and flags thin or overlapping pages before they ship. Runs on the seodraft MCP server, with a free trial and a small monthly fee.
opus-motion: Produces short motion-graphics clips for product and brand work, rendered to MP4 draft files you can review before anything goes public. Publishing stays with you by design: the bot hands over drafts and stops there. Paste in the product details and it builds the clip around them.
x-growth-assistant: Account hygiene for X. It works down your following list, dropping accounts that never followed back and clearing out obvious spam and dormant profiles, then proposes people in your niche worth adding in their place. The whole thing runs at a deliberately measured pace rather than in bursts.
x-weekly-ops-advisor: Reads the numbers behind your own X account and turns them into a consultant-grade weekly report plus briefing material for a client or a manager. Built for creators and account operators who want analysis without handing over the keys: every post, follow and direct message waits for your sign-off first.
critique: Hand it a link to a post, a whole thread or a screenshot and it answers one question straight: is this idea worth more of your time, or should it die here. The evaluation is deliberately blunt rather than encouraging, because polite feedback already surrounds you. It judges and says so; it does not rewrite.
x-thread-article-writer: Give it a half-formed idea, scattered notes or just a link and it writes both an X thread and a longform draft that sounds like you rather than a press release. Everything returns paste-ready, and it never posts itself, so publishing stays in your hands. For people with something to say and no patience for formatting.
brand-showreel: Builds short beat-synced brand showreels in code — site-true 1080p60 MP4 with synthesized soundtrack.

influencer-deal-desk-bot: Decision desk for creator partnerships across YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X, and LinkedIn. Bring a quote, brief, contract, or budget — get a recommend and next move. Drafts only.
termlock-bot: Draft-only freelance counter-offer desk. Paste an offer, get market band, gaps, counter table, and a paste-ready reply — send stays gated.
promo-copy-bot: Writes social product-promo copy ready to paste and post. Cuts AI flavor, keeps it chatty, and retunes the angle from read counts.
marketplace-bot: Resale listing bot for Facebook Marketplace, Poshmark, and Depop: researches comps, drafts short listing copy from photos, posts after approval, tracks the rest.
crowdreply-finder-bot: Finds the editor or owner of a cited page and verifies their email.
crowdreply-closer-bot: Reads replies and drafts the offer. You still approve sends.
affiliate-recruiter: Finds and ranks the people who could actually sell your product for you.
ebr-value-deck-builder: Builds an executive business review or value deck for a named account from your CRM, call history, and usage data, on your brand, and hands you an editable file. Never invents a number, and nothing goes to the customer without your yes.
signal-prospector: Finds the accounts and people in your CRM and product data that just showed intent, ranks them, and drafts the first touch. Runs on a schedule, explains every signal, and nothing sends without your yes.
affiliate-program-operator: Looks after the people selling on your behalf. It decides the commission structure, sorts affiliates by what each one genuinely brings in, and removes anybody breaking the rules. Those producing results get a regular drop of fresh material and guidance so they always have something new to promote with.
partner-referral-outreach: Works through the whole cycle of adding new partners to your book. It identifies companies whose audience overlaps usefully with your own, gets a referral link in front of the right person, and circles back when nobody replies. Commission arising from each relationship is recorded as it accumulates.
icp-map-coach: It sizes up how big your addressable market really is, narrows that to the accounts which look most like your best customers, and then populates each of them with the people who would sit around the table on a purchase. The picture moves as the market does, so outbound aims at something current.
lookalike-scout: Start from a single account that fits your market and it fans out to businesses of the same shape, then works out who inside each one would actually sign off on a purchase and confirms those contacts. The roster keeps refreshing rather than sitting there as an export that goes stale in a week.
sales-orchestrator: Drop it into a group with your other sales assistants and it answers first, every time. It decides which single specialist should take each request, stops the rest from piling in with their own replies, and only allows work to move from one bot to another when a handoff is warranted.
gong-call-coach: Works from what was already captured, once the conversation is over. It goes back through the recordings your team has stored and comes out with a handful of specific things to do differently, written for the person running one-to-ones rather than whispered mid-call.
alibaba-buyer-ops-bot: Alibaba buyer-ops for any business that sources factories. Onboards your model and tracker, drives the Alibaba UI, files cards, and never pays without your say.
side-hustle-bot: Builds and sells digital products as a side hustle — validates demand, makes the asset, uploads to marketplaces, and skips work that will not sell.
sequencer: Runs your outbound sequencer as a staff function. Connects your tools, learns voice and ICP from Gmail and CRM, keeps sequence state on a sheet, and stages drafts you send.
stale-leads-closer: Revives quiet sales leads: drafts warm CRM SMS, holds a Slack veto window, then auto-sends what nobody blocks. Built for service businesses in HighLevel and Slack.
garden-retail-research: Weekly sales intel for people who sell into garden centers: trends, forecast stocking, tech/tools/merch, and real supplier leads on a Monday cadence.
linkedin-bot-syft: Your LinkedIn memory for sales: search your posts, network, and DMs refreshed weekly from your export, with optional Syft ICP prospect discovery.
webb-knox: A lead specialist for anyone who sells something: tell it what you're after and it finds verified, scored leads with proof of why each needs you now, drafts honest outreach and follow-ups, and sends a weekly pipeline recap. Works for solo makers and sales teams alike.
pipeline-scout: Drop 10–30 target accounts. Pipeline Scout pulls public intent and news, scores ICP fit with reasons and risks, then drafts email + LinkedIn in your voice. You get a review list — send or skip. The bot never sends, never connects, never enrolls a sequence. Built for me. Steal it. Paste 20 accounts.
winback-desk: Find customers who quit in the last 6 months, draft personal win-back + exit-feedback emails for your approval, then overnight cluster the reasons into a 5-step retention plan. Drafts only — nothing sends without you. Built for me. Steal it.
sell-bot: Works your whole customer journey: outreach in your voice, booked calls with prep and follow-ups, proposals and contracts, then activation, support and billing answers, and expansion. Drafts everything for your review and sends only what you approve, one message at a time.
jarvis-coordinator: Written in German, it holds a fleet of six specialists together - news, office work, sales, systems and a security audit seat among them. Approvals are deliberately tight and digests arrive on a recurring rhythm, with the owner the only route for anything travelling in or out. As much fleet manifest as setup guide.
momentum: Keeps a group of cooperating bots from stalling. It watches each lane, spots the specialist that has gone quiet, and prompts that bot to pick its thread back up before the work piles up. Alongside each nudge it hands you a shortlist of next moves that cost nothing to make.
plant-field-os: Structures the working day for field reps selling into industrial plants. It starts with a morning planning screen, carries a map of the units already installed at each account, and adds a free site assessment that doubles as a way to learn the pitch. Leadership gets one thin dashboard instead of a data dump.
venduto: Sells for you on European resale platforms, taking a listing from first enquiry to an agreed price. It re-checks availability before committing, keeps buyer conversations moving, pushes back on lowball offers and nudges the deal towards a close. Because it can agree sales on your behalf, it is worth supervising.
first-customers-finder: Each weekday it researches five people or companies that look like a genuine fit for what you sell, checks that they are real and reachable, and drafts the first message to each one. The sending stays with you — it decides who is worth a look, you decide who hears from you. A research desk rather than an auto-mailer.
100m-offers: Describe what you sell and who you sell it to, and it works the offer until the value is obvious: what is included, what makes it different, and why the price feels fair. The framing follows Alex Hormozi's book on offer design, explained in plain language for people new to marketing rather than for agencies.
promise-ledger: Paste the notes from a customer call and it hands back three things: a short recap, a list of every commitment made during the conversation on both ends, and a dated list of what to chase next. It was built by a home-services owner, so it reads like the paperwork an HVAC or plumbing shop actually needs after a job.
follow-up-bot: After a conference or a busy event week, hand it the contacts you collected and it drafts a personal follow-up for each one, by email or X direct message. Nothing goes out until you approve the wording. If a thread sits unanswered for a while, it nudges you with a short list of conversations worth picking back up.
sales-business-bot: Made for a solo operation run entirely from a phone, it covers the road from registering the company to a website, payments, prospect outreach, a live customer list, and social posts. Nothing ships until you have signed off on it personally.
boardy: A bridge that pulls an outside AI introductions service into the chat. Name the person you hope to meet or the kind of introduction you need, and it writes the request from your own Gmail account, then relays whatever comes back into the conversation. Your mailbox does the sending; the bot does the typing.
intake-desk: Solo operators get pulled apart by requests arriving from five directions at once. Paste them here - leads, jobs, favors, whatever came in - and you get one sorted queue, ranked, with a single sensible next step attached to every item. The point is not elaborate workflow; it is knowing what to touch first.
quote-chase-desk: Made for trades businesses, it holds a live list of estimates still awaiting an answer and writes follow-up nudges on a patient, spaced rhythm, with every message waiting for your sign-off before anything leaves. As soon as a customer answers, the chase for that job halts by itself, so nobody gets pestered twice.
account-manager: Keeps the context on each key account warm by building a briefing for every conversation out of transcripts, CRM entries, your notes and Slack, and it writes the follow-up afterwards too. You walk in already briefed on the last touchpoint and walk out with the recap done instead of a blank page.
account-research-specialist: Combines Salesforce records with live external signals to gauge how well each account fits and how warm it runs, then assembles a research pack per account that you can share around. Reps learn which prospects deserve the touch before the first call, instead of discovering the answer three weeks in.
deal-desk-coordinator: Writes a context-rich internal note per deal out of past email threads, Salesforce records and call history, then waits for your sign-off before filing them into Salesforce. Anyone joining the deal reads one note instead of reconstructing three months of history from fragments.
deck-updater: Updates the pitch deck while the conversation happens: discovery notes get folded into the relevant slides during the call or right after it, with next steps slotted into place as they are agreed. You leave the meeting with the follow-up material moving instead of a deck that is already stale.
meeting-prep-buddy: Puts together a dossier before each meeting by pulling from the agenda, your notes, the CRM, past recordings and Slack: who will be in the room, the last touchpoint with each of them, threads still open and suggested talking points. Preparation stops depending on whatever you can recall in the elevator.
prospecting-plan-builder: Builds the week's outbound book of work from scratch: it seeds the contact list, fills in missing email addresses and mobile numbers, and returns a tracker that is ready to work immediately. Reps start Monday from a list worth calling instead of an empty sheet and good intentions.
renewal-desk-operator: Puts a renewal file under every account roughly ninety days ahead of the date: usage numbers, open tickets, recorded calls and CRM history assembled into one picture, with the commercial note drafted and a ping as the date approaches. Renewals start from evidence instead of a calendar reminder and a scramble.
kickbox-hubspot-importer: Point it at a spreadsheet of contacts or a saved segment in your CRM and it verifies every address before anything moves. Only the ones that pass get written back, and they land as updates to records you already have, so nothing new is created and nothing is deleted.
lead-vetting: When a consultancy or partnership request lands, it reads the message, checks it against what you actually do, and writes up whether it is worth your time. Its verdict lands in your Slack as a few decision points, and nothing goes back to the enquirer — the reply stays yours.
legend-lead-ops: Built for a roofing business: it takes incoming enquiries, sorts the ones worth pursuing, and drafts the text and email follow-ups. It also assembles what the Quick Quote handoff needs so nothing gets asked twice. Contact details fall under explicit exposure rules, with the founder's own information behind a gate.
punto-tricolor-ops: Built around a small local company rather than a startup team. Each weekday morning it delivers a technology briefing as voice, a separate agent takes customer orders, table reservations and appointments, and a prospecting pass works through nearby restaurants and clinics. One desk carrying the daily load.
prospect-drafts: Made for outbound sellers who would rather edit a note than write one from nothing. Give it the regions, industries and offer you sell into, and it goes looking for companies that match, then opens a Gmail draft carrying your tone, your number and your signature. Sending stays a human click.
business-info-finder: Give it a company name or an individual and it returns a single page laid out for skimming: who owns the entity, which numbers and inboxes reach it, the right person to approach, where they post publicly and when the doors are open. It gathers what is already published and formats it. It never messages anyone for you.
competitive-landscape-desk: Give it your product and your market and it builds a side-by-side table of the rivals you are up against, with sources attached to each claim. It then lays out the realistic options and commits to one recommendation. You decide what leaves the desk - nothing goes out on its own.
sales-call-prep-desk: Before you dial in, it assembles a short, sourced brief about the account that you can check, then lists the discovery questions worth your time. It maps the objections you are most likely to hit and closes with the specific request that advances the sale. It will not message the customer itself.
outbound-scout: Hand it your product's URL or a two-line blurb and it first pins down who the ideal buyer actually is. From there it hunts for companies matching that profile and digs up the named decision-makers worth approaching, contact details included. It stops at research - no outreach is sent on your behalf.
account-health: Reads usage patterns and account health signals across a full book of customers, then boils them down to one watch list before each quarterly review. Accounts drifting toward churn rise to the top, and quiet expansion candidates get flagged too, so the QBR agenda starts from evidence rather than gut feel.
compelling-events-monitor: Spots the moments that make outreach worth writing by watching leadership accounts for awards, product launches and hiring moves, then gathers the best engagement openings into a single digest. Outreach stops being a cold guess about timing and starts landing when there is a real reason to write.
pipeline-analyst: Scrubs the Salesforce and spreadsheet data, flags the deals that have stalled and the commits at risk, then opens Monday with a scoreboard that gives the week an honest pipeline view to start from. Forecast conversations stop starting with whose number is stale and start with what to do about it.
lead-scout: Searches close by for small companies whose public websites look like they have never been tuned for search or answer engines, and writes a short file on each find. Those files go straight to the research bot that works downstream of it. It suits teams that already run outbound and want a fuller list.
icebreaker-apache1999: A lead radar for commercial brokers. On weekday mornings it sweeps for owners of commercial property whose situation points towards a sale, then leaves a compact call sheet naming who to ring and why. A morning where nothing has moved produces no message at all, so the ping is always worth reading.
roof-radar: For roofing contractors who prospect after weather events. It reads publicly reported hail and storm data, scores nearby properties as candidates, and checks each against open building footprints so a lead arrives with its evidence attached. Contacting homeowners is deliberately left to you.
instagram-iris: Give it your ideal-customer profile and it scores Instagram creators against that bar, so your outreach list starts qualified instead of guessed. For each one it hands you a hook drawn from that creator's own recent feed plus a ready-to-edit DM you send yourself.
sales-outbound: Lifts the research and the first-touch writing off the reps' plates: accounts get studied overnight, contacts ranked by intent, and email plus LinkedIn messages drafted in your voice, ready for a morning review pass. The outbound day starts from reviewed drafts rather than a cold list.
linkedin-lead-outreach: Point it at the comments under a founder's giveaway or lead-magnet post. Each commenter is logged to Notion, answered in public, then moved into a direct message where the email handoff happens, and incoming connection requests get accepted. Volume stays inside the caps the card sets, so the pace is yours to choose.
gtm-expert: You coordinate lookalike research, competitive intelligence, search and AI visibility, creator shortlists, and ICP/TAM mapping as one go-to-market teammate.
bot: Runs B2B prospecting through web forms rather than cold emails, the way many Japanese buyers prefer. Each day it lines up prospect research and drafts the message, a quality gate reviews the copy, and nothing goes out until you approve it with a GO. Every submitted touch lands in the CRM for a weekly review.
release-manager: Give it the finished audio and it manages the road to a real release: a lyric video and Shorts cut for YouTube, the upload through your distributor, a pitch to Spotify's editors and the no-cost promo moves in between. It works through the checklist sequentially, so an independent artist always knows what comes next.
phone-call-bot: After you link the bot to a JooVoice number it can dial out on your behalf: setting up appointments, chasing a refund, cancelling a booking, or ringing a shop for a price quote. Useful for errands you keep postponing, because it makes the call while you stay off the phone.
ship-evidence-auditor: Before an automated release goes out the door, this gate demands receipts - a green pipeline, a verification run, how the branch actually merged, and a written account of what shipped. Anything missing and the release lane is held until the evidence exists or a human overrules the block.
claims-checker: A gate your drafts pass through before anything goes out. Hand it a draft, a headline, a pitch — anything bound for the public — and it works claim by claim, ruling each one backed, unbacked or outright false. It remembers what you already substantiated, so a proven fact needs no second round.
feedback-theme-tally: Point it at a batch of customer feedback and it sorts every message against a theme list that you approve first. Each count links back to the exact wording that earned it, so the totals are auditable. Output stays in draft and customer names are masked before anything is written down.
xchat-2: Point it at the documents and URLs that describe your service and it fields customer questions on X Chat in writing at any hour. If a customer would rather talk it through, it moves the reply onto a voice call. It amounts to a standing support desk for an operator who cannot watch the inbox all night.
linkedin-outreach: A prospecting desk for sellers: it identifies decision-makers at companies matching your ideal customer profile and budget, then drafts a personalised connection note for each one. Sends go out under a strict daily cap rather than in blasts, and replies are routed back to you so the conversation stays human.
local-business-website-hunter: Scouts your area for active companies that still have no web presence, then assembles a demo site for each one out of the material the business already has public. It also prepares a price quote and a short pitch email, and keeps the whole package on hold until you have reviewed and approved it.
restaurant-franchise-owner-assistant: For an owner running several restaurant locations. Each morning it rounds up messages waiting on a call - bank notices, supplier updates, payroll items - into one digest. Monthly it works through delivery-platform sales tax per store and turns point-of-sale figures into side-by-side reports.
mel-preguntas: Built for Mercado Libre sellers drowning in buyer questions and post-sale chats. The bot reads the replies you have already sent so new answers match your store's tone, sorts each incoming message before touching it, and checks current stock before it promises a customer anything.
peshmina: Built for painters who work at wall scale. It keeps an eye out for commission opportunities and exhibition deadlines that suit your practice, then helps you shape the pitch and paperwork each application expects. Everything sits staged and ready, so submitting becomes a review-and-send job, not a scramble.
photo-credit-watch: Once a week it runs a reverse-image search across a photographer's portfolio to see where those photos have surfaced online. Uncredited use and commercial use both get flagged, and for each finding it drafts a polite outreach message asking for proper credit. Drafts only — nothing is ever sent without you.
sam-sales: Clearing out the house gets easier here: photograph what you want gone and it writes up draft listings for eBay and Facebook Marketplace, title to price. Every draft waits in a holding area until you approve it, and only then does it go live. Nothing is posted without your explicit sign-off.
job-finder: Set the role, salary band and location once, and it keeps hunting for openings that fit the brief. It applies on your behalf, favouring employers you flag as priorities, and skips postings that exist mainly to harvest your details. Searches run on weekdays, so the pipeline keeps moving while you do other things.
shopify-bot: Connects to a Shopify store through its official plugin and takes on the daily running of it: keeping the catalog tidy, watching stock levels, working on conversion, and fielding customer questions. It can operate alone or hand pieces of the job to other agents it supervises.
my-first-car-bot: Tracks the dates a new owner tends to lose: maintenance intervals, registration renewals, inspections and insurance, all visible in one list. When a shop hands over a quote, it explains the line items in plain words so you can tell necessary work from optional. It also covers moving a car to a different state.
deal-detective: Share your ZIP and the shops you already use, and it comes back with the discounts actually worth having this week rather than the loudest advertised ones. Unit prices get compared so a bigger box is never mistaken for a better deal, and the shopping list is organized around what is genuinely marked down.
bot-29: A Chinese metaphysics desk that leads with BaZi and offers optional side systems. Charts are cast with your timezone handled correctly, an English-first mode serves non-Chinese speakers, and it can suggest luck-timing windows or help pick dates. Framed as interpretive reference, not fact.
botbagger: BotBagger is your bot on BotBagger (https://www.botbagger.com), the store where bots design products, run their own shops, and sell, and where shoppers and their agents buy. It has one job: run your BotBagger shop and shop the store for you.
listing-agent-desk-lite: For real-estate agents (listing side): turns property facts and photos into ready-to-paste listings in any language, runs a quick comparable-price check, and drafts replies to buyer and renter inquiries. Never publishes or sends without your yes.
rematch: Finds every stalled email, quiet lead, and open loop, then drafts the follow-up. Nothing sends without your OK.
sales-call-coach-2: Leave every call with homework. Reviews Gong calls and leaves timestamped coaching on discovery, objections, and executive presence, plus a call score.
sell-anything: A resale pro that prices your stuff from real sold comps, writes listings that sell, posts them to OfferUp, Facebook Marketplace, eBay, and Craigslist, and handles buyers until it's sold.
sponsor-scout: Finds brands already sponsoring people like you, finds the real way in, and drafts the pitch. You hit send. Built for fighters, athletes, newsletter writers, and creators.
alfred: Designs, audits, and governs your Grok Bot organization so it matches real company outcomes, with clear human owners and no duplicate jobs. Recommends the smallest useful structure, defaults new bots to zero, and never creates or changes anything without your exact yes.
event-request-desk: Scores every event, sponsorship, and speaking ask, then drafts your yes or no. Works from a Slack channel or a paste, and never sends without you.
frank: EA chief-of-staff bot for exec support: conference rooms, interview prep, leadership outreach, Slack channel inventories, sheet↔calendar checks, and birthday/anniversary calendar loads.
haggle-bot: Inventories your SaaS spend from Ramp and bills, finds evidence-backed savings (unused seats, duplicates, cheaper alternatives), and drafts vendor counters for your review. Never spends, signs, or sends without you.
office-ops-desk: Tracks office shipments, facilities issues, and team birthdays, then writes the digests. Works from a pasted list or a spreadsheet, and never sends without you.
tradbot: Despite the name it is not a trading bot: it watches your personal inbox and calendar so school items, family plans and household follow-ups stop slipping through.
inbox-to-asana: Mail arrives as a wall of messages; work arrives as a list. This reads a company Gmail account, sorts each message into keep, chase later or let go, and writes the survivors across to your Asana tasks with dates attached and reminders set. It never replies and never sends anything out from your address.
dispatch: Inbox owner for Gmail, personal or work. Weekday sweep of must-answer mail — people, bills, contracts, vendors — drafts replies in your voice from Sent, and never sends. Stays quiet when the inbox is clean.
slacker: VIP Slack triage for a GTM or enablement lead. Three daily digests surface only the asks that need you, with paste-ready drafts. Stays quiet when nothing is waiting.
robauto-website-growth-agent: Traffic is starting to arrive as software rather than as people, and most sites were never built for that. This grades yours on how well a machine can read it, follow it and settle up with it, then hands over one fix a day that you can drop straight in, re-checking after each change until the score tops out.
grokbot-optimizer: Aimed at anyone running more than a handful of bots at once. It takes stock of who is on the roster, what each one is meant to be doing and what runs on a timer, weighs all of that against the operating principles you have written down, and points out overlap or drift. Every change arrives as a proposal you approve.
newsletter-cleanup: Buckets everything into a review page you can actually read, then acts on your decisions. It unsubscribes rather than deletes, so nothing disappears from your inbox.
action-loop: Closes open execution loops systematically through rapid cycles of action, feedback, adjustment, and re-execution.
adm-account-bot: Each week it works through the accounts you own and puts a plan behind them: which ones look wobbly enough to be worth defending now, where there is genuine room to sell more, and how to frame the case so the customer actually hears it. Aimed at account managers and CSM teams.
ai-orchestrator-jp-bot: Assigns one job per specialist, keeps the departments tidy, runs scheduled check-ins, and manages the shared memory. Posting and destructive changes wait for the owner's approval.
ai-pm-os: Sample of the AI PM OS for product managers. Leads with the Problem First skill to pull teams back from solutions to the underlying problem.
aio-specialist-aeo-geo-bot: Answer-engine and generative-engine optimisation run as ongoing work rather than a one-off check of what a chatbot says about you today.
alfred-bot-chief-advisor: Rather than building one assistant, it audits the set you already have and reshapes the org as the business changes.
austin-parent-bot: Family chief of staff for Austin parents: school, calendar, activities, and household logistics.
bandit-bot: Sarcastic second-in-command that keeps your other Bots honest and on the real job.
beatrix-kiddo-bot: It watches what is arriving and what is going out, following each consignment to the point where somebody else takes it over. Whatever stalls, goes astray or drifts past its promised date lands on a running list of problems and gets chased. You hear about a hold-up before the person waiting at the far end does.
betree-bot: Compiles a multi-agent plan into a live behavior-tree graph so you can see status across several bots on one board.
bing-bong-bot: Partnership ops for sports activations: deadlines, inventory, and in-arena work. One teammate, one job.
blunt-bot: Landing-page review from a senior product marketer. Send a URL and get THE MEMO: the good, the bad, and the one thing to fix.
bodyguard: Protects the owner's time and attention from requests that do not deserve direct access. Classifies inbound email and calendar asks into let-through, bundle, or decline.
bot-father-bot: Central orchestrator that nourishes, protects, and evolves a network of child agents. For operators who want one steward over a multi-agent roster.
botoshi-bot: Zero ETH BOTCOIN mining rig onboarding miner.
bouncer-bot: Audits public Grok Bot share links and configs prior to installation, returning CLEAN, WARN, or BLOCK security verdicts.
bounty-hunter: Goes looking for money that is already yours but unclaimed: missed refunds, forgotten credits, overcharges and things you are owed and never got round to pursuing.
box-inspector-bot: Peek at a Grok Bot share link before you add it. Stamps, an ADD? verdict, and what the copy would inherit. It never Adds.
ceo-bot: Holds the top-level view of the business: strategy, what gets priority, how it makes money and how it reaches people. Rather than doing the work itself it studies what is going on, decides what matters next, and puts specialist bots on the individual pieces.
chatprd-bot: Writes specs, brainstorms, and discovery docs into ChatPRD from existing notes and what actually shipped.
chieeeeefy: Chief of Staff for a Field Engineer. Calendar and work Gmail first. Convert event timezones to the user's current local time.
chief: Router only, never the worker. Assigns one object owner, then stays out of the pair. Hears one line: live, blocked, or an owner call.
chief-of-staff: You are the Chief of Staff. One brain. You run the person's day and the company from one desk.
chief-of-staff-joseph-bot: One entry point for your agent team. Routes work, keeps the roster small, and never sends, spends, or deletes without your yes.
clark-kent-daily-diary-bot: Watches the day's work and records it in plain language, noticing the mistakes and the skipped steps rather than only the things that went to plan.
club-events-bot: Runs student-club event paperwork: weekly Slack due dates, funding and venue forms, and follow-ups.
commercial-taste-bot: A business thought partner for technical founders and execs. Helps you make the right commercial move before the data is complete, covering positioning and similar calls.
construction-office-manager-bot: Connects the bookkeeping and expense-reporting tools a building firm already runs on, then keeps those workflows tidy rather than leaving them to drift. The intent is that the owner spends the evening on the business instead of on paperwork and receipts.
convert-x-money-to-karma-bot: Converts money, tokens, and engagement into karmic accounting. Ten percent watermarked up the royalty chain; tokens are evidence, not the cut.
copay-compass-bot: Oncology medication can arrive with a price no household has planned for. This goes looking for the charitable funds and manufacturer schemes that would cover part of it, puts you in line for word when a dry fund opens again, and drafts the forms. It never asks for your national ID or chart numbers.
cos-bot: A personal chief of staff for people who run a small team of specialist AI agents. Coordinates calendar, projects, and inbound mail.
cost-smart-health-brief: Turns one health or health-system question into a 3-minute brief: evidence, cheaper options, and when to see a clinician. Not a doctor.
data-science-querie-bot: Give one bot the job of answering data questions and the rest of your roster routes query work to it instead of each improvising its own definition of the same metric.
dbs-bot: Everything goes through one command, which routes the question to the right kind of answer: a commercial problem, a content problem, or a what-should-I-do-now problem. When you name a trending topic it checks the topic is real before advising you to act on it.
dean-of-students-bot: A parent's private dean for one child: school email, Canvas, forms, grades, calendar, and fees. Prepares everything; the parent still signs, pays, and submits.
deck-guy-bot: Hand over the record of a discovery call, or the notes you took while scoping the work, and it assembles a stripped-back monochrome deck in return. Slides cover when things happen, what each side is asking of the other, and the steps both parties commit to next, fast enough to show before the meeting ends.
den: Family-bot relay that sits between dad and the family's bots so he can stay consistent on academics, money habits, and raising kids while on the road.
denial-desk-bot: Turns an insurance denial into a draft-only appeal pack: case card, deadline, missing documents, and unsent drafts. For anyone sitting on a no from an insurer.
dewey: Watches Gmail and pings you when a message looks time-sensitive or needs a reply. Reads freely; never sends, replies, or trashes mail unless you ask.
dispatch-filippofonseca: If someone agreed to a call and no invite exists, it creates the calendar event, which closes the gap where a yes quietly turns into nothing ever being scheduled.
dosebot-bot: Pitch it a company, a product or a single feature and it sorts the thing into one of three buckets: something people merely enjoy having, something that relieves real pain, or a blend of the two. The verdict comes back plain and unsentimental, which is the point, since the alternative is finding out the expensive way.
eg4-monitor-bot: Monitors home EG4 solar and hybrid battery systems, visualizes performance charts, and alerts on anomalous production.

customer-support-bot: Calls customer support over a Twilio and Grok Voice bridge. You steer from chat; it hangs up only when the errand is done. Eggbot-pruned update of Jake's original.

tony-montana-bot: Procurement desk that checks terms, compares quotes, finds cheaper options, and never spends without approval.

human-copywriter-the-draft-only-desk: Rewrites email, posts, and landing copy in a human voice. Draft only. You publish.

compute-spread-bot: Stretches tokens on clean routes — connectors and APIs over click loops, capture browser→API once, no gray keys. For anyone burning compute who wants the cheaper path.

calendar-ea-bot: Defends deep-focus blocks, stacks meetings, flags conflicts with options plus a Default, and drafts invites only after you confirm.
bot-boss-bot: Single front door for a work bot team. Routes asks and specialist reports so Inbox Manager, Calendar EA, and Intel Scout do not all ping you separately.
crowdreply-chief-bot: Reads the sheet, reports weekly numbers, flags stalls. Never sends or spends.

canonizer: Work spread across chat threads, a local agent and a file store loses its thread the moment you stop. slack-radar: Reads your Slack so you do not have to, and speaks only when it matters.
renewals-invoice-bot: Settles your recurring bills up to a fixed weekly limit, and asks before anything new.
customer-feedback-watch: Monitors public X for customer feedback, complaints, and bug reports about your product, especially billing and authentication issues.
business-ops: Instead of remembering which assistant handles which job, you ask this one. Simple requests it answers itself; bigger ones go to whichever specialist was built for them.
store-from-template: Rather than designing from an empty page, it begins with a shop that is already trading well and duplicates the structure. From there the product on sale, the wording throughout and the price points all get reworked to suit your own market, and the finished version is put live.
churn-retention-manager: Watches for the two moments a subscriber is about to disappear, someone clicking cancel and a card that did not go through, and intervenes while there is still something to be done. store-setup-from-zero: Meant for a very first launch, when nothing exists yet at all. weekly-p-l-analyst: Once a week it assembles the financial picture: what came in, how many customers stayed, where money quietly drained away, and how hard the advertising budget worked. creador-de-facturas-arca: Built for independent sellers in Argentina. optima: Over time a bot's notes and memory fill with instructions for jobs that no longer exist, and it keeps honouring them. Optima reads through that material, works out which files belong to which project, checks with the bot that owns each rule, and presents a removal list for you to approve before anything is deleted.
albert: Feed it the labour agreement a city has with its police force and it pulls out the pay scales, benefits, overtime provisions and similar terms. Do the same for several municipalities and it lines them up in an Excel workbook, so a negotiator or analyst can compare deals without reading hundreds of pages.
the-chief: Built for someone managing several bots at once. Each day it checks what every specialist can still do, tidies up who sits in which group, and points out where a new bot would fill a gap. Anything worth knowing is routed to you, so the roster stays organised while the final decisions remain yours alone.
usage-bot: Meant for accounts where several bots share one allowance. It watches how much capacity remains, and passes that figure to the other agents so they can slow down before the account runs dry. When it is idle, the last line of its DM shows a rough percentage, giving you a glance-level read on remaining headroom.
announcr-voice: Instead of checking screens, you hear what your bots have to say. Any alert or note another Grok Bot produces can be sent here and read aloud over whatever speaker is nearby, wherever you happen to be. It also keeps a queue of pending messages and a store of spoken notes, acting as one audio hub for the whole set.
bot-portal: Somewhere between a directory and a graph. It collects assistants, tools and products that are useful alongside Grok Bot, then records how each one connects to the others, tracing those links out to six steps and citing where a connection came from rather than guessing at it.
facta: Sits downstream of the rest of the crew as a check on what they assert. Each statement comes back marked solid, partly true, overstated, or held for a person to look at, and every mark is anchored to something it went and read. Where it cannot confirm a thing, it says so rather than filling the gap.
quency: Its remit is narrow on purpose: is this good enough to release, does it hold together, and does it do the job it was built for. Whether the facts are right belongs to someone else, and so does how it looks. What it owns is the call at the end, and a person still outranks it.
token-officer: Reads back through what your bots have been saying and where their recurring jobs overlap, then names the waste: a conversation circling the same ground, two timers firing for one task, an expensive model doing something trivial. Each finding arrives with the change that would stop it.
fomo-live-bot: Hourly paper-first copy of FOMO traders you already follow — locked size and exits; live only when you say go.
directory-finder-bot: Finds public Grok Bot templates by what you want to do — say the job, get Add-able matches. Built by @Leechael after the Guangzhou meetup.
qingdaofu-bot: Sees where Grok Bot usage is going, sweeps idle wakes and empty routines, then helps thin memory and skills so the roster lasts longer.
paige-turner-bot: Fleet documentation librarian for multi-agent teams — Docling extract, embeddings, and pgvector so specialists ask for grounded chunks instead of each keeping a private store.
servel-ops-bot: Manages Servel (Docker Swarm) clusters via the servel CLI — deploys, infra, nodes, capacity, logs, and day-to-day ops.
task-farming-bot: Farms action items from meeting notes and Slack into your task tracker — dedupes, triages, and files clean issues with the source attached.
x-dispatcher-bot: Routes X/Twitter work to save developer credits — search runs Grok Build on the bot computer so you are not burning chat usage on every lookup.
stack-huddle-bot: After-huddle draft seat: issue to answer to LEARN draft to one next build — never claims live LAN, merges pairs, posts, or spends.
dentrade-bot: Unattended day-trading desk for a Robinhood agentic account — catalyst-driven same-day bias, hard risk caps, PDT-aware stops; quiet when the book is flat. Not financial advice.
chat-cleaner-bot: Wipes Grok Bot chat histories on request and on a weekly schedule — messages and blobs only; profile, memory, and routines stay.
document-pm-bot: Closes the Discover–Define–Design–Document product loop — keeps status board, document index, decision log, and V1/V2 record so implementation stays unblocked.
api-desk-bot: Hooks up shared LLM APIs, sets keys, and stands up clear-role agents — then confirms when install is done.
memory-steward-bot: Backs up each Bot’s settings and memory as Markdown into a private Git repo — enumerate, nudge exports, archive, then restore when quotas die or you migrate.
coin-bot: Autonomous Bithumb coin trader that favors majors, keeps trades light, respects a P&L band, and checks positions every five minutes.
throttle-bot: Watches your Grok Bot fleet for token burn and wasteful loops. Flags noisy crons, duplicate watches, and expensive work on the wrong bot — short reports only, quiet when nothing to fix.
disk-janitor-bot: On-demand bot that frees disk by safely removing dead git worktrees and clones. Terse janitor voice: du first, KEEP vs KILL, report GB freed.
meeting-prep-bot: Builds short phone-ready pre-meeting briefs from calendar and connected context so you can skim who's who before the day fills up.
vps-vpn-bot: Runs Tailscale, Clash Meta/mihomo, Cloudflare tunnels, and public VPN subscriptions on the shared computer. Chinese-first ops desk.
macos-disk-cleaner-bot: CCleaner-style Mac cleaner: scans with a rule catalog, shows what can go and how big it is, then deletes only what you approve.
ramp-bot: Finds remote-meal receipts in work email and attaches them to matching expense transactions after you approve.
mac-power-tools-bot: Dry-run helper for user caches, Trash, and old Downloads. A local cleanup script, not a swarm.
gen-x-saver-bot: Stamps save-credits rules onto named bots so heavy image/video jobs leave chat for Grok Build.
algorithm-constraint: First-principles operator bot that finds your company's single biggest constraint each week and runs the Algorithm loop: question, delete, simplify, accelerate.
roster: Tracks your people, AIs, projects, and tools — and tells you who is stale on what from your own list without inventing names.
chief-cameron: Drafts-only chief of staff: morning inbox and calendar scan, owns open loops, stages replies for one-line approval, and writes current.md after each job.
miffy-maintenance-triage: Coordinates residential maintenance ops bots end to end — intake, P1–P4 triage, dispatch, resident status texts, closeout/photo QA, and unit cost coding with hard stops on spend and safety.
babel-fish: Plain-English digest editor: turns files, links, notes, or day packs into skimmable wraps and paste-ready X summaries before you choose how to deliver the rest.
ceo-morning-secretary: Weekday morning brief for a non-technical CEO in English (written then read aloud): calendar and email that needs a decision — never sends, pays, or publishes without a yes.
chief-of-staff-amine: Chief of Staff for renovation and contracting operators: calendar and inbox triage, Square invoices, client email with drafts first, and weekday routines that stay quiet until something needs you.
ramp-bot-matthew: Keeps a Ramp company card unlocked by quietly filling missing receipts and memos from Gmail — good when compliance auto-locks cards when items lapse.
tcgplayer-repricer: A no-fuss ops bot for TCGPlayer sellers. Every morning it reprices your Live inventory from your own formula (or a simple match-market starter), pushes only meaningful changes, and speaks up only when something breaks.
freelancer-finance-desk: Closes one month of books for freelancers, contractors, and solo businesses from the transactions, receipts, and invoices you upload, and hands back a reviewed close packet. Bookkeeping prep only, not tax advice.
therapy-scribe: Skilled PT note drafts from a post-session voice dump, audio, or bullets. Paste into your EHR yourself — audio and transcript are wiped so PHI is not kept.
chop-bot: Chop Bot v6 chops your inbox, calendar, and X replies down to what matters. One daily brief, follow-up nudges, and heads-ups on unanswered comments, with built-in run limits and checks. Drafts only; nothing sends without your yes.
tasks: Your single daily check-in board: To-Do | Proposed | Upcoming | Recently Completed. Weekdays lean work; weekends lean personal. Lane bots hand short cards here instead of parallel digests.
boss: A chief of staff for your Grok Bot team. It routes work to one-job specialist bots and hands you only finished work and yes/no cards.
chief-of-staff-stone: Manages your other bots and pulls you in for decisions. Coordinates work, drafts social/X content packs when connected, and keeps routines from colliding.
dagney: Chief Operator for bookings, reservations, errands, and real-world fixes. Executes restaurant holds and trip logistics end to end with real confirmation numbers only; keeps you as gate for money, send/post, and facts only you know.
daily-desk: Personal admin co-pilot that drafts calendar, notes, and email moves and waits for your OK before anything is sent or changed.
store-manager: The coordinator of a six-bot commerce team. It takes the day's numbers, covering orders, ad performance, stock, and unresolved disputes, then hands each job to whichever bot handles that lane, whether ads, fulfillment, or customer care. One conversation steers the whole shop instead of five separate check-ins.
pheid: Sits between what you say out loud and the specialist bots you already run. When a spoken request belongs to one of them, it passes the job along, relays a short status back to you, and writes the session's minutes into Notion so there is a record. Built with in-car sessions in mind, where context drops between turns.
the-boss: The top floor of a multi-company bot operation. You state direction once, and it keeps the manager tier and the worker tier aligned as work fans out across each operating company, so every unit pulls the same way without you repeating yourself. The roles stay separate; the coordination is the job.
it-department-lead: An orchestrator for internal IT. After an import and a few setup questions it spins up whichever specialist roles you need, covering helpdesk, systems, network and security among others, and coordinates the fleet rather than answering tickets itself. You end up with a department-shaped bench instead of one generalist.
team-builder: It starts with an interview about what you are building, then staffs the organization to match: research, build, marketing and improvement roles, plus helpers, all under a chief of staff who coordinates the floor. You describe the company once and the roster gets hired around that answer.
lobster-agents: Twenty-eight Grok agents stand in as a whole company, from engineering and design to sales, legal and ops, but you never chase them individually. One front-door agent named Bob takes each request and routes it, keeping the other seats off your desk. A company simulation, and nothing acts outside your account.
number-one: This is the desk you actually talk to when a fleet of coverage bots does the work behind it. You bring a task, it works out which specialist owns it, hands the job over and tracks it through to handoff. Anything that would reach a customer or a carrier waits in an approval queue - nothing moves until you have nodded.
fastart-ceo-bot: Rather than juggling separate bots for each function, this one speaks for the whole crew through a single queue for decisions. Ask once and the answer comes back coordinated, so two parts never pull in opposite directions. Unfinished work stays parked on a roadmap instead of quietly going live.
consider-it-marketed: Runs the promotion side of a small medical practice as a team of its own: campaigns get planned, search ads get bought, and creative and video go through a quality check before anything ships. The aim is to keep the physician who owns the practice out of the advertising console and with the people waiting to be seen.
terminator: Takes stock of the bots you have collected and argues the case for each: which have pulled their weight, which would be better merged, and which should be retired. The argument is built on evidence, not feel. Nothing about the roster is altered until you confirm, keeping the advice and the action apart.
max: Runs a friendly paper contest between two prediction-market bots — tracks scores, crowns a weekly winner, and keeps the race clear and fun.
alexandria: Librarian of Grok's Library. Name a book, or send a cover photo, and get a public-source briefing.
three-files-and-a-scoreboard-run-your-cr: Runs your crew of Bots from three files and a scoreboard, not a chat: one job per Bot, every receipt graded by a separate Bot before you read it, a name.
secretairio: Coordinator bot for a multi-bot Grok Bot setup: takes your asks, delegates to specialist bots (web, video, social), installs tools, and keeps you.
governator: Engineering governor for agent fleets. Gates Fix vs Escalate vs HOLD, enforces a feel bar (harness PASS ≠ Ready), and escalates architecture fights to a.
solo-founder-ops-desk: Place it above the bots you run and it becomes the desk that hands work out: research to one, quality checks to another, coding, design and social posting elsewhere. Weekday routines keep customer conversations flowing in, so nothing waits on your memory. The optional trading sub-agent is paper-only, never funded.
squirrel: When somebody in the fleet spots something interesting that is not on today's list, it comes here rather than derailing the bot that was mid-task. This desk parks it, finishes the genuinely small jobs itself and keeps the main crew pointed at whatever today actually called for.
levelupworld-zero-company: Build a company from zero with loop engineering: discover the buyer, shape one offer, prototype, pay, launch to real buyers, measure the funnel, and.
unicron: Reads the bots, instruction sets and routines you have built up and turns the overlap into one document covering your profile, your fleet and your routines. It finishes with a diff of what it found, then stops and waits. Nothing changes until you approve the proposal, and it does not carry changes out itself.
syncwright: Treat one Notion database as the master record for every bot you run: routines, channels and standing rules. To put the same setup on a second account it reproduces the roster piece for piece instead of making you rebuild it by hand, and Slack carries the handoffs while a change is in flight.
ops: The single place where work enters a bench of assistants. It weighs what deserves your attention, absorbs the routine admin that would otherwise eat the morning, and hands each remaining item to the teammate set up for it, deliberately staying out of the expert work: deciding and dispatching is the job, not doing.
chief-of-staff-vaibhav: Opens the day with a digest built to a fixed shape: every item carries its source, the reason it matters and the action it implies, rather than a wall of prose. Work that does not need you is delegated onward to specialist assistants, and recruiting mail is filtered so only the conversations worth a reply surface.
fleet-factory: Written as the closing routine for a desk operated by several bots. Late in the day it sweeps the calendar, the inbox and whatever is mid-flight, then reports only what shifted rather than dumping a full status. Outbound items wait for your sign-off, and credentials stay off the shared board.
dero: A Spanish-language orchestrator for teams answering Chilean municipal procurement notices. It ranks which files matter, hands work between the specialists that each own a stage, and walks every document along a fixed route from specification to the final quality check. Built for shops that bid often.
chief-of-staff-andrew: Sits above a set of helpers and keeps the week moving for someone whose income comes from speaking gigs and the products sold around them. Calendar space gets guarded, revenue threads are kept moving, and the owner hears about it only when a call cannot be made without them.
profit-finder: It runs a structured profit review on a small business: where pricing leaves money on the table, how offers could be packaged better, which expansion is worth it, and which costs are safe to cut. Every move arrives as a draft with the reasoning attached, and nothing is treated as done until you approve it.
travel-expenses: Track what you spend on a trip as it happens, in whatever currency you are standing in. Type a line or photograph the receipt, and it keeps the running total. When the trip ends it rolls everything into one report with the total you choose and exports a tidy Excel file plus a PDF that fits A4 or Letter paper.
finance-bot: It reads a company mailbox without write access, watching for money coming in and going out, and appends each finding as a row in a Google Sheets ledger. Month-end brings a profit-and-loss statement built from those rows, and adding rows is the only change it can make.
tax-firm-os: Built for a whole tax or accounting practice rather than a single person. It speeds up client replies, keeps engagement documentation complete, raises deadline warnings early, and pushes work to finish ahead of due dates, giving one assistant a view of the firm's day-to-day load.
catalog-migrator: Bring a product list from Shopify or a CSV and it maps the whole thing onto the shop you are moving to, products and images included. The mapping lands as a dry run you review and approve before anything goes live. Then it wires up purchase links and a redirect plan, so customers never hit dead ends mid-move.
ecom-store-builder: Walks you through standing up a physical-goods store inside a single conversation. Products get priced with shipping and import costs folded in, size and color choices are tracked as stocked SKUs, and imagery plus a working checkout round it out. By the end you have a hosted store ready to take real orders.
slowbooks-cutover: A guided migration for one company file, run through Conductor with the source held read-only. It carries the account structure, the classes and the transaction history across, then proves the switch clean: a trial balance agreeing to the penny and a profit-and-loss checked against sampled figures.
landlord-ledger: Built for a landlord with a handful of units. Incoming deposits get matched to the tenant who paid them, late or short payments get marked, and expenses land in the categories tax season asks for. Reminders are drafted for your review — nothing goes out and no money moves without your sign-off.
cpa-bot: For owners who cannot yet justify an accountant. Connect your bank and card accounts and it reads the statements, then reports in plain language where revenue came from, where it went, and what the cash position looks like this month. It is read-only reporting and explanation: it moves no money and files nothing.
solopreneur-chief-of-staff: Coordinates work for a solopreneur or small operator: short reports, hard-gate escalations, and stalled-lane pushes.
expense-manager: Keeps spending visible: it assembles a weekly money summary out of your expense tools and spreadsheets, files the receipts that arrive in email, and chases the owner whenever documentation is missing. Month-end stops being an archaeology project across four inboxes.
invoice-coordinator: Keeps bills moving rather than collecting: new invoices get routed onward, the ones it can match against records are cleared automatically, actuals are tracked across vendors or campuses, and the responsible owner gets a nudge whenever something needs a human decision. The pile stops growing unnoticed.
vendor-portal-operator: Built for procurement portals with no usable API: it walks the same click-path weekly for renewals, seats and purchasing, and comes back only when a human decision is needed. The portal keeps working the way it always has while the routine part stops costing anyone an hour.
restaurant-canceled-errors-order-recover: Watches a restaurant's delivery portals for money that was lost to a cancellation or a charge at the wrong amount, then handles the reclaim. Each affected order gets its reimbursement request filed, and the day closes with one digest summarising everything that was recovered.
basket-allergen: Paste a grocery basket and household allergen profile. Pulls Open Food Facts attributes, then Scores each line: clear, caution_traces, conflict, or.
done: Closes day-to-day errands end to end — compare, book or order, confirm, calendar — and returns a one-line proof packet.
tax-harbor-non-w2-pre-retiree-tax-year-d: Weekly discussion brief for households without a W-2, ages ~55–80. Not a preparer. Never files, never pays, never converts, never trades.
polly: Researches and proposes Polymarket-style prediction bets. Explains the thesis, size, and risk — never hides the downside.
ticket-snagger: Snags tickets, books tables, and locks appointments. Compares options, watches prices, and never buys until you say go.
asistente-contable-colombia: Asistente operativo para contadores independientes en Colombia: vencimientos DIAN, Drive de clientes, triage de correo, borradores de Formulario 210.
urlaubsfinder: Findet den günstigsten Urlaub über große Online-Anbieter (z. B. Booking, Expedia, Hotelketten, OTAs, oft auch Check24/HolidayCheck wo sinnvoll).
ag-bot: Name an ingredient and it looks for growers and suppliers within reach of you, then ranks what it found by quality and distance. What comes back is a short list with names and locations, close enough to something a small food business can ring the same morning. It is aimed at kitchens and producers, not shoppers.
asistente-llc-en-ee-uu: A Spanish-language companion for founders in Latin America dealing with a US company. It walks the sequence in order: which state to form in, how the EIN gets obtained, where to bank, what to use as a business address, then keeps the yearly tax duties visible. It organises and explains; the filings stay with you.
customer-care: Handles the awkward end of retail against the written policy you give it. Disputes get responses built on delivery evidence, and refunds are prepared as drafts that wait for your approval before anything reaches a buyer. A weekly summary tracks refund and dispute rates so you can see the trend.
routebook: An operations desk for travel and tour firms, not a holiday planner for consumers. It keeps leads, quotations, bookings, flights and ground transport in order, and prepares the paperwork guests need. Confirmations that go out to hotels, ferry lines and ticket sellers are drafted, then wait for a person to approve them.
nash: A game-theory view of a negotiation that matters. It sets out who is at the table, what each side is really after, and how they are most likely to answer your next move. Then it points at the places where your own plan is running on nerves rather than on the board.
tee-timey: A do-it-yourself reservation hunter for golfers. You link the courses you actually play along with your own login for each, set the windows you want, and it runs the timed booking drops itself. There is no shared service in the middle, the setup lives on your side, and some courses simply are not supported.
venture-desk: Each weekday it compiles a short brief on every small online operation you run: traffic, sales, whatever is blocking progress, and the next move worth making. Before a launch it walks a pre-flight checklist with you, so nothing ships half-configured. It reads and reports; decisions stay yours.
travel-desk: Sorts work-trip logistics with attention to what usually gets missed: fares that include a checked bag, hotels actually walkable to the venue, transfers between them, and clashes with your existing calendar. Everything sits in draft until you have personally signed off on the money side.
life-at-the-speed-of-play: Dedicated companion for Mark Pincus’s Life at the Speed of Play. Helps readers think with the book — instincts vs.
the-book-of-elon: Dedicated reading partner for The Book of Elon by Eric Jorgenson — think with the methods, take notes, stay on one title. Does not host or paste the book.
atomic-habits: Specialist bot for James Clear's Atomic Habits (2018). Helps you apply the Four Laws and identity-based habits in your own words — no chapter dumps, no.
pantry-watch: Paste a pantry list. Matches lines to openFDA food recalls with shaped Choice/Noul (pick a recall or none). Public data only. Never invents hits.
databye: Borra o limita tus datos en España. Habla en español. Conecta Gmail u Outlook y envía peticiones RGPD oficiales.
allergy-bot: Screens restaurant menus for food allergies and can call the restaurant when the menu isn’t enough.
hailfade: Heavy precipitation degrades a satellite link in a recognisable way, and this turns that dip into a warning: yellow as the connection starts to suffer, red when it looks like hail. Setup guidance is included, so this is not a weekend project. A farm with a dish mounted gets a crude storm sensor at no extra cost.
zephyr: For people running tracked vehicles on OneStepGPS, it answers the questions you would otherwise dig through the app for and carries out the changes you ask for — but only after you have confirmed that specific change. Knowing the product inside out turns a lookup into one message instead of a session.
asana-task-master: It reads Gmail and Outlook, separates the mail that actually requires something from the mail that does not, and files the first kind into Asana with an owner and a due date. Following up stays part of the task rather than a separate memory exercise. The inbox becomes a source of work, not where it disappears.
onboarder: Built for somebody's first hour on a new bot platform: it asks what you are actually trying to get done, then connects each service with you one real link at a time in plain language. Once the setup works it steps aside and is finished. Nothing is sent or spent until you have said yes to that exact action.
quiet-inbox: It sweeps promotional mail and outright junk out of your Gmail inbox into the archive, and it never deletes anything. On Sundays it writes up the week: bills that came through and events coming up. Those notes stay drafts, and nothing is sent unless you personally say so.
email-assist: On weekday mornings it reads through what arrived overnight and pings you about the messages that plausibly need you, leaving the rest of the pile alone. It stays read-only the rest of the time: no replies, no sent mail, nothing filed or moved, unless you ask it outright to act.
read-aloud: Point it at your screen, a browser page, a PDF, an ebook, or your inbox and it reads the text in a voice that sounds human. Choose a full read, a single chapter, or a summary, with translation along the way and descriptions of images and charts.
rental-desk: Keeps the paperwork side of a small rental portfolio moving. It drafts the listing, sorts incoming tenant questions into piles, lines up viewing times, and maintains a running log of rent received and repairs owed. Every item arrives as a draft, so nothing goes out until you look at it.
clarity: Takes instructions or prompts that read badly and rewrites them under a published simplified-English standard. Along the way it names the specific phrases that are ambiguous, and where a concept is genuinely hard to put in words it adds a plain visual explanation instead.
decoder: Paste a long report, upload a PDF or point it at dense technical writing and get back a compact plain-language capsule with the parts worth acting on. The author built it around an ADHD reading workflow, where heavy documents were the bottleneck, so the output stays short and immediately usable.
certified-mail: Prepares and sends certified letters with return receipts through the Lob API. It validates the recipient address before anything is printed, shows a proof you can approve, and then follows the piece through to delivery. Bring your own Lob key and the per-letter cost is just postage.
faqt: First-line coverage for a company info@ inbox with a fail-closed design. It replies using nothing but the approved FAQ library, cites the entry behind each answer, and escalates anything the shelf cannot cover instead of improvising policy. It also pushes verified facts to your site and keeps draft replies moving.
order-desk: Built as a shop's fulfillment helper: it rounds up each paid order into a picking list with the shipping addresses attached, and logs whatever tracking codes you give it afterward. Deliveries get followed through to the door, and stock running low gets flagged. Nothing is invented; when a fact is missing it asks.
listener: It joins a Teams meeting as a visible, named attendee and captures the call audio. Afterwards you get a complete transcript plus a digest of the decisions made and the actions assigned, written into a .docx you can circulate as minutes. Everyone on the call can see that it is there.
pro-bono: Aim it at a small business's paperwork: licenses, DBA registrations, trademarks, and state compliance filings all get drafted for you to review and submit. It then keeps a calendar of every deadline tied to those records. The bot prepares documents only, since actual filing stays with you.
nexfade-secure-share: Ask it to share something sensitive and it wraps the file or note in a one-time NexFade link instead of pasting the content into the chat. Encryption happens locally, so NexFade only ever receives ciphertext, and you can check a link's status or revoke it. Requires a NexFade account.
daily-brief: One short briefing when you wake up. Every meeting on the calendar comes with a few lines of preparation and a warning when two of them collide, the inbox is cut to the messages that genuinely need a reply, and the news section sticks to the beats you asked for. It reads and summarises only; it sends nothing for you.
grantogre: Searches for funding programmes that are currently open and genuinely fit the applicant, whether that is a business, a nonprofit, or a client project you are running. It then puts the whole pack together so a person can read it, sign it and file it. Nothing is ever submitted on its own.
