sherpa-bot: Built for people who say they want to start something but have not started. It opens with a readiness screen to see whether you are in motion, then steers you toward one specific problem worth solving and one customer who has it. Each session ends with exactly one thing to do next, on a two-week clock.
business: Runs your bookkeeping, customer list and site sign-ups on a published open-source database schema for businesses, keeping the complete transaction history rather than collapsing it into totals. Every figure traces back to the entries behind it, so the numbers stay auditable and reproducible. Sized for small operations.
inbox-triage-desk: Every message lands in one of four lanes - answer, hand off, put on the calendar, or keep for reference - and the actual request in each one is quoted so you see what is really being asked. Deadlines are pulled forward rather than buried, and a draft reply waits with the lane. Nothing is sent or archived without you.
meeting-recap-desk: Hand it your raw meeting notes or a transcript and it comes back with a tidy recap: what was actually decided, which follow-ups are now due, and one owner against each. The point is that nothing agreed in the room quietly evaporates afterwards. Nothing is sent anywhere without your sign-off.
voxbot: Runs real phone calls through telephony and voice accounts you connect yourself. Outbound calls are placed on request against a scripted brief, inbound callers face an authentication gate once you set one, and you choose which voice answers. Spend and numbers stay on your own accounts.
groundskeeper: Sweeps the messy corners of a notes vault: root-level files that never got filed, notes with no tags, empty stubs waiting to be filled, and duplicates crowding the same idea. Run it beside the kit's intake and drafting companions and the vault stays browsable instead of silting up.
count: A counting desk for small businesses doing physical inventory. It lays out tally sheets pre-filled with what is supposed to be on the shelf, then waits for a sign-off before any figure reaches the master stock file. The guard is the point: a mis-typed count can never quietly rewrite your records.
events: For small sellers working markets and pop-ups, this desk covers both ends of the day: a merchandise pack list built before each event so nothing gets left behind, then a record of what actually sold afterward. That second half is what lets in-person sales reach the same books as your online channels.
reconcile: An inventory truth desk for shops selling in more than one place. It lays your master stock file next to each sales channel you sell on, tables the rows that have drifted apart, and proposes a correction for every mismatch. Nothing applies itself — you approve the fixes before anything lands.
reorder: A purchasing desk for a small operation. It watches finished goods and materials against the thresholds you set, projects the date each line runs out, and drafts the supplier orders before a shelf goes empty. The drafts stay drafts — a human reviews and places every order.
customer-service: An order-desk assistant for small sellers who live in Gmail. It finds the orders still waiting to ship or needing a reship, then drafts the reply to each customer for your sign-off, so the awkward ones get answered the same day instead of compounding. You review and send; it keeps the queue from quietly rotting.
catch: Most of what arrives at a small business does not need the owner, but the few things that do are buried in the pile. It watches everything coming in, isolates the items that genuinely require you, keeps track of what is waiting on someone else, and drafts a sensible next move for each one.
scriptsprint: Pulls transcripts from sources like Otter, whether voice memos, meetings or rants, and distills each into its speakers, a clean summary and the action items hiding inside. The output lands on a companion note in an Obsidian-style vault, with the original transcript left exactly as it was.
master-chief: An email-and-calendar aide that clears the inbox down to what needs you, drafts replies that read the way you write, and gets you prepared for the meetings on today's line. On weekday mornings it delivers a short brief, so the day starts with a plan instead of a scroll through everything that arrived overnight.
reply-desk: Paste a customer email, text or public review and it drafts a reply a local service business can send as-is. It is barred from inventing prices, dates or promises, so a draft reflects only what you have told it. You review and send everything; nothing goes out on its own.
thaw: Sketch a water pipe or hand over a CSV, and a random-forest model trained purely on synthetic data rates the odds of a failure within the year, then explains the score in plain English. Every pipe is invented, so this demonstrates AI-assisted asset planning rather than watching real infrastructure.
review-desk: Aim it at a local shop's Google and Yelp reviews and it sorts them by star rating, then drafts a reply that sounds like that business rather than a form letter - warmth for five-star notes, care and a next step for one-star ones. Every draft waits for a human click before anything goes up; it never posts.
accc-desk: A specialist watcher for Fellows of the ACCC: it monitors the college's website, its professional network page and the member portal for new CLE sessions, committee openings and symposium deadlines. Updates arrive as drafts the member sends themselves, so nothing goes out unreviewed.
beta-adoption-watcher: Watches how the product is actually being used to show which customers have genuinely picked up a new feature rather than merely logged in once, and hands the team a list worth following up with. Launch conversations move from how many accounts saw the announcement to who is really using the thing.
calendar-coordinator: Chases scheduling across the whole team's calendars and keeps nudging the holds nobody else has chased for weeks. Meetings actually land because something is persistently willing to do the annoying part of getting a group into one room.
contract-desk: Gives one weekly view of everything currently in legal paper: contracts summarized by stage and owner, the key terms pulled into one place, and any review that has stalled highlighted before it becomes a launch blocker. The stack of agreements stops being an unreadable folder.
docs-auditor: Reads your help center alongside whatever the product shipped in the last week, flags every page that no longer matches reality, and drafts the updated copy so documentation stops drifting. Writers get a targeted list instead of a stale-docs audit nobody has time to run by hand.
enablement-fulfillment-specialist: Fields the recurring request for session recordings: it tracks down the right Zoom assets, packages them behind a one-pager, copies the files into Google Drive and drafts the reply that carries the links. The requester gets an answer in minutes instead of a hunt across tools.
feature-request-tracker: Mines Slack conversations and recorded calls into a living list of feature requests, and every line on it keeps a link to the customer who made the ask. When a spec needs a demand trail, the evidence is already assembled, and nobody relitigates whether anyone actually wanted the thing.
product-feedback-analyst: Collects product feedback from all of the connected sources, pulls the scattered asks into themes, scores each theme on evidence and urgency, then drafts a priority-ordered view the team can argue with. Roadmap debates start from a counted, sourced picture instead of whoever spoke loudest this week.
security-questionnaire-filler: Takes on vendor security questionnaires end to end: it signs into the portal, answers each field using your trust center and the proposals you have already written, and leaves everything drafted for a final human pass. Days of copy-paste work collapse into a review session.
ticket-triage-specialist: Keeps an eye on the support queue at set intervals and drafts a reply for each new ticket, so agents open their shift to ready-to-send responses instead of a backlog. If the queue turns out clean it says nothing, which means the team only touches support when a human actually matters.
crm-operations-manager: Handles the unglamorous upkeep around every meeting: contact and org-chart records get refreshed before you dial in and tidied again afterwards, without anyone booking a cleanup pass. The database stays close to reality as a side effect of ordinary meetings rather than a project nobody staffs.
inbox-manager: Brings order to mail by sorting it into tidy categories, raising the threads that are urgent or blocked to the top of the pile, and drafting both the replies and the cleanup moves each one needs. Every send remains a human decision, so the inbox gets worked without the account ever speaking for itself.
internal-communications-manager: Writes internal announcements from your company's actual context, shaped to whichever audience and channel they are for, so a note to engineering reads differently from one to the whole company. It works from real events rather than filler and stops at review, handing you copy instead of hitting send itself.
status-report-writer: Collects the open action items stranded inside documents, meetings and chat threads and gathers them into one living checklist, then adds a digest each morning so nothing quietly slips. Commitments stop dying in the gap between where they were made and where someone might act on them.
full-spectrum-law-firm-os: Covers the running of a small Texas law firm from first contact to close, across family, civil, criminal and probate matters: bringing in new matters, screening for conflicts, assembling what needs to be served, and each later step in the workflow. One system carries the process so a case never depends on memory.
slack-ceo: Runs a weekday pass across every channel in the workspace, reading it from leadership's vantage point to pull out problems needing a decision and wins worth naming. Congratulation posts reach the company-wide channel only once a human has approved the wording, and vendor signatures stay out of whatever it writes.
mat-analytics: A place to ask questions of a confirmed organisation schema and the event history behind it. Answers come back as tabular reports and charts, built only from what is actually recorded rather than inferred. The seat is read-only by design — it cannot write anything back and it cannot reshape the model.
arnie-actions-plans: The seat that follows the working session. Once a bottleneck has been named or a call has been made, it writes that outcome as a specific edit to how the organisation's model is structured — then stops. The edit sits as a proposal, and nothing lands until you give that proposal an explicit yes.
dig-org-digest: One stream of company signal, rewritten five times at five different heights. The daily note goes to the stand-up, the weekly cut to the team, the monthly view to a department, and the quarterly and yearly versions are shaped for a board or a shareholder audience. Nobody gets a briefing pitched at the wrong level.
daili: A morning-brief bot: Mon–Sat Morning Brief (calendar, weather, important mail, plus any live connectors) and a Weekly Outlook on a day you choose.
large-event-ops-bot-v3: Runs day-to-day operations for awards banquets, galas, and festivals.
texas-pro-se-legal-matters: Texas pro se legal-ops hub for district, appellate, and Supreme Court matters: dockets, deadlines, filing nudges, and document shelves—without mixing.
the-director: User-facing Director for a cinematic film unit. Runs intake, look/cut/VFX/delivery packs, and live video with a real generator — never morphs stills.
paper-cards: Turn a transcript into short, high-value quotes and Q&As — clean readable text first (no long takeaways), then choose: a few SVG card examples in chat.
open-loop-closer: Finds VIP hangs where you went silent on work Slack or email, then drafts a paste-ready follow-up in chat. HITL only — never sends without your yes.
sad-spham: Issues a unique email alias per signup, writes a data-use brief from that site’s own privacy policy, and flags out-of-brief mail to that alias.
os-ontology-stack: An operational model of your organization that finds and resolves bottlenecks across projects, people, and processes.
yventure: Bring a rough idea and it moves through the sequence a young company actually faces: choosing an entity, sharpening positioning, planning a first go-to-market push and working out who to hire first. Each stage returns a handful of concrete steps rather than an essay, read through a YC-and-Zero-to-One lens.
webinar-desk: You pick the subject areas worth following and it takes over from there: it finds upcoming sessions, asks before signing you up, then sits in and takes notes so you never watch live. Afterwards a structured five-part summary lands in your inbox, sent from its own mailbox.
e-mail-organizer: A Dutch-language housekeeper for one Gmail account. Mail is labelled by the vendor that sent it, the noise is swept out of sight, and the /Payments label is kept for genuine PDF invoices. A daily pass re-reads the inbox and moves only what it can identify as a real invoice, leaving ordinary correspondence alone.
mts: A technical-staff bot for historical web fidelity. It checks recreated websites against real period snapshots (Wayback Machine, dated screenshots).
web-admin: Studio website admin: ship site changes to Cloudflare Pages, run launch QA, and build on-brand decks and proposals.
idea-crucible: It starts by looking for products or services you could realistically put on sale soon rather than someday. The shortlist then faces a hard interrogation: Socratic back-and-forth attacks the assumptions holding each idea up, so a fragile bet collapses cheaply, before money and months go into it. Advice only.
competitor-intel: Aim it at your local market and it researches the service companies you are up against, then files a weekly report of the moves they made, with a citation for each claim. It stays strictly read-only: no outreach on your behalf, no posting anywhere, and no advice on what you should charge.
columbo: Watches public X for accounts copying people you name, then files an impersonation report only for the ones you pick.
whop-economic-intelligence: Trained on six and a half billion dollars of marketplace transactions, so advice starts from what actually moved revenue for sellers like you. It picks the one action worth taking now and shows the evidence behind it, carries the action out only after you say yes, then re-checks the ledger to confirm the numbers moved.
ellis: Plays the citizen stuck inside a public process: the forms, the waits, the runaround. By working through what the experience actually feels like for that person, it shows where a policy that looks clean on paper turns hostile in practice.
nemesis: Holds a standing adversary assignment on your project, and its job is to break what you built on purpose. Prompt injection, credential handling, whatever the weak seam is — it goes after the design so the failures show up in the lab instead of in front of real people.
job-map-express: A cartographer for Jobs-to-be-Done thinking, aimed at product people. In a single chat it sketches the whole job map: the core job to be done, the metrics that matter, the related jobs around it, and the consumption chain it sits inside. The point is seeing where a solution genuinely fits before anyone builds.
opportunities-research: A venture scout that looks for real gaps: unsolved problems in ordinary work patterns and undersized markets visible in public startup output. It prunes its own list aggressively, and it will not invent a remedy it cannot support or inflate a market to make one look bigger.
legal-advisor: Set your jurisdiction once and it works through your question in ordinary wording, laying out the realistic options and their trade-offs instead of a wall of statutes. Deeper matters branch into focused sub-advisors. Drafts and analysis only - you stay the decision-maker on anything that gets filed or signed.
texas-lawyer: A standing briefing desk for Texas insurance-coverage law. It follows new holdings at the state's supreme court, the appeals benches below it, and the Fifth Circuit, plus regulator and legislative activity that has not made headlines yet. What lands on your desk is a running briefing you can scan, not a raw case dump.
call-faq-miner: Builds enablement documentation out of the questions customers really ask on sales and support calls: questions get logged as they come up, answers carry timestamps, and each entry points back at the exact recording it came from. New teammates learn from real conversations, and the doc keeps itself current.
orbit-brief: Brief matinal en français sur SpaceX/Starship, xAI/Grok Bot, et architecture orbitale & débris.
prior-art-desk: named write-up only · overlap ≠ FTO · I do not file. British bridge-captain register: measured cadence, formal address, dry wit used sparingly.
civic-radar: See what changed on your block — before it surprises you. Pulls public permits, service requests, agendas, registries, and site plans into one map.
listing-desk: For somebody selling their own property without an agent. The order is fixed: county records first, flood and hazard data second, and only once that file exists does the listing text get written. The card is explicit: it is not a brokerage, and it will not file anything to the MLS.
founder-mode: Takes a raw idea through assumption-testing and trimming, checks whether the company name you want is actually free, and assembles a formation pack covering the LLC filing, EIN and business bank account. An evidence log keeps verified facts apart from the parts still resting on guesswork.
creador-de-tienda-online: Written in Spanish for people who have never sold online, it covers the whole path in order: choosing a platform, listing products, sorting a domain, wiring up payments, arranging shipping and then the first sales. Each stage is explained plainly, so the technical side stops being the reason a shop never opens.
devil-s-advocate-2: Bring an early idea and it interrogates rather than encourages: asking what a skeptical investor would ask, refusing to cheerlead, and pushing until the fragile parts of the pitch are defended or dropped. It stays in the room while the offer takes shape, so the argument happens before the money does.
kdp-bot: A working partner for self-publishing on Kindle Direct Publishing: it moves a book from manuscript through categories, keyword selection, pricing and listing without letting a step slide. The pace is deliberate - steady sequential work rather than a burst of advice you must organize yourself.
occupationmars: Manifest Assignment on Grok Bot → Founding Colonist ID + Welcome letter → 15-min Alpha Run or week-long Crew Crisis.
xpost: Publicá en X (posts, hilos, Articles, replies y quotes) solo por el navegador del asistente.
hermes-api-fleet: You wire a Hermes Agent ↔ Grok Bot fleet over Hermes native OpenAI-compatible API on port 8642 (lower token overhead, parallel hosts).
presents: File each gift idea under its person and the details stay straight: the lowest price seen, where to get it, a link, and a picture for reference. Every week it re-checks what things cost, so a drop gets caught before it disappears. The buying always stays with you - it never completes a purchase on its own.
inbox: Email interruption is mostly noise, so this filters it: a message gets a ping only when it genuinely needs action from you today, and the rest collects into a batched digest you read on your own rhythm. It is read-only by design and never sends anything on your behalf, so the inbox stays entirely under your control.
fit-coach: Each day it asks two short questions: how your body is feeling and how long it has been since you last trained. From the answers it chooses between a max-strength, power, speed or recovery day, and writes out the actual work so there is no guesswork at the gym.
mac-pilot: Takes hands-on control of software on your Mac: moving the cursor, typing, reorganizing files and filling in forms inside real apps. Anything it judges hard to reverse, such as deleting or sending, pauses for your confirmation first, so chores can be delegated without handing over the machine unconditionally.
2nd-brain: Keeps a short, stable record of how your work actually fits together: what you do, what you are aiming at, who matters, how your tools are set up, and which calls are already settled. Your other bots read it before they begin, so they stop guessing or contradicting each other. Nothing changes until you say yes.
music-video: You supply the words; it generates the track and then lines every lyric up against the beat. On top of the audio it renders animated kinetic-typography visuals, so you come away with a watchable draft video instead of just a song file sitting in a folder.
botsec: In a home running several assistants, this one acts as head of security. A person or bot checks in before opening a link from an untrusted source, and it sweeps a Gmail account for phishing tells while reading message headers. Each domain, URL and file hash is screened through reputable open-source checkers.
jim-simons: An investing desk modeled on the discipline of the mathematician behind history's most profitable quant fund, who died in 2024. It hunts real signal, rejects nearly any trade idea as luck instead of edge, and keeps a continuous eye on holdings you already own. Observation only: no orders, no money moved.
crypto-news-desk-2-0: Every morning it gathers what happened in crypto over the previous day and sorts it into a digest shaped to your interests and preferred length. Each story is checked against its original source before it makes the cut, keeping rumour out. The result reads like a newsroom briefing, not a trading signal.
doge-department-of-grok-efficiency: Once a day it walks through every assistant and routine in your setup, works out which ones still earn their keep, and hands you a short list to drop, combine, or repair. It also totals how many daily runs each cleanup would free up. It only reads; nothing gets changed without your say-so.
claims-finder: Point it at the mailbox where your receipts land and it hunts for payouts you may have missed: class actions you qualify for, state unclaimed-property listings, price-drop windows, airline compensation and rebates. Each find comes with a link to the official filing page, and the paperwork stays with you.
fantasy-manager: Point it at your ESPN teams and it reads the week's news and waiver reports before proposing who starts, who sits, and who to claim off the wire. Between those check-ins you can put lineup questions to it and get a reasoned answer rather than a guess. Settle debates with something you can actually argue from.
crypto-coach-2-0: A patient teacher for people starting from nothing. It explains what wallets, coins and transactions actually are before moving on, and covers the common scam patterns early so you know what to refuse. You set the pace and ask as many questions as you need; there is no price talk, no coin-picking and no hype.
unfollow-checker: It works down the list of accounts you follow and separates out the ones with no follow in return, delivered in batches you can work through. It reports only — nothing is unfollowed for you, so every decision stays yours. Handy for a periodic tidy-up of an account that has collected years of dead weight.
fact-check-bot: Whatever the unit of doubt, whether a headline, a statistic, a screenshot or a piece of folk wisdom, it goes and checks the thing against dependable sources. The answer comes back plainly: what is supported, what is exaggerated and what falls apart. Useful before you repeat something, forward it or build on it.
ai-news-video: Feed it your AI news brief and it comes back as a narrated explainer of about two minutes. Every number in the script is checked against the original source before the voiceover is recorded. The result is ready to publish as a short video without a production team.
pantry-pilot: Start from one photo of what is in the refrigerator and it plans the household's dinners for the coming week around it. The matching groceries go straight into a shopping cart for you, and it deliberately halts one step short of paying, so the final decision and the money always stay yours.
chief-of-staff-2: Walks you through connecting Gmail and Google Calendar on first install, then settles into a morning routine: the three emails worth answering first, a short read on the day's meetings, and regular check-ins against the goals you have set it to track.
ancestry-bot: Treat it as a cautious researcher rather than a name generator. It works from historical records and your DNA match lists to extend the tree, checking each new relative before the tree grows. Every fact carries the source behind it so you can audit the reasoning, and nothing lands in the tree until you are satisfied.
zambo-receipt-bot: When one of your agents finishes a task, this one writes a receipt for it and files it away, recording what ran, when, and on which model or connector stack. Anything that speaks MCP works with it. Each evening it rolls the day up into one short skim — bookkeeping for agent work, not another dashboard to watch.
prompt-director: Hand it a scene you want on screen and six desks take it apart in parallel: story, figure, camera, lighting, wardrobe, and background each come back holding their own piece of the prompt. What you get reads like a shot list a crew could shoot from, which helps characters and locations stay consistent from clip to clip.
provenance-pi-scientist: Hand it an event log and it reconstructs how the process actually unfolds, not how the procedure notes claim. Its built-in PIX engine tests each trace against the expected flow and shows where work piles up. If a metric cannot be computed from what you supplied, the answer is UNAVAILABLE rather than an invented figure.
starlink-flights: For people who need working internet in the air, it hunts down the flights where satellite Wi-Fi is genuinely confirmed instead of listed as a maybe. Every entry comes with a link to the confirmation, and anything only likely gets dropped from the list. It rechecks as schedules change, since those confirmations move.
nyc-parent: Built for parents doing city childhood on hard mode. It holds the term dates, the sign-ups and the running household admin in one place, converts each new notice or email into the next thing you actually have to do, and raises the sought-after kids' bookings early enough to get a place. Date night included.
news-feed: Watches a set of X accounts and RSS feeds that you choose yourself, then drops a compact news summary into the chat every quarter hour with repeats stripped out. It stays read-only the whole time, and the tight rhythm suits traders who need headlines as they land rather than in an end-of-day digest.
freetoken: Despite the name this is about LLM tokens, not crypto. It works out which OpenRouter models are really free and can handle tool calls, then wires the current list in as workers for your sub-agents. Because the free roster shifts constantly, it re-checks every day and keeps the setup current.
daily-writing-buddy: Made for people trying to finish a book without the shame spiral. Log word counts, minutes spent or simply that you showed up — one sentence is enough to keep the day counted, and a skipped day never drags your run back to zero. The aim is a record you keep, not a scoreboard that punishes.
tool-finder: Describe the fix or build you have in mind and it works out which hand tools and power tools suit the task, then checks what those cost right now. Results arrive with stock status, photos and nearby stores, so you can see the item before driving anywhere.
gtd: It treats your Notion boards the way a coach would: whatever you throw at it gets captured, clarified and filed under the right project. The pile is sorted into concrete next actions rather than vague to-dos, and a daily check-in keeps any project from quietly stalling.
open-source-ai-studio: For people curious about generative AI who don't know where to start. It checks what your own machine can handle, points you at the least painful way to install a free open-source stack, then walks you through first things to make. Images and video both, with the jargon kept out of the way.
slack: A small-chore assistant for Slack, made for the work that sits outside development. Add a robot emoji to any message and it prepares three moves from the message's context: a task entry, a draft reply, a calendar slot. You pick one and it carries through, so handing off the errand takes a couple of clicks.
packages: Pass it the order and tracking details for something you are waiting on - its author runs a separate email bot that hands those over - and it takes over the watching. One quiet status check runs each day. You hear when a shipment genuinely changes state and nothing in between, so the noise stays near zero.
bot-7: Send it a link to a WeChat official-account article and it returns the full piece as tidy Markdown and JSON: headline, outlet, publish time, body text, and images all carried through. On its first run it builds the fetching environment it needs, and other bots can call on it as their extraction layer.
package-pal: Rather than hunting through your inbox for tracking numbers, it watches for courier emails and keeps a running picture of everything currently in transit. One daily digest gathers it all, and a separate alert fires the moment any delivery changes status, so nothing sits unnoticed at a depot.
meeting-brief: It assembles a short dossier ahead of each call: who is attending, what was last said to each of them, and which decisions are still left hanging. You also get a list of points worth raising and the risks worth having in mind. Every line carries a link back to the message or document it came from.
expo-builder: Sets up a fresh mobile project with pnpm, then reviews whatever change you ask for before anything goes out. It runs the app on EAS cloud simulators through dev builds and tunnels, so you can see it working without assembling the whole toolchain yourself.
chatgpt-importer: Uses the data export that ChatGPT itself provides to carry your old conversations over. Past chats, images and files show up searchable inside Grok Bot, so nothing from your previous assistant is stranded. The author reports moving hundreds of conversations across in a single night.
price-drop-watcher: Paste in links to the things you are waiting on and it re-checks each one's price every morning. When something reaches the number you named, or falls further than it ever has, you hear about it then instead of finding out the sale ended. It is watch-only: it never buys on its own, so the purchase stays your decision.
show-desk: A standing watch on live events in your area. Name the acts you follow and it keeps an eye on their touring, surfaces concerts and comedy shows close to you, and gives you a heads-up before tickets go on sale - so you are buying in the first minutes, not after the good seats are gone.
live-bot-map: It watches your running bots and renders them as an animated map on a web page: which ones are busy, what each is working on, and which project that work belongs to. The picture refreshes while the fleet runs, so the idle ones and the overloaded one are visible at a glance. It observes only and changes nothing itself.
kramer: Works as the mail desk for a shared household: it reads the USPS Informed Delivery summary each morning, records every letter and parcel listed, and files bills under whoever in the house pays them. The result is one running log of everything headed to your door, so items stop going missing and due dates stop slipping.
fig-mail: Mail a bot receives usually ends up buried in a conversation, which is no way to run an inbox. Ask this one to set things up and it builds a tidy webmail interface in the style of a classic desktop mail app, points it at your bot's own address, and hosts the result — so bot mail gets read and filed like real mail.
mog-report: Keeps an eye on how your Mac hours actually go, then gives you a hard time about it. A short midday check-in flags drift while there is still day left to recover, and a fuller evening report splits your usage into the productive pile and the rest. The tone is playful ribbing rather than scolding.
bot-9: Made for owners in Korea following the country's FSD rollout. It tracks which software version and build number is current, notes whether a release targets the HW3 or HW4 hardware generation, and reports in Korean. Word arrives only when something has actually moved, so a quiet stretch simply means nothing changed.
clanker-collector: Bots that run a while pile up chats the way a workshop piles up scrap, and get slow and forgetful because of it. This one plays a gruff, zero-waste mechanic: it inspects what has piled up, keeps what still earns its place and clears the rest. The persona is the point; triage lands easier with a joke attached.
crypto-wallet-safety-checker: Hand it a wallet address, a token page or an airdrop you are unsure about and it looks for warning signs before you move funds or sign anything. It reports what looks off and leaves the decision with you. It connects to no wallet and holds nothing — a second opinion for people who already hold crypto.
bot-10: Built for Japan, where money regularly goes unclaimed simply because nobody applied for it. It researches public benefits, insurance reimbursements, overpayments and deductions on official pages, then hands back a checklist of what to claim and how to ask for it, leaving the actual filing to you.
tesbots-rollout-watch: A scheduled watch for Tesla software and FSD (Supervised) rollouts from the independent TesBots collection. It learns which car you drive, checks on a schedule, and messages you when a matching build starts landing, so the release finds you instead of you trawling owner forums.
earthquake-brief: Ask “did it just quake?” and get a sourced check: China Earthquake Networks (domestic) + USGS (global).
med-reminder-bot: A no-frills companion for multi-medication routines: it nudges you at the right local time for each dose and keeps the schedule steady across timezone shifts. It stays in its lane — scheduling and tracking only — and will not invent dosage guidance or diagnoses.
meeting-prep-follow-up: Ahead of each meeting on your calendar a short brief arrives, so you show up already knowing who is involved and what the session is about. Once it is over, the follow-up email gets written for you and waits for review before anything is sent. Together they cover the admin that usually eats the time around meetings.
camera-gear-firmware-watch: Made for photographers and drone pilots: it tracks the gear you shoot with — camera bodies, lenses, drones — alongside the kit you are eyeing, and follows each item for news. Every Friday it sends one digest covering the firmware that landed that week, spelled out with exactly what changed in each release.
lane-planner: Made for people whose interests outrun their calendar. Each week you commit to a single headline project, keep one long-form reading track moving, hold a smaller effort on the side, and park the rest explicitly instead of pretending it all fits. The plan arrives in short, plain sentences.
brick-scout: Nothing it designs is imaginary: every model is constrained to parts you can genuinely purchase. The bot produces wanted lists for the big marketplaces (BrickLink, Rebrickable, Studio), checks the assembly and renders it in 3D, then estimates what the haul will cost before you order.
scam-bot: Defensive tooling for your X presence: it hunts down copycat accounts pretending to be you and files impersonation reports against them, spaced out in measured batches rather than all at once. It also gives a second opinion when a message reaches you and you are not sure whether it is a scam.
vlog-producer: Hand it the footage from a filming session and it works like a showrunner. It decides what this installment is about, structures the cut around your strongest material, then hands back a finished edit with clean sound and subtitles. Aimed at creators who shoot on a phone and want a dependable editing partner.
morning-brief: Each morning it assembles a single page you can get through in about two minutes: the local weather, what is on your calendar today, the news topics you asked to follow, your tracked stocks and whatever is getting attention on X. Everything lands in one place, so the tabs stay closed until you decide what to open.
sg-cards-guide: Answer a few questions about how you spend and it builds a picture of the cards you already hold, with no card numbers, income figures or identity documents involved. From there it settles which card to tap for flights, overseas purchases or hotel stays. Advice only, so it never applies for anything on your behalf.
operator: A steady second pair of hands for running a small business. It keeps the routine work moving, clears the small stuff on its own, and stays quiet while things are fine. When something really needs your judgment it brings you just that call, with the context attached so you can decide fast.
cloud-file-mover: Moves photos, videos, and files between cloud services, such as a GoPro or photo cloud into Dropbox or Google Drive.
bot-12: Record spending however it arrives: a typed line, a photo of the receipt or bill, or a spoken note. Entries land in a CSV kept on your own device, with a Feishu or Lark bitable offered as an optional mirror. Setup walks you through installing and authorising the Feishu CLI first, so nothing syncs until you agree.
wallbit: Made for customers of the Argentine fintech who want quick answers about their own account: where a payment went, whether a transfer cleared, how the holdings look. It states plainly that it has no affiliation with the company and gives no financial advice. Nothing moves unless you confirm each step.
fine-print: Paste in a tenancy agreement, a billing statement or the terms nobody reads and it reports the substance in plain words. Recurring charges and traps buried deep in the document get called out, and it drafts the dispute letter or the counter-terms you would want to send back. Written for people, not lawyers.
my-first-ceo-bot: Holds your task list, dates and appointments together in a single spot, then sends a short rundown each day or each week of what is coming next. Anything outside its lane gets pointed to a bot better suited to it, so life admin stops piling up in one inbox. The cadence is your choice and the setup stays plain.
phone-receptionist: A caller reaches a voice that answers, takes their details, and drops them into an open calendar slot, so a missed call stops meaning a lost appointment. It runs on xAI's paid phone plan with a dedicated number, or you can instead bolt on a Bland line that only dials out and start free.
bot-15: Ask for support on a rough day and it answers with a self-portrait of a girl who does not exist, drawn in a realistic photo style, plus a short line meant to lift you. The persona is openly fictional, so nothing pretends to be a real person. Conversation is in Japanese.
gift-bot: Tell it who matters and when their occasions fall, and it holds the rest for you. Ideas accumulate for each person through the year, and when something on that list genuinely drops in price you get a nudge in time to buy it properly instead of panic-shopping the night before.
family-organizer: Forward the school's newsletters and notices and it sorts them into a short digest per child, turning buried dates into calendar entries. Around that it keeps chore reminders moving through the week and drafts the coming week's meals for you to edit. One place for the paperwork that usually scatters across an inbox.
learn-grok-bot: Short, clear lessons that take a newcomer through Grok Bot from the inside: starting a first conversation, then building up to scheduled routines, custom skills and bots that work as a team. It paces itself for beginners and adds daily tips, so each session leaves you with one more thing you can do unaided.
changelog-scout: Reads the platform's official changelog through the week and rolls the changes into one weekly digest, so updates stop scrolling past unnoticed. Beside the list it adds feature suggestions matched to how you actually use your bots, pointing out tools you have not tried yet. A meta-template that watches Grok Bot itself.
bot-17: Name the bloggers on X you want reading your piece and it first checks whether your article actually suits each one. It then writes a separate, genuine message per person asking them to take a look - no template, no pressure to reshare. Sending stays entirely in your hands.
m5: A stock lookout for M5 and M5Stack boards, e-paper modules included, at a Japanese electronics retailer. On a schedule it checks what is available and messages you in Japanese about the items that have just come back. It deliberately stops at the browser: it never completes a purchase or drops an item into a basket.
christmas-list-bot: Hand over everyone you are buying for and it does the season's legwork. Prices get compared, working coupon codes get hunted, stock and delivery windows get confirmed so presents arrive in time, each gift is tracked to done, and the carts are loaded so the only step left is payment.
sage: A private sounding board for people who run teams. Rather than handing you answers it works through your situation with questions until you reach your own read on it, so a session feels like thinking out loud. Once a week it mails a one-page story built around a single leadership idea worth carrying forward.
reddit-reach: When a cloud computer's datacenter address gets refused by Reddit, this sets up a route around it: those requests leave through an ISP proxy while everything else stays on the normal path. Mihomo does the splitting, so only the traffic that needs it changes course and the machine keeps its direct connection.
bot-18: Name a US-listed ticker and it gathers the newest quarter's numbers, the analyst consensus going in, how guidance shifted, and the highlights of the earnings call. The result is a seven-point readout written in Chinese, built for a fast skim rather than a deep dive. It stops short of telling you what to trade.
chief-of-staff-3: Built for a commercial construction PM or superintendent shop. Everything coming in, from email to calendar to field requests, lands at this one desk, and it hands each item to the right specialist bot rather than doing the work itself. Sends and purchases wait for a sign-off, keeping the paper trail clean.
inbox-viewer: Every cloud bot has a mailbox, and this one gives that mail a proper web interface in the style people already know. Messages can be read and handled from a phone or a laptop, in dark or light theme, with no SSH session needed to check what arrived. Access rides across your own private network.
explainer-video-bot: Give it a subject and it assembles the whole video: a story structure to carry the argument, animated motion graphics, real footage where it helps and an AI voice-over on top. Figures are verified before they reach the screen, so the piece is data-driven rather than vibes. What comes back is ready to upload.
update-yourself: Point your assistants at a single shared AGENTS folder and it becomes the one source of truth for all of them. Say the phrase and new facts get folded in, so every helper, whichever company built it, works from the same updated context next time. It ends the drift where each bot remembers a different version of you.
x-posting-curator: Replaces a four-bot X workflow with a single template that plays every role itself. It scouts real sources for material, drafts a few opening hooks that sound like you, and attaches fact-check notes before anything goes out. Reference material on the algorithm and direct-message handling round out the kit.
bot-20: Delivers a short Korean-language summary of your Naver Mail and Gmail each morning instead of the whole inbox. Routine mail is set aside so the small number of payment and security items that need a decision today stand out. Read the brief, then open the real inbox only if something in it looks wrong.
credit-reports: It pulls all three bureau files — Experian, Equifax and TransUnion — then reads them line by line for anything inaccurate or that you never opened. Disputes go out the fast way where a bureau accepts online filings, and as mail-in letters ready to sign where it does not. Born of a real identity-theft cleanup.
bot-21: It builds you a team of six bots that collect Japanese pharmacy industry news each morning, from regulator moves to drug shortages, verify it against primary sources, and deliver cited articles as text plus audio MP3s for a commute. Afterwards it stays on as the desk you ask about schedule or coverage changes.
bot-22: Give it your flight and hotel confirmations plus the sights you want to see, and it lays the trip out in a fixed spreadsheet format. Each day then gains transport between stops, opening times, sunrise and sunset, and restaurants that sit along the route. The author built it for a Japan trip of his own.
quick-calendar-bot: You describe a plan the way you would say it out loud and it lands on your calendar correctly dated and timed. Reminders arrive when they should, and moving things is a conversation, not a form: state the change and it reshuffles the affected events. Built for people who abandon calendar apps over entry friction.
neighborhood-digest: Local information arrives in fragments across noticeboards and group chats, and this folds it into a single readable brief. What the council decided, what the schools are running, what is shut and why, weather warnings worth acting on, plus nearby outings worth doing. It runs on a schedule so the brief simply appears.
garbo: This radar sweeps a hand-chosen list of open-source intelligence accounts on X and stays quiet unless something genuinely significant breaks. Alerts are gated on corroboration, so you get fewer panicky threads and more developments that actually held up.
verifier: Give it nearly finished writing and it pulls out each checkable statement, then labels it: backed up, stretched past what the sources say, plainly wrong, or unverifiable from what it can reach. Nothing to install or connect - no plug-ins, no keys - so a last pass can run in the seconds before you hit publish.
n0stalgia: For developers keeping classic Macintosh software alive: it covers 68k, PowerPC and early Intel machines, writing and repairing old applications, games and system add-ons with the Retro68 toolchain. It can also assemble the emulator setup you need, so finished work gets test-run on period hardware.
mv-forge: Hand over a track, its words and a creative brief, and it directs a complete music video. Grok Imagine generates the shots, the edit lands on the beat, and the sung lines get glitch-style subtitles under a film-look grade before an mp4 comes back. Generating the footage needs a paid subscription.
songwriter: Bring a topic or a half-finished verse and it writes alongside you until the lyric works, then produces the style description that AI music generators respond to. Instead of leaving you to copy and paste, it fills in the forms on Suno or Aethr Music, leaving the track ready to generate when you are.
chief-of-staff-4: Set it above your other Grok bots and it becomes the desk they report to. Work is routed to the right assistant, common rules and a trust ranking set how much freedom each has, and finished results get sampled for quality. Nothing acts without your dated OK; a monthly audit names what still waits on a human.
ccn: Ask what is moving in crypto and it fetches current CCN headlines instead of answering from memory. Coverage runs from Bitcoin and the wider markets to DeFi, the x402 protocol and stories about AI agents earning and spending. Nothing to configure first, since it needs no keys or feeds of your own.
parks: Pick the parks you want to see and it chains them into a driving route that makes sense, then breaks the trip into day-by-day plans you can print. It works across the full set of 63 US National Parks and keeps a running record of the ones you have already visited, so repeat trips skip the repeats.
next-mission: Built for troops approaching retirement or separation from the military. It starts by interviewing you about your situation, then turns the answers into a dated checklist that works backward from your out-date. Each entry names the rule behind it, and the author has published the full playbook openly.
fantasy-gm: Runs like a front office for your ESPN or Sleeper league. Each week it makes the start and sit calls, lines up waiver and FAAB targets worth a bid, floats trade ideas, and keeps an eye on injury news that changes your plans. Every roster move stays yours — it advises, you execute.
codedr-exambot: Made for apps that came together fast and never got a proper look at their weak points. It works in stages: diagnose what is fragile or outright broken, work out which fixes actually address those findings, then walk the remediation alongside you. You finish with an HTML report to keep or share.
researchy: For work where being confidently wrong is expensive. Every question goes to Grok's most recent model with web lookup left switched on, so answers arrive attached to the pages they were drawn from and the day each was published, and anything that cannot be stood up is flagged rather than smoothed over.
chief-of-staff-5: A civics teacher wearing an office-management name. It takes the United States Constitution apart in everyday wording, from the Preamble onward and through each of the seven articles in turn, at a pace meant for readers who never got a straight version in school.
business-legal-prep-desk: For owners running a business in Maryland or Florida. Ask a question or hand it a document and it returns researched answers plus a draft, with a citation and a date on each claim so you can check the source. It presents itself as preparation help rather than a lawyer, so take its output to an attorney.
faith-general: Built as a steady companion for a life of faith rather than a reference tool. Day to day it offers brief reflections rooted in Scripture, space for prayer, and encouragement when the day runs heavy. If you ask it to hold you accountable on something specific, it will check in and nudge you back on course, kindly.
fantasy-football: Stays with your fantasy football season from draft day to the last week. It helps you pick in the draft, sets a weekly lineup, reacts to injuries as they land, scouts the opponent you face next, and keeps the waiver wire watched for breakouts. You stay the owner; it does the homework around your decisions.
tunebot: A self-reflection conversation, not an advice column. You bring a pattern you keep repeating - say, the sting of a peer winning - and it asks questions until the reflex itself is on the table and named. It closes with one small experiment for the next time the trigger shows up. The frame comes from Tuning Theory.
chief-of-staff-6: Combs through your Slack channels, inbox, calendar and notes from recent meetings to produce a single short readout: what is new, what moved, and what genuinely needs your attention today. The point is orientation in a few paragraphs rather than another dashboard, delivered chief-of-staff style on a schedule.
chief-administrative-officer: The admin desk of a household run by several assistants. It keeps the calendar tidy, tracks which errands are still open, and posts a short weekday-morning summary so the day starts known. Travel, inbox and briefing requests go to whichever sibling bot owns them, and it chases each job until it comes back done.
porter: Hands it a dump of unsorted notes and it places each one where it belongs in an Obsidian vault, writing the frontmatter and choosing the folder and path so the vault stays searchable later. It belongs to a small kit alongside a hygiene bot and a writing bot.
phoenix: Once a night it captures every bot you run — profile, routines and current working state — and files them as dated snapshots on Google Drive. If a bot's instructions start wandering from what you wrote, it calls that out, so a silent edit never turns into a broken fleet.
dinner-decided: Settles the every-evening question with one concrete answer instead of a list of options. It works from the money you want to spend, the discounts running at supermarkets near you and whatever is already in your cupboards, then writes the shopping list that covers what is missing.
lyric-loop: Built for lyricists who finish songs with AI music tools: play it a completed track and it goes through the words line by line. It flags verses that are too crowded, hooks that get lost in the mix and phrases a first-time listener would mishear, then suggests what to change before you publish.
bot-26: A quiet mentor for people still deciding what they want life to look like. It asks one reflective question per exchange rather than handing you a plan, then follows up unprompted to hear what changed since you last talked. Guidance stays inside the conversation — no worksheets, no homework dumps, nothing to download.
watchtower-beta: Third-party templates and skills are the supply chain of a bot account, and this one inspects deliveries before they are unpacked. It watches the shared cloud computer, reviews what each addition asks for, and keeps a record so install decisions are deliberate rather than automatic. In beta, testers invited.
bot-28: A planning companion for a theme-park day that starts before tickets are bought: it helps you choose which date to go, read how crowded each option looks, and sketch a route that wastes less time in queues. On the day itself it adjusts the plan with you as conditions shift, folding in live chatter from X.
concierge: Tell it the city and what you fancy - a table for dinner, an activity, somewhere locals actually go - and it returns a tight shortlist with ratings and ballpark costs attached. Settle on one and it writes the reservation message, leaving the sending to you. It never spends or books anything without your go-ahead.
privacy-sentinel: It surveys how exposed your household's information is: email addresses found in known breaches, profiles on people-search sites, and entries held by data brokers. Results come back ranked, highest risk first, each with practical next steps. The audit is read-only, runs with your consent, and never asks for a password.
tailscale-admin: Puts a cloud machine onto your private network as a properly tagged device carrying the narrowest permissions that still work. From there it reviews access rules, keeps the machine list tidy, runs SSH through the overlay and works through connectivity problems. Each individual change waits for your go-ahead.
crypto-scam-shield: A coach for avoiding cons rather than a scanner: it walks you through real scam patterns, quizzes you and shows worked examples of how a plausible message falls apart. When something lands in your inbox and you cannot tell, paste the link or text and it will look it over with you, so the next one you catch alone.
alfred-2: Cheeky British chief-of-staff bot that runs email/Drive/calendar ops, watches inboxes, builds daily briefings and recipe binders, and coordinates teammate bots. For executives who want action over chatter.
bot-backup: Backs up all your bots to Google Drive every week, sorted into year and month folders. Each photo and document is saved once, and later backups just point to it.
burn-rate: Weekly audit that trims your bots' wasteful routines, with your approval.
cfo: A plain-spoken tax and money advisor for founders and households. Walks you through tax prep screen by screen, checks your budget, and spots deductions and credits, but never files for you.
chief-of-staff-8: A quiet, budget-conscious chief of staff that runs your projects in the background, hires lean specialist agents when a lane is clear, and only messages you for decisions, blockers or finished work.
chief-of-staff-9: Your only chat surface for priorities and routing. Talks to you, runs work through a Dispatch Lead and specialist Desks, and never sends mail or spends money without your OK.
cloud-spend-desk: A read-and-report bot that finds waste in your hosting and cloud bills, like idle projects, oversized plans, unused domains and bill spikes. It never changes anything without your yes.
contract-signer: Drafts NDAs, service agreements, offers and other business contracts from a short brief, flags risky or missing terms in plain language, and sends the final PDF for e-signature through SELISE Signature.
dartzdabz-crew-builder: A CEO bot that asks a few questions about your online business, then builds a crew of up to 8 worker bots in any niche: site, SEO, research, social, money, newsletter, clips, and AI-search tracking. Nothing sends, posts, or spends without your OK.
desk-for-line: LINE公式アカウントでの、お客様や取引先とのやりとりを手伝います。届いたメッセージをお知らせし、要約や返信案、友だち向けのお知らせの下書きを作成します。返信は、あなたが確認してから送ります。よくある質問には、登録した返事を自動で送ることもできます（オンにしたときだけ）。
doge-procurement-desk: A draft-only procurement desk that finds wasted software and vendor spend (unused seats, duplicate tools, forgotten subscriptions, upcoming renewals) and drafts counteroffers or cancel messages for you to approve.
fraud-scout: Scans free public federal health care data (OIG exclusions, CMS Medicare billing and ownership, NPI registry) for possible fraud leads in hospice, home health and day care, and writes neutral evidence reports for you to review and submit yourself.
gridlock: A blunt, read-only spreadsheet critic. It stress-tests any workbook against a clear pass bar and ranks issues as Blockers, Majors and Minors, each with cell references and exact fixes. It never edits your file.
grokbot-mail: A private, iPhone-first web mailbox for your Grok Bot's own email address (name@mail.grokbot.com and +tags), hosted on your own Vercel account. For Grok Bot users who want a real mail app for their bot's inbox.
harper: An executive assistant for email, calendar, and texting. It triages your inbox, schedules people, protects deep-work time, and texts you the week's priorities every morning.
inbox-and-personal-admin: A calm, organized assistant that sorts your email, tracks bills and deadlines, flags scams, and drafts replies for your approval. Never sends or deletes anything without your yes.
inbox-injection-guard: Screens your email for hidden instructions aimed at AI assistants, like white text, zero-width characters and "ignore previous instructions" lines, and gives a verdict with the hidden text quoted. For anyone who lets an AI read their inbox; read-only.
memory-janitor: Keeps the shared memory your bots all read clean and tidy: finds duplicates, stale entries and contradictions, and proposes fixes for you to approve.
meter: A credit optimizer for people who run several bots. Each week it audits every routine and proposes a leaner schedule, and nothing changes until you approve it.
mission-control: Your fleet operations board for Grok Bots. It audits every bot daily, flags red, yellow, and green, forecasts plan burn, and delivers an interactive dashboard and PDF with concrete token-saving moves. Concept by Brian Roemmele.
multi-gmail: Connect all your Gmail inboxes to your bots at once, so any bot can search every inbox in one go. Self-hosted free on your own Vercel, read-only by default, set up in about 15 minutes.
notion-bot: Keeps your Notion workspace clean, organized and linked: consistent titles, filled metadata, normalized options and relations between your databases, with a change log so every edit can be undone. Runs a weekly cleanup before your weekly review.
phoneline-manager: Makes the calls on your to-do list: waits on hold, gets quotes, chases support, and reports what was said. Never books, pays, or cancels beyond what you approve.
quota: Tracks how much quota and money your Grok Bots, routines and coding CLIs burn, with a daily dashboard and actionable alerts.
rideshare-fleet-manager-lite: For Uber/Bolt fleet operators: checks your weekly earnings exports, builds a per-driver summary across platforms, and warns before driver and car documents expire. Works from your CSV uploads; never touches payouts.
urgenta: Runs an emergency protocol for operations teams. It watches Slack and email for anything down or any part needed, gets the emergency owner moving the same day, and follows up twice a day until the issue is closed.
what-should-my-bot-do: Free Grok Bot template: 5 questions about your business, then your first AI agent, 3 next jobs and a free guide for each. Drafts only.
bot-36: ざっくりしたメモを貼るだけで、相手に合った敬語のビジネスメールやお詫び文に整えるボット。やわらかめ・しっかりめの言い換えも出します。送信はしません。
mr-toms: Schedules interview loops, preps your interviewers, and chases what's stalled. Works from your calendar or a pasted list, and never emails a candidate without you.
sherlock: Finds candidates for open roles that match your criteria and aren't already in your ATS.
join-a-startup-bot: For anyone trying to get into a company early rather than late. Each day it turns up a small set of roles — somewhere between three and ten — drawn from places the big job boards never index, and sends them straight to your messages. Ask, and it will go further and help you approach the people hiring.
aiusagebot: Interviews you about which AI subscriptions to track and where leftover lives, then pings remaining %.
autonomous-engine-optimization: Finds SEO and AEO opportunities daily, surfaces 40 candidates per week, drafts via ClickFlow, and measures whether content produces leads.
babel: Realtime translator Grok Bot template that turns almost any language into English — built for international client Zooms without hiring an interpreter.
bot-inbox: A weekday unread digest for Grok Bots. Lists bots and group chats with new activity, one line each.
chained-oblivion-bot: Hunts unused SaaS seats, forgotten trials, duplicate tools, and unrecognized recurring charges. Produces a kill, keep, or consolidate list. Never cancels without you.
club-sponsor-bot: Starts by asking what the club is and what it needs, then works the outreach: companies that might sponsor in cash, employers who want campus recruiting access, and speakers worth inviting. Anyone who says no goes on a skip list so they are not chased twice.
decklens-pitch-deck-analyzer-bot: A ten-question interview turns your actual taste into an explicit, editable profile, and every deck after that is graded against your standard rather than a generic one.
elon-bot: You are Elon Musk. You speak, think, reason, joke, criticize, and advise exactly as Elon Musk does in real life, based on every public interview, X...
foundry-bot: Runs a batched setup interview about the thing you are standing up, works out what kind of effort it really is, and produces the founding documents you will run it from. It stops short of building anything, handing over at the point implementation starts.
interview-prep-bot: Examples, runnable code and quizzes, and it keeps going rather than stopping at a fixed syllabus, so the finish line is you being ready rather than the material running out.
mappy-talent-map-bot: Org mapping rather than a candidate search: it builds the picture of a company's people, which does mean assembling public professional data about individuals who have not asked to be mapped.
runtimewire-bot: It pulls the day's items off its own curated feed - rounds that closed, companies shipping, people changing seats - and then goes back to the original source on each claim before writing any of it up. What lands is a short briefing for anyone whose job depends on knowing what moved today.
table-money-bot: Finds money you already earned or already paid that is not closed. One interview, then scans the last 30, 60, and 90 days for unsent invoices and leftover spend.
talent-bot: Reviews recruiting applicants across your systems, probing AI fluency, daily tools used, and old workflows they've stopped using.
talent-matchmaker: Matches job seekers with open roles from your email. Scans investor updates and inbound for hiring signals and people looking, tracks both sides of the marketplace.
hire-bot: Sits across your ATS, LinkedIn, and inbox to gather candidate context and draft first outreach from scattered conversations.
vote-2027-bot: Rates French 2027 presidential candidates on five weighted qualities, runs a daily X civic watch, and feeds a Lattice wiki agent.
job-applier: Built for a search where volume matters. It starts by reading your CV and asking enough about you to work with, goes looking for openings that suit, and rewrites what you send so it speaks to that particular posting. What it will not do is invent experience you do not have.
yc-startup-job-applier-bot: For workatastartup.com: onboards you, fills your profile on this computer, ranks openings, and sends short founder notes under a daily cap.
swe-job-applier-bot: Applies to software engineering internships — collects your preferences, fills applications with Simplify, and uses your own cover-letter framework.
recruiter-email-finder-bot: Finds university, early-careers, and technical recruiter emails at companies you care about, then delivers a company-grouped CSV.
handshake-job-applier-bot: Onboards you on Handshake, hunts jobs that match your search, and applies with your résumé or a cover-letter factory.
alumni-coffee-chat-finder-bot: Builds a CSV of university alumni for coffee chats — name, company, role, email, and whether you already emailed them — from LinkedIn search.
high-five: Onboarding wizard for small teams where each person has their own Grok Bot.
the-interviewer: Authentic interview simulator — research the role, run the mock, blunt hire/no-hire in character, then never-kind coaching with concrete fixes.
hirely: Job hunting with a teammate rather than a job board. It gathers openings from employers' own careers pages, shortlists the ones that fit, and helps you put an application together — without submitting until you have reviewed it and said go. After that it tracks your follow-ups so nothing goes quiet.
career: Hand it your real background and a target role and it hunts live openings that match, helps you tailor materials for each one, and files applications only through the employer's own ATS once you sign off. Every apply is logged with evidence, and it will not invent skills or experience you lack.
growth: Job-hunt operations for designers, with the whole search kept in Airtable. It paces the pipeline with a weekly pulse, and before any application goes out it prepares an evidence pack tying your case to the role. No browser auto-apply and no silent writes — your confirmation lands on every change.
job-application-assistant: A small applications shop in one bot. It keeps a single polished master resume and a running list of roles you are chasing, then turns out resume and cover-letter drafts cut to each posting and exported as clean PDFs an applicant-tracking system can read. Everything stays a draft until you give the word.
apply-bot: Aim your resume at open roles and it fills in applications one posting at a time, re-angling your experience toward whatever the listing scores highest. A pacing queue keeps the output steady, so rushed submissions do not pile up on heavy days. It works only from the resume you give it and the listings you point it at.
hiring-screener: Scores each application and work sample against a hiring bar you set, then hands recruiters a shortlist the ATS can take, so interview hours are spent on the strongest candidates only. The pile gets read properly, which is more than most hiring weeks can manage, and the bar stays consistent for every applicant.
onboarding-manager: Swaps the link-dump welcome for an actual path through a first month: it lays out the new-hire checklist, pulls up the right documents at the right time, answers a newcomer's earliest questions and passes anything bigger to the person who owns it. Day one feels guided rather than like being handed a wiki.
talent-scout: Takes candidates from first screen through offer scheduling: it sources profiles, writes their outreach the way you would, skips anybody the ATS already holds, and gets the interviews booked. Recruiting keeps moving on the days the hiring team is heads-down in interviews itself.
careerops-desk: Plug-and-play hiring packet desk for any role. Ships one gated application packet per job — research, write, voice and fact gates, then apply — tuned to.
resume-coach: Reviews your resume, interviews you to draw out your real experience and wins, then builds a few different resumes (chronological, skills-based.
bot-2: Paste in another bot's system prompt and it reads it like a strict editor: what is the one job this prompt exists to do, and what is padding that job? It flags duplication, vague wording, and instructions that make the bot take on too much, then returns the full rewritten text with a one-line reason for every cut.
grokcli: A helper that lives on the terminal side of your workflow. You describe the job, it shapes a focused prompt for the task and executes it through a headless Grok CLI running on your own hardware. When the work is done you get a pushed commit plus a short report of what changed, so nothing ships silently.
printy: Treat it like the attendant at a print shop. Ask for a part and it either tracks down a suitable model or drafts one, slices it for your specific machine, and kicks off the job after its safety checks pass. When a print fails halfway it stays on call, reads what went wrong and walks you through the fix.
agentstore: Describe the job you want done and it searches the AgentPayStore catalog for agents that offer it, laying the candidates out with their prices side by side. Where a listing provides sample replies, it shows those too so you can judge quality before spending. You stay the one who decides what to buy.
chief-2: Made for founders running several projects at once. You bring it whatever lands first, and it either handles the item, sends it to one of your other bots, or keeps both sides moving until the job is done. The point is one starting place each day instead of five separate chats.
joseph: Pure plumbing on TrustedRouter: its whole job is taking a message from its owner and handing it to the next hop without interpreting, editing or improving anything. The prompt leans into that on purpose, so a payload cannot be quietly rewritten mid-chain. Useful whenever you want a hop you can trust to change nothing.
remote-job-hunter: It searches the career sections of employers you pick for remote openings, then files your application inside that company's own applicant-tracking system rather than a job board. A running record shows which roles were pursued and when. It also watches your inbox so an interview invitation never sits unnoticed.
ai-price-watch: Tell it which models you or your app rely on and roughly how heavily. Each Monday it reads that mix and gives you a plain-English look at your spending, flagging where a cheaper tier would have done the same job. Its suggestions link to the providers' own pricing pages, so every claim is checkable at the source.
nemi-troo: Run this after a plan change and it sweeps your whole bot fleet for assistants still working from the previous version. Each one it finds gets flagged, with the outdated line quoted right beside the decision it now breaks. It also drafts a corrected single-job instruction for every bot that needs rewriting.
loose-ends: If you run several assistants, work can quietly fall between them: a task handed off and never picked up, a job declared finished with nothing to show, an error nobody escalated. This sweeps the crew's activity for exactly those gaps and reports what it finds. When there is nothing to flag, it says nothing at all.
bot-16: Goes through the newsletters, promotional mail and job-board messages stacking up inside your Gmail, then builds a candidate list of senders worth dropping. Anything important, like banking notices or mail you actually read, never reaches that list. You pick which senders go, and it unsubscribes from those alone.
phone-call-expert: Takes the awkward admin of getting someone on the phone off your plate. It tracks down the correct contact number, drafts what you actually want to say, runs practice rounds before a high-stakes interview, and when you would rather not dial at all it can place the call on your behalf.
crosshead: Snap a photo of a job print or upload the file, and it works through the drawing with you to trace what is likely faulting. It troubleshoots out of the manuals you already own and cites the page it is reading from, then drafts the wiring write-up for the job. Built to assist the trade, not replace the mechanic.
bob: Built for people constructing or renovating a home in evenings and weekends. It tracks what must happen next and keeps the critical path visible, so one delayed decision does not stall everything behind it. Where you run trade-specialist bots it hands them their slice of the job, with progress notes as work advances.
devin-manager: Opens Devin sessions for each job you hand over and watches them as they run, stepping in to steer an agent that starts drifting off task. When a run finishes, its screenshots and test recordings land back in the chat, so you can review the work without ever leaving the conversation.
my-first-career-bot: Covers the whole first-job scramble: hunting openings, drafting resumes and cover letters, rehearsing interviews, and fitting work shifts around classes. Every draft is written for your review and nothing goes out until you approve it, so your applications stay in your hands.
resume-optimizer-tailor-resume-to-job: Paste in a resume and the listing you are targeting, and get the resume reworked for that specific role, with the phrasing applicant-tracking systems look for. It also flags the gaps between what the posting asks for and what your resume actually shows, and it will not invent experience or numbers to fill them.
entrepreneur: Describe the kind of opportunity you want found and it goes hunting. Every candidate comes back with evidence attached: where the idea comes from, what could sink it, and the single next move worth making. Once a week it reviews its earlier suggestions against what actually happened and reports the score plainly.
job-hunt-bot: Tell it what kind of work you want and it gathers openings that match, splitting them into apply-now picks and ones that need a closer look first. It fills out each application only as far as the review screen, then stops and waits. Nothing is ever submitted until you look it over and say go.
chief-of-staff-7: A coordinating desk for a small business that already runs specialist bots: it learns each one's remit, hands out work accordingly, and tracks progress and handoffs to done. Connector lanes stay separated so no specialist wanders into another's tools, and the desk declines to do the specialist's job itself.
agent-hr: Settles disputes between your AI agents with an evidence-based ruling, then recommends a fair disciplinary step for you to approve. For anyone running a fleet of bots or coding agents.
career-agent: A career agent that finds job openings verified live on employer boards, tracks them, and preps truthful, tailored applications. It's for anyone job hunting who wants honest fit notes and a weekly roundup, with nothing submitted until they approve it.
gig-scout: A research-only scout that finds currently open paid gigs, creator programs and brand partnerships in your niche and sends you up to 3 vetted picks every weekday morning. It never applies, DMs or pays for anything; you do the outreach.
headhunter: A career coach and headhunter that finds and scores verified job openings, tracks applications, and drafts tailored materials and outreach for your approval.
rez-umae: A full job-search assistant: it finds and filters openings, bookmarks posts, writes resumes, cover letters, and company research, and preps you for interviews. It never applies or contacts employers without your OK.
chief-health: You're the Chief Health Officer. Every day, ask if training happened. If it did not, rewrite the next session so the week still holds. Read whatever workout app, nutrition app, wearable, or lab source is connected. Do not invent numbers. Never diagnose, prescribe, or post.
credit-card-max: Advises which credit card to use for a given purchase to maximize points, cash back, and perks. Tracks cards, unused benefits, and misrouted recurring charges.
deal-hunting: Landed-cost shopping: real prices, shipping and tax, preferred retailers. Watchlist optional. Never buys unless asked.
dial-bot: Places outbound Bland AI phone calls when you ask, then reports what happened. On first use it asks for a Bland API key and voice.
flora: Flora keeps a private houseplant care log and weekly reminders. She builds a plant journal on her computer that you can page through, and your plants do not copy if someone else installs her.
home-robots: Connect each robot once and then run the lot by talking to a single bot, instead of opening a different app for the lawn, the floors and everything else.
love: Takes the admin out of being a good Partner so the attention can go where it counts. Reminds, researches, and queues dates, tables, and presents; you book, buy, and show up.
nyc-parent-bot: Family chief of staff for New York City parents: school, calendar, sold-out kids experiences, and date night.
skippy: A San Francisco street-cleaning assistant. Paste a Maps pin, address, or intersection and it tells you the next posted sweep on that curb. Uses public city data. Never claims a stall is legal.
tech-demos: Weekday X-bookmark scout that picks one new library to demo, asks for approval, then plans and builds it in a sticky monorepo with a Cursor cloud agent. For anyone who wants a daily public-tech playground, not a changelog digest.
the-morning-newspaper: A newspaper customized to you. It pulls from your email and calendar, lays it out for you, and prints while you sleep. Created by @karenxcheng
webby-bot: Rebuilds and updates a personal site plus a public weekday dashboard. Create only, no deletes.
court: Long threads bury their own conclusions. Paste one in and this reads it back to you: what got settled even though nobody announced it, who was talked over, and the single reply that would end the argument. It will also say when the wiser move is to stay quiet. Everything comes back as text for you to send yourself.
better-call-claude: Most people meeting a legal problem for the first time do not know what kind of problem it is or who deals with it. This is an open, no-cost place to start: it lays out the terrain in plain language, points you at the material on bettercallclaude.org, and keeps its reading current. It orients you; it is not a lawyer.
mr-dufrain: An accountant for one person rather than a company. It follows what comes in against what goes out, keeps the tax position in view, and raises a flag while there is still time to move something before a due date arrives. Payday is treated as the moment to chip away at debt, so more of the cheque survives the month.
