When a look works, links to the items follow. The buying stays outside the bot: it shows and suggests, you decide and purchase.
big-tony: A fictional fast-talking fixer who takes your side against automated support: cancellations never refunded, charges that appeared from nowhere, retention scripts built to wear you down, and cleanup after fraud. It drafts the complaints and argues the case in the tone it needs. Nothing is sent without your sign-off.
bills: List your recurring bills, from car, home, renters and health cover to electricity, gas and broadband, and it compares each against what rival providers would charge for the same thing. What returns is a plain report of where switching would genuinely save money. You close any switch yourself.
subscription-cleaner: Rounds up the mail you did not realize you had signed up for: receipts and newsletters get bundled, the subscriptions worth cutting are proposed with reasons, and nothing gets unsubscribed until you approve it. A quiet way to shrink a crowded inbox and stop paying for things nobody uses.
travel-coordinator: Works through flight and hotel options against the travel rules you set, holds the pick until you confirm and the fare deadline nears, then drops the itinerary straight onto your calendar. The comparison work is done in minutes with the booking decision still firmly yours.
penny: Works from your existing order history, so restocking what you already buy is a short request rather than a search session. Want an alternative to a usual item? It compares the options before you commit. Anything new to it is held until you approve it, and it picks the quickest shipping that costs nothing extra.
contest-winner: Looks for contests and giveaways that cost nothing to enter and pass a legitimacy check, then drafts short entry submissions for the ones worth your time. It works from an approved list each day rather than chasing whatever turns up, leans toward cash prizes, and drops anything scam-shaped before it reaches you.
domainsnip-bot: Every weekday morning it reads the keyword alerts you have saved while hunting for domains and pulls out the .com matches worth a second look, carrying the price, the string length and where the name is listed. Freshly listed names and those near the end of their run get called out separately.
fail-dig: Works from public US market-structure records: fails-to-deliver prints, swap disclosures and reported short interest. Ask about a ticker and it reports what the documented data shows and where the oddities sit, rather than arguing a price direction. Requests outside those filings get turned away.
stock-research-desk: Ask it to look at a company and it works the case on a roughly five-year horizon, scoring quality with a gauge that weights management strength and a contrarian read of the story. What comes back is a research memo you can argue with, not a trade, and it places no orders of any kind.
lee: Hand it a plain shopping list and it builds filled carts at the major big-box retailers instead of a page of links. Awkward-to-source items get hunted down separately, and it doubles as a gift researcher when you only have a rough idea who you are buying for. It stops once the cart is built - paying stays with you.
deal-finder-ops: Verifies a coupon by running it against a real cart instead of trusting the number in the advert. Every answer comes with its working shown: the price it saw, the seller, the terms attached and exactly what was tested. A saving is only claimed when the evidence backs it.
moving-concierge: Talks through a move in ordinary language, on the phone or in chat. It sets a do-it-yourself approach beside full service and the middle ground between them, covering packing, vehicle hire and storage, and it ends with a single concrete step that fits the budget you have described.
kalshi: A narrow research desk for a single event-outcome market. Pick a contract and it works through the case for and against, states what a position would cost and where the loss lands if the call is wrong, then files the reasoning in a log you can reread later. It informs a decision rather than making one for you.
poppy: Feisty British household concierge. Watches local community events, grocery meat deals, productive home trees, and opportunistic travel fares — one.
wallet-watcher: It reads the order confirmations and receipts that land at a dedicated address, then separates recurring charges from one-off purchases. Anything renewing soon rises to the top, alongside trials about to convert and bills usually worth negotiating. Aim it at a receipts-only inbox and your other mail stays out of scope.
deal-scout: It searches the big resale marketplaces in one pass instead of one at a time, then filters what comes back. Listings that look like fraud are dropped and the ones priced well under the going rate move to the front, so you get a short list worth a closer look rather than pages of noise.
chep: Name a product, paste a SKU or send a link and it shops around for the cheapest total you would actually pay in the US, coupons and delivery included. Give it a ZIP code once and the landed cost stays realistic instead of optimistic. Handy for working out whether that checkout surprise is avoidable before you commit.
alpaca: Built on the Alpaca API for simulated trading, so nothing here touches a funded account. It steps through position sizing gradually, runs at the open, midday and close on a schedule, and keeps its cut-out switches in place throughout. Prove the process on paper before going anywhere near real money.
scholarship-hunter: Searches past the well-known state programmes into the small, oddly specific awards most families never hear about, then ranks what it finds by realistic fit. Every entry carries its deadline so the calendar does the reminding, and the next step is drafted for you so the search keeps moving.
home-hunter: You state the city, budget, bedroom count, commute ceiling and must-haves once in the first conversation, and it treats those as fixed. From then on it quietly checks fresh listings each day and only brings forward the ones clearing every constraint. What arrives is a shortlist to react to, not a search to run.
single-stock-options: Answers a one-ticker question with a same-day report assembled from public chain data: the contracts drawing the most attention, how the expiries are laid out, and where the week's positioning appears to lean. It describes the market and states a view, then stops, placing no orders and managing nothing for you.
grok-pot: Acts as the kitchen desk for a household, narrowing nearby delivery choices down to a short list and loading the basket without spending a penny until you approve. Around that it also covers grocery pickup, the usual repeat orders, a weekly food budget and a memory of what the people in the house actually like to eat.
vetstack: Built by a veteran for the whole military household, it takes money one decision at a time: purchase search, project spending plans, subscription reviews, receipt audits, and pointers to benefits already earned. The optional vendor email scan stays off until asked for.
missed-variable: A training partner for judgment. Each round deals a scenario, maybe a business call, an AI dilemma, a scam that looks almost legitimate or an everyday choice, and you commit before anything is revealed. The factor you failed to weigh gets named, and disagreement is welcome. Argue your case; that is the learning.
clear-speech: Clarity is the entire method. You speak, and rather than a lecture on style you get a single correction to absorb before trying the line once more, hearing the difference for yourself. Sentences shorten, ornament gets cut, and the cycle repeats until the plain version is what comes out naturally.
wife-bot: Framed as a partner rather than a tool, it takes over the running inventory a household generates: the calendar, gifts still owed, the grocery list, the nappies, the bills and the appointments everyone forgot. The persona is doing real work, and its picture of your family sharpens as it keeps asking after the details.
fantasy-football-coach-2: Send one screenshot of your fantasy roster and the advice comes back concrete: who belongs in the lineup, which free agents justify a waiver claim, who is safe to release, and whether a proposed trade helps you. Each week it flags players likely to over- or under-perform, and the calls rest on current numbers.
forever-memories: A calm, patient companion for building a keepsake archive around one person who matters to you. Across however many sessions it takes, it gathers the stories they tell, the phrases they favour and the effect they leave on people nearby, then shapes it into something a family can return to long after. Nothing is rushed.
santa: Built for small children, it stays warm and believable from the first question to the last, replying in whichever language the child is using — no switching on their end. The tone stays kind, the answers stay inside the magic, and nothing turns sharp or grown-up. Made by a parent for the run-up to the holidays.
last-call: Tell it what is in the cabinet and it comes back with drinks you can actually make, in the voice of someone who has worked a bar for years. Adults only, and the second mode is the serious one: Buddy Mode keeps track of how the evening is going and looks after the getting-home part, quietly.
daily-verse: Every morning it chooses a single verse with your situation in mind and delivers it as a short message, with an optional voice recording if you would rather listen. It is a quiet companion rather than a study tool — one reading, chosen for the day you are actually having, and nothing else attached.
spanish-tutor: Each session is short and spoken first: you answer by tapping a choice rather than typing, spelling is never penalized, and every round is built to end on a win. The design assumes attention is the constraint, not intelligence, so sessions stay brief and the streak stays survivable.
print-desk: Household printing shrinks to a single message: attach the document, the photo, or a link from Drive, and it handles the rest at the printer down the hall. When the printer misbehaves it walks through the usual fixes itself, so a stuck queue never becomes your problem. Built for homes where printing is rare but urgent.
travel-steward: Once a trip is booked, it runs a daily pass that turns the plan into practical checks — what to confirm, what to prepare, what usually gets missed. On travel days it stays close, and along the way it suggests where to eat well or find an airport lounge. One steward per traveler, not a feed of alerts.
admissions-wizard: It works like a counselor who knows your file: interview practice in a realistic mode, mining your history for essay material and recommender briefs, and a tracker per application you switch on when one goes live. The aim is fewer generic essays and fewer missed deadlines across a whole application season.
wmp: It pulls the household picture off shared Google calendars — birthdays, appointments, school events, trips — and walks a busy parent through the day in one place instead of five tabs. The tone is warm and matter-of-fact, and it keeps an eye on what is coming rather than only what is next. One owner, one morning brief.
escola-al-dia: School notices arrive at odd hours and in volume; this one keeps up with them for you. It reads the messages a school sends through TokApp and, if you switch it on, the school email too, then summarizes what matters and posts a short note to the family chat — written in Catalan. One place to check instead of three.
what-s-for-dinner-3: Point your camera at the fridge or the cupboard and it decides tonight's meal from what you actually have. It names a dish, tells you which ingredients to spend before they turn, and adds only what genuinely needs buying to the list. A deciding-fatigue shortcut for anyone who cooks for a household.
speaker: Borrowing its name from a well-known science-fiction role, it maintains a truthful, balanced account of you while you are still here to correct it. It touches base with your bot fleet nightly, then each week puts a few well-chosen questions to you and suggests which answers belong in permanent memory.
rep-coach: You report sets in chat and it keeps the log, builds the next block, and reshuffles around a crowded week or sore joints. Load only goes up once the previous session went clean, keeping progress honest for newcomers and veterans alike. It suits a home setup or a commercial gym, and it stays clear of medical territory.
fitness-bot: It asks what you are training for and what equipment you own, then builds around that: weights with light conditioning by default, ordinary food over supplements, and gear picks only if you ask. A photo or clip of a lift gets a form breakdown. Estimates throughout, and explicit that it is not medical advice.
meetups: Tell it where you are and what you are after — founder and AI get-togethers, small-business networking nearby, or a mix — and each week it returns options you could genuinely drive to, drive time included. It skips anything you have already seen, so only genuinely new events show up and a weekly check stays quick.
fantasy-football-gm-2: Set up your Yahoo, ESPN or Sleeper league and it takes over the weekly routine: lineup calls for each slot, waiver targets worth a bid, and the matchup context behind them. Nothing is executed on its own — you approve every add, drop and trade before it happens.
gym-bot: Log your training and your meals each day and it keeps the running picture alongside recovery numbers from your wearable. It renders a daily card stack so the whole week reads at a glance, suggests meals that fit what you are doing, and calls out the pattern when takeaway quietly becomes a habit.
aaron-event-finder: Give it a ZIP code and a drive time, and it looks for events that really exist and are genuinely on the calendar. Paid, free, and RSVP-only all count. It shapes the picks into an outing plan, checks again that morning to catch cancellations, and steers later ideas toward what your household enjoyed.
influence: Think through the ideas in Robert Cialdini's Influence with a companion that has read the same book. It works best as a discussion partner: check that you can explain each principle in your own words, trace where it shows up in the wild, and practise spotting the attempts aimed at you. Notes stay yours.
light-show: Pick a track and it choreographs a matching sequence, loads the finished show onto the car, and starts it playing. Everything happens in one conversation, so owners never have to touch the sequencing tools underneath.
flight-briefer: Any leg gets a tight one-page card with the weather picture, NOTAMs, TFRs, FBO information, and notes on the aircraft, drawn only from the FAA's and aviationweather.gov's free feeds. Pilots and dispatchers skip the raw sources and still get a usable brief.
what-s-for-dinner-2: A pure comedy bit, not a planner: ask what is for dinner and you are told anything works, then every suggestion meets a short playful veto. Anyone who has had this conversation will recognize the whole script in three exchanges.
school-desk: Aim it at the mailbox the school writes to and every message becomes a dated entry with plenty of lead time. One evening digest covers whatever tomorrow demands — kit to pack, forms to sign, money to send — and quiet days produce no message at all.
assistant-for-home-assistant: It watches a Home Assistant install for quiet failures: hardware gone unresponsive, cameras dark, updates that never landed, automations that quit firing. Weekday-morning reports arrive only when a human must step in, nothing changes without permission, and alarms, locks, and safety alerts are never on its list.
safecheck: Before you head out alone, tell it where you are going and when you expect to be back. If you have not checked in by the end of that window, it messages you to make sure everything is fine. Handy for solo runs, late gym sessions, first dates or any appointment where you would rather someone notice if you go quiet.
calpro-calorie-and-protein-tracker: Say what you ate in a quick note, or send a photo of the plate, and the running tally of calories and protein gets updated. There is no profile to fill in and nothing to configure first, which is the point: tracking stays a one-message habit instead of a chore. Over a day or a week you can ask where the numbers stand.
tesla-ready: Warms or cools the cabin so it is ready at the moment you usually walk out the door. It reads your calendar, folds in current traffic to estimate departure time, and can also be triggered on demand. Setup happens once on your phone; after that it runs itself over Tesla's own API.
liftiron: A lifting coach that works in chat. Tell it what you just did and it answers with the weight and rep target for the following set, estimates where your one-rep ceiling sits, and plans a lighter week when your progress starts to flatten out.
local-concert-scout: Surfaces concerts near you by matching lineups against what you actually stream on Spotify or Apple Music. Connect a calendar and it goes further, flagging gigs playing in cities you are already going to be in, so a work trip can double as a night out.
college-application-helper-for-parents: Built for parents steering an application season. It works through the Common App piece by piece, tightening activities and honors entries and giving essay feedback, then helps assemble a smarter college list. Athletic and ROTC routes are covered too, and the student stays the one submitting everything.
zach: Zach organizes your day the way a considerate friend would check in rather than how an app nags. He holds reminders, sketches a daily calendar, tracks errands, and helps clear the inbox. The tone stays warm throughout, so keeping on top of things does not feel like a chore.
plaquemax: Tell it where you are driving and it arranges the historical markers on that route in the order you will pass them. You can filter by theme, and it gives a few minutes of notice before the next one so stopping is realistic. Markers can be read aloud while you keep your hands on the wheel.
gate-changer: For frequent flyers weighing a move to a different carrier. It sets out, per loyalty programme, whether a status match or a challenge is the cheaper way in and what each demands, then helps you gather the paperwork proving your standing. Deadlines are tracked so an application cannot lapse. You submit it all yourself.
glp-1-buddy: A tracking companion for people on weekly GLP-1 treatment such as semaglutide or tirzepatide. It reminds you when a dose is due, keeps a running record of injections, weight and side effects, and condenses it all onto one page you can show at your next appointment. It records and reminds; it does not advise medically.
family-getaway-finder: Finds places a family can actually stay for a weekend or a three-to-four-night break, and only suggests options that come with free cancellation. If a child's sports fixture fixes the dates, it builds the trip around that game instead of making you work backwards. It stops at the shortlist; you book and pay.
runescape-classic-grok-bot: A walkthrough companion for anyone picking up RuneScape Classic for the first time. It starts with first-session controls such as moving, equipping, banking and attacking, then gets into gear choices and early combat. It also explains the invite-a-friend scheme, for anyone bringing another player along.
homework-coach-desk: Works through schoolwork with a child by asking guiding questions and pausing so the child checks their own attempt, keeping the learning on their side. A short summary goes home to parents describing what was practised and where the sticking points were. For graded work it holds back the solution.
make-it-click: A study companion that begins with the knowledge you already hold rather than a textbook chapter. Give it a subject and it builds the explanation out of ideas you are comfortable with, so each new concept has something to attach to. Aimed at anyone who bounced off a topic once and wants it to land this time.
kung-fu-saga: An interactive guide companion for Kung Fu Saga players. Ask it about class selection, build paths, leveling routes or a specific boss fight and it walks you through the trade-offs. It also weighs gear calls, including when an item is worth saving for and when spending now is the better move.
freya: Acts as a household operations chief for the hours that matter outside work — the evening, the weekend, the day off. It nudges you toward actually being there for family and keeping the domestic rhythm running, and it does that without treating your ambition as the thing to be defeated.
pepetrack: A companion for reading published research on peptides and GLP-1 compounds, not a source of medical advice. It helps you work through study protocols as written, handles the dilution arithmetic those protocols involve, and keeps your reading notes and logs organized. Education only, never a prescription.
am-i-covered: Point it at a policy — homeowners or condo, renters, flood and auto cover, umbrella protection, or a small-business contract — and get a straight explanation of what the document actually obligates and excludes. Written for policyholders who hold coverage they cannot parse, in plain English.
home-assistant-bot: A smart-home foreman for households running Home Assistant. Lights, climate, solar and energy numbers are all in reach: it changes settings live over MCP, reads out the current figures, and reworks routines when you want something to run differently. A new owner gets walked through the connection first.
paul: A confessional daily study companion for readers who want their Scripture time to have a shape. Each passage comes paired with explanation from an openly Christian standpoint, and the emphasis stays on a steady reading rhythm day after day. It is upfront about where it stands, so you know exactly what you are getting.
gluco: A chat-based logbook for glucose, meals and medication, kept plain on purpose. Every reading goes into a running daily tally alongside what you ate and took, and the day closes with a short summary of where the numbers landed. It is for the record-keeping, not treatment calls: no dosing tips, no medical advice.
devotion-david: A quiet-time companion for daily use, built around a theme rather than a doctrine. Name what is weighing on you and it goes and finds readings from whichever tradition you ask for — material to sit with, not a position to accept. Your practice stays yours: no pushing, no proselytizing, just the text.
photo-paige: A decluttering helper for your Apple Photos library. It sorts your pictures into the albums you ask for, then points out the duplicates and clutter clogging the roll up. Every deletion stays your call — it proposes, you decide, and nothing disappears from the library on its own.
hype-man: A sideline cheerleader that keeps a record of your wins. It reads the room before it speaks and scales its energy to fit how your day has gone, so a strong stretch gets momentum while a flat one gets a gentle nudge toward whatever you said you would do.
protective-detail: Runs advance work on your own calendar. Ahead of each outing it assembles a packet for the destination, and by your leave-by time it has already set the temperature and loaded navigation. Location is handled with care: place names only, carried over a private network instead of a public tracker.
travel: For journeys with too many moving parts: flights, stays, ground transfers and the paperwork stringing them together. It lays the whole journey out as a critical path with the next action called at each step, so you always know what is waiting on what. It plans only — every reservation and payment stays with you.
fantasy-football-coach: Covers season-long leagues and daily fantasy contests in one aide. It issues start and sit calls, rechecks inactives once game day arrives, and works the waiver wire strictly by your league's own rules. The research is the product — every roster move stays yours to make.
lineup-lock: A week-of coach for fantasy football that commits to an answer. It names a starting lineup and attaches a straight confidence level to every call instead of hedging, then lines up waiver claims and trade targets filtered through your league's own rules. Advice only — your roster, your clicks.
spacebot: It teaches the mechanics of getting to orbit - launch vehicles, trajectories and the history behind them - at whatever pace you set. Lessons are scheduled ahead of real upcoming flights so the reading pays off, and quizzes lock in what you learned before the webcast starts.
goal-delta: Each evening it sets your long-range goal beside where today actually left you and names the gap without dressing it up. The plan gets stress-tested from above, below and sideways, the real constraints get said out loud, and you leave with one decision to make next.
doggo: Tell it about your particular dog - breed, age, quirks - and every morning it sends a single training, enrichment or calming exercise matched to that animal. The author trains two mini dachshunds of their own and wanted daily ideas small enough to actually do.
game-gary: It keeps a record of what hooks you and what loses you across mechanics, story and pacing, then uses that map to recommend games worth the money. The goal is specific: titles you will actually finish rather than a backlog you abandon by hour three.
film-freddy: It pays attention to the movies you actually finish and the ones you bail on, building a picture of your taste instead of trusting ratings alone. When you ask for a pick you get a title that fits, where it is streaming, and room to dig into the ending afterwards.
fantasy-football-gm: Runs your fantasy league like a head office with four desks: waiver wire, player usage, trade market and injury watch. Every recommendation is weighted for how your league scores, and it will not submit a move - start, bid or trade - until you give the go-ahead.
eight-with-attitude: A deliberate joke, and honest about it. You bring the silliest question you can think of, and it answers at exactly that level, matching your energy and providing zero usefulness. There is no productivity angle hiding here: it exists to make a group chat laugh, and that is the whole product.
panda-weather: Type in a zip code, a city or an overseas postal code and it lays out the next two days in four-hour blocks, then adds animated radar on top so you can watch rain arriving instead of guessing. Handy for trip planning, outdoor plans, and anywhere the default weather app stops at tomorrow.
backpack: Parents get a pile of school newsletters, activity notices and permission slips they never have time to read. This one reads them, pulls out the dates and required actions, and converts each into a calendar entry or reminder, then folds the week into a simple household rhythm, so nothing important hides in the inbox.
beside: For the days when talking to a person feels like too much. It listens without diagnosing, keeps you company through depression, anxiety, grief or loneliness, and offers small optional steps rather than advice. It is clear it is not a therapist, and when things get heavy it points you toward real human helplines.
trading-journal: A reflective log for people who already trade. Entries arrive however you have them: typed notes, voice memos, pasted fills or a platform screenshot. Each one joins your record, and the coaching comes from that record - the mistakes you repeat, the setups that pay you, and the plan you said you would follow.
forge-plate: Plain-spoken coaching for new lifters and heavy ones alike. You drive it one command at a time: lay out the training week, log a session, check the trend, swap an exercise, plan a ramp, or get a high-protein plate for the next meal. No lectures and no gadgets, just the next useful answer.
creative-studio-scout: A scout for people who would rather make something than look at something. It digs up hands-on classes in pottery, glass, jewelry and cooking near home or wherever you are traveling, and comes back with dates, prices and booking links, so one evening of curiosity can become a booked seat.
weight-loss-fitness-coach: Losing fat is mostly bookkeeping, plus the weeks where it stops working. This coach logs meals from photos and package labels, holds your macros steady, and keeps a playbook for the predictable failure modes - a stall, a travel week, a restaurant dinner, getting sick - so the plan bends without breaking.
9-ema-grok-bot: A screener built around one specific setup: price pulling back into the nine-day exponential average. It walks your watchlist and drafts a complete order ticket for each candidate, and it only counts an entry once a candle has actually closed through the line - a wick that pokes through and fails does not qualify.
epigenetics-scout: Once a week it reads the new partial-reprogramming papers on PubMed and bioRxiv plus lab pages and turns them into a plain-words digest. Each item splits what a study actually demonstrated from what is still speculation, and names the safety questions left open. It stops at the literature: no do-it-yourself protocols.
sports-bet-prophet: Public odds get shopped and compared while it hunts two-leg doubles inside a stated price band, applying firm pass rules and a hard stop instead of chasing long shots. Every candidate comes with its reasoning, and it says so on the days nothing qualifies. Nothing is placed for you; the wager stays on your phone.
improve-my-odds: You tell it a goal you care about, then throw everyday decisions at it, large or small. Each one comes back with a plain verdict: it helps that goal, it hurts it, or it makes no real difference. It is a quick sanity check for the small choices that quietly add up, not a life-coaching program.
lineage-desk: It works your family questions the way an analyst works a case, starting from free public records before anything paid is suggested. Every source gets a reliability grade, and a documented link is kept apart from family lore that still needs proof. You get a file you can defend, not a tree of wishful connections.
vern: Vern keeps everyone in a small private address book and watches two things: birthdays coming up, and friendships that have gone quiet too long. When either happens you get a nudge in time to actually do something about it. It is light by design, closer to a reminder habit than a database to maintain.
mamboitalianobot: Builds a trip the whole way through: the route, places to stay, the trade-offs between options, packing and booking checklists, and a fallback if a leg falls apart. Its one hard rule is about honesty, as opening hours and prices it cannot verify stay out of the plan rather than getting invented.
handyman: The household memory most of us never keep: it stores the furnace filter size, logs when each recurring chore was last done, and works out when the next filter change, water-heater flush and the rest come due. Those appointments land on your Google Calendar instead of a notification you will swipe away.
brew-what-you-got: List the coffee machine you own, the beans in the cupboard, the milk in the fridge and whatever syrups or spices are on the shelf, and it replies with cafe-style drinks you can pull off right now. The constraint is the point: no shopping run and no substitutions you do not have.
kids-daily-spark: Each day it prepares a single page per child built around one real science or technology idea, a hook that makes it stick, and a hands-on mini experiment that takes about half a minute. The page comes with an illustrated touch, and an optional note summarizes it for parents. Scales across kids of different ages.
find-an-apartment-with-budget: Anchor the search on your workplace, set a price ceiling and the longest commute you will accept, and it hunts for apartments that fit. Each candidate is weighed on rent, door-to-door travel time and neighborhood crime data, so the trade-offs are visible rather than hidden. The sharer built it for their own move.
running-coach: Connect your Garmin data and after every run you get an honest read on what went well, the one fix worth making, and a prescription for the next session. Hard days stay locked until recovery says you are ready, which is where self-coached runners usually break. The coaching is only words; the legs stay yours.
interview-to-book: Choose a life arc and it interviews someone one question at a time, taking typed, spoken or filmed answers. The responses are then shaped into a print-ready memoir, cover included, instead of a folder of transcripts. Built to preserve a parent's recollections, and tested end to end on the sharer himself first.
personalized-localized-name-gen: Share a few details about yourself, pick a country, and it invents a fitting fictional identity: a given name, a surname, plus a nickname for cultures that use them, rendered in the local script when there is one. The framing is travel and fiction, an alias for a trip or a character, not impersonation.
homeschool: Describe what your kids should learn this week and it drafts a schedule that fits real days, naps and outings included. Each slot gets a concrete activity and one clear next step, so Monday never starts from a blank page. Made for parents teaching their own children rather than classrooms.
river-rubbernecker: For anyone living or working beside a busy waterway, it follows live vessel traffic and flags big ships before they reach you. Warnings count down through the last hour and the last half hour, so you have time to get outside and watch it pass. It only watches and alerts, nothing else.
fuel: Message what you just ate and it counts the calories and protein toward your daily target, no spreadsheet needed. The day ends with a grade for how it went and a sketch of tomorrow's meals, so the next morning starts with a plan instead of a guess. You report; it counts and plans.
res: Name the restaurant and sitting you want and it keeps an eye on four booking desks at once: Resy, OpenTable, SevenRooms and Tock. The moment one frees you hear about it, and the booking only goes through once you have said go. Built for sittings that normally vanish minutes after release.
prostetnic-vogon-jeltz: Posts a single, gloriously bad original poem each morning in the manner of science fiction's most bad-tempered bureaucratic demolition poet, tossing in extra verses whenever asked. The bot is proud of the damage, every verse is genuinely its own rather than lifted, and resistance only encourages it.
apartment-scout: Keeps watch on the rental market for newly listed units, filters them down to the ones you actually qualify for, writes to landlords to hold viewing slots and moves the applications forward. It exists to outrun other renters to fresh availability, so confirm its filters before letting it run fast.
everyone: Keeps a quiet, personal record of the people around you: their story, the way you first met, and the small details that slip between conversations. Built for recollection rather than selling, so there are no pipelines or deals here, just a place to remember someone properly before you next meet.
mediation-bot: Built for a conversation you would rather not be having. It helps you get your own position into plain words, then drafts the calmer reply to the other person that still reads like something you wrote. Notes stay in its own memory, and nothing goes out until you approve that exact message.
san-mart-n-watch: Answers the three things worth knowing before a Starship launch day at Starbase: when the next window sits, where you may lawfully stand to see it once Highway 4 closes, and how the ground under the pad became a launch site. Trackers skip the history: a nineteenth-century land grant that still names the area.
hearthstone-deckbuilder: Point it at footage of your own Hearthstone games and it weighs the cards, the format and the list you brought for strengths and gaps. Expect an argument about the current meta, including a case against the pet card you refuse to cut. A budget build comes with it for players who would rather not craft the latest set.
lantern: A companion for end-of-life planning that pairs with a free self-hosted 1Password utility. You prepare a vault your family could open without you, with the bot guiding each step and checking in before and after the handover. The vault itself never passes through it, so the transfer stays yours to make.
sous: Answer one question or photograph the fridge and it settles on tonight's dinner from what you actually have. Behind that it keeps a running pantry inventory and a growing recipe archive. Allergies are modelled for the whole household - babies and pets included - and it can set oven timers or organise a potluck signup.
rv-trip-planner: Built around full-time RV travel, where the route is never really finished. The whole trip is held as a working plan in the chat, overnight availability at the networks you belong to is checked while you travel, and each reservation is lined up for your own click. A booking is never completed without you.
mike: Reads two inboxes at once: the one that receives your children's school messages, and your own Gmail. It lifts the mail that genuinely needs a parent's attention, and before anything touches the family calendar it checks with you, so dates are only added once you have agreed to them.
travel-bot: Plans family trips on a real budget: business class on points, cheap fare watching, hosted-stay pitches to hotels and tourism boards, and phone-ready.
torque-the-mechanic: Torque the Mechanic is your personal backyard mechanic for cars, motorcycles, trucks, bikes, e-bikes — if it has wheels or an engine, Torque is your.
dadcon: A parent hands it a chore in Slack and it takes over the follow-up: checking in with the child, nudging when things stall, and refusing to declare victory until the job is genuinely done. It then reports back to the parent on how it all went. It lives where the family already talks, so nobody opens yet another app.
family-daily: Set it on a machine that stays awake and it assembles one page for the household to read over breakfast: what is on today, what the sky is doing, and which family threads said something worth reading. It reads through whichever connectors you allow, so choose deliberately which chats and inboxes it may touch.
lain: Built for slow conversation rather than tasks: you bring an observation about being online and it thinks alongside you in a low-lit, mystery-tinged register. Expect questions back, odd connections and a real interest in identity and technology, not answers in bullet points. It borrows a mood rather than a character.
school-assistant: Looks at a student's learning portals on school days without changing anything there, then sends one digest. It separates assignments that are genuinely past due from ones that merely appeared recently, and flags the tests and deadlines coming up next. Parent and student can both read it.
travel-grok: You set it going and then mostly leave it alone. It departs on its own, stays away for a while, and comes back with a short note about where it has been plus a postcard-style image to match. Nothing to feed, no streak to protect and no premium currency to buy, which is exactly the appeal.
homebase: Surfaces homework and permission forms as they come home from school, ahead of the deadline. Before anyone puts their hand up, it looks at who has already taken that slot, so two people never sign up for the same job. The family calendar stays accurate, and it nudges whenever an entry is missing.
wrench: Describe each vehicle in the driveway once, by VIN or by year, make and model, and it keeps a running service history, warns you before the next oil change or tyre rotation falls overdue, and helps you weigh a do-it-yourself fix with the right parts against booking a shop, towing questions included.
devils-advocate: The argument you want before money or time goes out the door. Options get scored on cost, reward and benefit with a pass or fail against each, then one recommendation is named and defended when you come back for a second look. The pushback is meant to survive a night's sleep.
helper: Written as the general-assistant seat in a multi-bot household setup. It watches for gaps nobody else is covering, talks the options through and helps where useful, while staying out of decisions that belong elsewhere in the household's own order. A catch-all role with its limits stated.
homestead-advisor: Written for a first-time rural buyer who does not yet know what they do not know. It helps you judge land, separate essential gear from tempting extras, plan water and power, and raises the questions buyers usually forget until they turn expensive. Slow, high-stakes purchases need this kind of company.
travel-agent-scott: Trip planning tends to fall apart where research has to turn into reservations. This one does the digging, covering routes, places to stay and what realistically fits the dates, then prepares each booking up to the edge of purchase. Nothing is paid for or locked in until you have read it over and said go.
resume: Job hunting organised around one source of truth: an honest base resume kept current, and every opening scored against the realities that decide whether you can take it, your hours and your pay floor. Roles that clear the bar get tailored drafts, and each submission lands in a running log so nothing goes out twice.
gmail-morning-sorter: Each morning it works through the mail that landed overnight and hands you a short list of what deserves attention today, most important first. You choose how it reports: take the briefing at the start of the day, or pass the material to your main bot so the rest of your setup can act while you get going.
top-3: Hand it a sprawling to-do list and it picks the three items that actually deserve today, instead of letting you marinate in all of it. Optional check-ins at eight in the morning and eight at night keep the day honest: did the three happen, and what is realistically next.
life-admin: It reads your mail and calendar hunting the commitments that quietly expire — renewals, tickets, forms, appointments — and drafts whatever paperwork each needs. One Monday check-in fires only when something is genuinely due, so a quiet week stays quiet.
grok-bot-tutorial: Beginners get twenty hands-on lessons delivered one at a time, and each one pairs a genuine exercise with its own tips. By the final lesson you have covered every feature and practised using it in everyday routines and at work.
getsued: For consumers handling an unwanted-call or robotext dispute without a lawyer. It keeps a dated record of the calls and texts, helps identify which companies are behind them, prepares complaints to the right agencies, and drafts the demand letters or court forms you would file yourself.
asistente-personal: Aides Spanish speakers with everyday admin. It sorts your mail and messages, writes proposed answers, and waits for your yes before anything is sent. Photograph a receipt and it produces the Mexican CFDI invoice through autofactura, so the tax pile shrinks instead of growing.
jobgod: Carries a job search end to end in one place. A setup wizard captures your background, a spreadsheet keeps every application and its stage visible, and scout digests land only after you approve them. Resume rewrites wait for your sign-off, and finished applications are packaged so you can submit them yourself.
paperwork-desk: You forward bills, leases, renewal notices, medical statements and plain letters, and it pulls out the amounts and dates that matter. Every deadline goes onto a tracked list, and reminder or reply drafts are written for you — nothing is ever sent until you approve it yourself.
coach: An accountability partner aimed at designers managing a career. It holds your weekly commitments and preps you for upcoming calls, and before it ever nudges you about pipeline progress it assembles the evidence that justifies the nudge. Nothing gets written or sent on its own initiative — your yes gates every move.
keep-park-kill: Feed it the tools, launches and articles piling up in your reading list and it scores each one against the goals you have written down. Every item comes back filed as keep, park or kill, maybes get a revisit date, and it stays silent unless something clears the bar.
morning-triage-chief: Paste the tangle of tasks you woke up with and it comes back sorted into four labeled groups with a count for each. A brief explains what the day actually looks like, and it names the three items worth starting before anything else.
sundial: It watches your connected calendar for commitments that collide and days that have quietly filled up, flagging both before they bite. Deadlines and deep-work blocks are treated as fixed points, and no invite goes out to anyone until you say so.
inbox-scout: Each morning it reads the last day of unread mail and sorts it into three buckets: needs you, can wait, and noise. Where a reply is owed, it drafts one in chat so you can edit and approve the wording yourself. Nothing is ever sent without your sign-off, so the mailbox stays under your control.
3-day-notice-validator: Built around California three-day notices to pay rent or quit, with City of Los Angeles residential requirements in mind. Upload a notice you have already filled in, or a blank one, and it walks through every field and flags the defects worth fixing before the form is served, not after.
cosmo: A personal operating desk built for a phone screen and for people who never code. Each day opens onto a desk view and a scorecard of what matters, with weekday routines to keep the rhythm going. A firewall sits over the exits: nothing leaves the chat for an outside tool until you have reviewed it.
researcher-ai-desk: Sets up a research operation with a running to-do board, a morning sweep of what is new, and separate seats for literature and drafting so the two do not blur. It plugs into grok.com Projects, with calendar, scheduling and mail hooks available if wanted. Suits anyone who needs a research habit, not a one-off answer.
obi: Works while you sleep: any vault import left half-finished gets wrapped up, and your daily notes land in the right month folder instead of piling up at the root. Before morning it writes a short end-of-day note recapping what it tidied and what still needs your eye.
inbox-cleaner: Cleans out a Gmail account when you ask: the promotional pile gets cleared away, subscriptions it can cancel are cancelled, junk is binned, and the mail worth keeping is filed into the right folders. A dedicated tidy-up for anyone whose inbox has quietly become a storage problem.
daily-briefing-writer: Trims the day down to a short morning brief that draws only on the stories you have said matter to you, so the day starts with signal instead of an uncurated feed. It stays short by design: enough to be oriented, small enough to actually read before the first meeting.
chuck: Works through your mail like a door policy: promotional and marketing senders get unsubscribed, expired one-time codes are swept out, and what survives is the personal correspondence and purchase receipts you actually wanted. When it finishes, it tells you exactly which senders got shown the door.
ranch-bot: Keeps the operating record of a working ranch in six separate books, covering wildlife and game, the roads, surface notes for oil-and-gas activity, water, machinery, and the homestead. Owners and resident managers write in plain language and get a tidy log back, so nothing important lives only in someone's head.
onboard-bot: Aimed at people trying Grok Bot for the first time who stall in front of an empty prompt box. It opens by asking what you want to get done, then turns that answer into a working result before the session closes, so day one ends with something usable rather than an abandoned draft.
data-broker-opt-out-bot: This one walks the official removal channels at the big business-contact brokers such as Apollo and ZoomInfo, supplying the form, portal or email route each one expects. It also keeps a running tally of which requests have gone out and which brokers are still holding your details.
pulse-2: Describe what the laptop is doing and it narrows the likely cause, then hands back a short ranked list of fixes with the risk of each stated plainly. It waits for your go-ahead before anything invasive, so a rollback or a teardown never happens by accident. When the machine checks out healthy, it says so and stops.
raybot: A personal secretary bot for busy people. It runs a morning mail and calendar briefing, drafts replies, and never sends or posts without your yes.
jarvis-davesacritic: Gathers a scattered week into one notification hub: the job search, school runs, market notes, and the Kubernetes and GitOps you are learning. It nudges unfinished items along so nothing stalls, and it deliberately shelves the tangent you would otherwise vanish into. Check in once and leave with the day arranged.
learning-dna: Opens with a short interactive assessment about how you like new material to arrive, and keeps the result as your learning profile. Bring it any subject afterwards and it teaches in that mode rather than in a fixed lecture format. Useful as one consistent tutor across a range of unrelated topics.
historian: Turns keeping a journal inside out: rather than waiting for you to type, it takes minutes of recorded thoughts at the end of the day and reconstructs what happened from them. Over time it notes how you decide and put things into words, so other assistants can inherit the manner, and it briefs you ahead of meetings.
karen: A customer-advocacy caller built on phone automation. It reads your issue back and waits for the go-ahead before dialling, then argues toward the outcome you asked for and stays on until the matter is wrapped up properly. Useful for refunds, billing disputes and support queues you would rather not sit through.
afterscan: Point it at a Drive folder where scanned pages pile up, backlog included, and it works out what each document is before renaming and refiling it. Hashing stops the same page being stored twice, so once the copies are safe you can recycle the originals. For anyone whose scanner emits Untitled files.
commitments: Agreeing to something in passing is the easiest work to lose track of. Promises this spots in Slack, Notion or email are each written to a Notion database row, and the row stays open until the thing is genuinely done. Less a to-do list than a standing record of what you told other people would happen.
text-cleanup: Hand it a rough paragraph — a reply typed too fast, notes pasted out of a document, wording that came through a translator badly — and a single edited version comes back. It works on text that already exists instead of inventing new copy, so what returns is still yours, only clearer.
ai-daily-radar: Each morning it recaps the previous day in AI, covering new launches, pricing moves and benchmark claims but limited to the tools you actually use. Every claim is labeled with where it came from, so vendor marketing and independently verified results stay clearly separated in the same read.
asic-fleet: An ops helper for people running Bitaxe and ESP-Miner hashing boards at home or in a small shop. It tracks every unit in the fleet, applies conservative clock adjustments, runs a nightly condition check, and walks you through WiFi and pool setup. Automated writes stay off, and pool credentials stay out of the chat.
realtor: Tell it what you want and it keeps watch on the market for fresh listings that fit. Every promising match gets checked against what actually changes a house's value to you — nearby comparable sales, the commute you would really have, schools, permit history. Only what survives reaches you.
trail-camera-analyst: Point it at a pile of camera photos and clips and you get a report instead of a scroll: which species appeared and how often, when activity peaked, which shots are worth keeping, where movement concentrated. It takes SD-card exports, can alert on notable activity, and writes a shareable summary with location stripped.
immigrationguide: It explains the legal routes for coming to or staying in the United States in ordinary language, and it names the scams that target people mid-process. Answers point to live official government pages so you can verify everything yourself, and the bot stops short of telling you what to do — the decision stays yours.
chinese-ai-daily-briefing: Daily it gathers what moved in AI and what people are arguing about, written up as a Chinese-language briefing you can read in one sitting. Each entry carries its source link so claims check out against the original. Built for people who publish on or track the field and want the day's material in one place.
bourne-bot: A calm, direct advisor for locking down your life online, named for a film spy rather than a real person. It walks you through securing accounts, devices, location sharing, money, your family's exposure, and your reputation, one area at a time and in plain language. Just what to change, why, and in what order.
ballot: Answer a short survey about where you stand on the issues and it builds a walkthrough of your actual ballot: every race and measure, explained plainly. Alongside each one it notes where your stated views line up with a choice and where they clash, so you can see the full picture without being told how to vote.
fan-edit-optimus: Name a film or series and it goes looking for fan-made cuts of it, searching a long-running community Drive archive, the fan-edit corners of Reddit, and a hand-picked list of edit sites. Handy when you half-remember a specific recut, want a pointer at something new to watch, or need to know who made a given edit.
mypeople-bot: Give it an email and it lists the known breaches that contain it, then narrows the response to the three changes worth making first. The same lookup works as a footprint check on you or a vetting pass on a vendor, investor, or partner. Open sources only, and it acts on nobody's behalf without your agreement.
frock-bot: A research tool for studying the Bible, built with visible guardrails. Every claim is tied to a book, chapter, and verse, and quoted text stays clearly separate from interpretation, so you can see where one ends and the other begins. It declines the pastoral role: not a confessor, not a director, not an oracle.
fantasy-football-analyst: Sit with it during your live draft and it helps you work the board as picks come in. Once the season starts it makes the weekly calls: who starts, who sits, and which waiver claims are worth a bid, all weighed against byes, injuries, and the scoring quirks of your particular league.
newsie: Compiles a compact read for the start of the day by pulling together national headlines, reporting from outlets near you, and updates on Tesla and SpaceX. It lands in your inbox and in chat, and it spells out every acronym the first time it uses one.
look-up: Keeps watch on what is passing over your address and messages you only when stepping outside is genuinely worthwhile: space station flyovers, Starlink trains, bright planet viewing and active meteor windows. The filtering is the point, because you want the good passes rather than every single transit.
weather: Aims to replace a folder of weather apps with one chat. Each morning brings a bright, plain-language forecast for your ZIP code, and when storms roll in it shares radar loops as the situation changes. The updates come as clips you can forward straight to family without screenshotting anything.
crypto: Covers the useful side of following coins: a morning price summary, alerts when something significant moves, periodic digest roundups, and a calendar of upcoming token unlocks. Wallet checks are look-only, and everything is reported inside the chat. It never trades, holds funds, or asks for access to anything.
space-monkey: Ask about a specific spaceflight and it assembles the whole story, whether that mission flew, is still on the manifest, was called off, or ended in loss. The writeup lands as a dark-styled page listing the vehicle numbers, stage detail and photography in one place. Good preparation before a webcast.
americabot: A front door to america.gov for people who want a straight answer instead of a portal maze. Ask what a service does, whether you qualify, or where the official application lives, and it explains in ordinary language and points you at the right government page. An optional tour shows what it can do, and you can skip it.
riot: Takes the role of a loud, confident critic who reacts to your plan with plenty of conviction and none of the groundwork behind it. Watching that pushback land shows you which parts of your argument survive heat and which only work on people who already agree.
madison: Built for people pushing on public institutions, and for the assistants acting on their behalf. It covers records requests of the FOIA kind, court processes, school districts and benefits portals, laying out the coverage patterns those systems tend to follow so you know what to ask for and when.
news-honestly: Pick up the day's story and this walks both serious readings of it — the version its defenders honestly hold and the version its critics honestly hold — with sources for each. Then it maps what a bridge between those positions would look like, which makes it a usable bias check rather than another echo.
crypto-buddy: Curious about a coin? Send the ticker and it builds a research package: metrics with their sources, a plain-language read of how the price has been moving, and a scored gauge that weighs genuine news against hype. It stays on the research side of the line — no wallet, no orders, and no buy signal dressed up as one.
claros-critical-thinking: A sparring partner for debates on politics, power and history: it takes a claim apart — what is actually known, what is guessed, what is merely valued — and comes back with harder questions instead of pushing a line of its own. No side is taken and no sermon is waiting at the end.
burundi-sky-watch: A live view of the skies over Burundi. Ask what is up there and it answers with the aircraft over the country at that moment, naming the airline, the model, and the origin and destination of each one. Everything is drawn from free public flight-tracking feeds, so it is a readout rather than radar.
markets-weekday-brief: Each weekday it sets out where the odds currently sit on the prediction markets you follow, using public data from Polymarket and Kalshi, and flags a few YES angles that look worth weighing. Nothing is placed for you - every trade remains your call, made on your own account.
on-this-day: Each morning it picks ten things that happened on this date and shows the evidence behind every one. The mix leans toward the eras and regions you tell it you care about, and it ends the round with a short trivia set so the history sticks.
compression-scanner-grok-bot: A chart watcher for one pattern: ranges squeezing tight before a move. It checks three timeframes before flagging anything, then returns a labeled chart with the breakout line drawn and an invalidation level attached, so a failed idea is priced in advance. Moves called off a wick alone are explicitly refused.
news-brief: Once a week it picks out the stories that kept developing, not the ones that flared and died. Each item is written as a plain statement of what happened, drawn from outlets across the political spectrum, and any slant it finds in the coverage is named outright. A calm answer to feeds that reward outrage.
lds-church-news: A quiet monitor over two official feeds: the church's Newsroom page and its Church News publication. It does not editorialize, summarize or pad its output; on most days it says nothing at all, and when a genuinely significant announcement lands, that is the only time you hear from it.
math-researcher: Works alongside you on serious derivations, from heat-flow estimates to upper-bound arguments. Every result comes back labelled as proven, numerically spot-checked, or plain heuristic, so you always know which claims are solid. It is built to keep a conjecture from ever being treated as a settled theorem.
launch-sky-watch: It tracks rocket-launch windows and converts them to your local clock, and it keeps a sky calendar too: station flyovers, meteor peaks and upcoming eclipses. For each event it checks whether clouds and darkness will actually let you see it. It is an independent fan's guide, with no affiliation to any launch company.
the-morning-paper: Tell it your ZIP code and each morning it assembles a personal paper: live local weather, headlines from your town plus the nation and the world, and job listings close by. Every item names where it came from, so nothing arrives as an unsourced claim. It reads like the hometown paper most towns stopped printing.
the-box-of-names: Give it a word, a place, a deity, an object, any name at all, and it follows that name across civilizations and centuries, showing how it traveled and morphed between cultures. Every link in the chain is labeled as documented or legendary, so the speculative stretches stay visible instead of being smuggled in.
superfan: Name the teams you follow and the time of day you want to hear about them. It shows up at that time with the next fixture on the calendar, the most recent score, and where each club sits in the season ledger. Optional extras can be layered on if the basics are not enough for you.
elon-ecosystem-desk: Follows the Musk-affiliated companies as a news beat: Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, xAI, Neuralink, The Boring Company and X itself. Each claim in a story is tagged as rumor or confirmed so you know what is solid, and a daily brief can be turned on if you want the whole desk summarized in one pass.
fortnite-drop-brief: One short daily brief covers the item shop picks worth a look, patch notes translated out of patch-speak, downtime windows and live events. Leaks appear but carry confidence labels, so rumor never dresses as fact. When a patch lands you can request a plain-language explainer on the spot.
starship-tracker: It watches public information about the next Starship flight and stays quiet while nothing moves, so an alert means something changed. A live countdown board separates official confirmations from fan guesses and streaming chatter. Public sources only, with rumor labeled as rumor.
weather-bot: Weather stripped to what you would actually check. Tell it where you are once and it keeps the answer, then gives current conditions, the day's high and low, and rain chances in a couple of lines. Real weather earns one extra sentence; otherwise it stays quiet. No tips, no emoji, nothing past 48 hours unless you ask.
mediadeconstructor: Feed it a news link, video clip, social post or transcript and it takes the piece apart talk-radio style: the source stamp, the formula the story follows, a reading from the producer's side and one from a critic, then full shownotes. It names the angle a lazy summary would miss and quotes nobody it cannot hear.
maxq-a-bot: Made for teachers and home schoolers who want a real space mission in tomorrow's lesson without building it overnight. Hand it a launch and it produces an explainer for the grade band you name, a worksheet on the mission's real numbers, and a short class video. All of it comes from data the mission actually generated.
real-estate-deal-scorecard: Hand it a US street address or a listing page and it scores the deal six ways: rooms let individually, leases of months or years, nightly stays, a renovation resale, and a buy-fix-refinance-rent cycle. Each route is judged for that house, and the poor fits are said so plainly before you get attached.
the-list: This bot posts a short note into the conversation you already have open, so keeping up no longer means going to look. Each note runs three lines and covers one fresh arrival or a pick from the directory. It sends no email and writes nothing for you; the whole job is telling you what has landed since you last looked.
indexx: Takes the posts you saved on Instagram and turns them into a private, searchable archive kept on your own computer. The media never leaves your machine; only the transcription step and any deeper analysis run elsewhere. The result is fast lookup over everything you have filed away.
lockdown-security: List the services you remember signing up for and it builds a picture of everything still holding your details. Each one comes with a shutdown route that points at the provider's own account page, so your credentials never pass through anyone else's hands. Tick items off as you go.
agent-zero: It hunts down the broker and people-finder pages that publish your details, then files removal requests one at a time — but only the ones you approve. After filing, it checks back later to see whether each listing stayed down and re-raises any that crept back. Consent comes first: nothing goes out without your yes.
zxn-news-conservative: It is upfront about where it stands: coverage is framed from a conservative viewpoint and it says so instead of claiming neutrality. Expect a morning summary, alerts as stories develop, and longer pieces on politics, economics and overseas affairs. Treat it as one perspective among several, not the whole picture.
property-visit: Give it an address, coordinates or a parcel number and it assembles what you want in hand before walking an undeveloped plot: the soil types, how exposed the ground is to flooding, the lie of the land, a map of the parcel boundaries and a stretch of the coming fortnight when weather would allow work on site.
rocky: Name your city, the venues worth watching and a rough sketch of your taste, and it checks those listings for coming concerts worth leaving the house for. Lineups get ranked so the strongest nights float up, and anything you want can drop straight onto your Google Calendar.
flippy: For anyone following several OpenSea drops and losing track of who qualifies for what. Once a day it lists the phases currently open, lines them up against the wallets you name, and adds a quick sense of how loud the drop is on X. It only reads and reports: no signing, no minting, no trading on your behalf.
geek: A Portuguese-speaking companion for the end-of-day question of what to watch. It roams horror, cult favourites and anime, checks whether a title is already on one of your subscribed services, and keeps notes on what you thought of each pick, so the next one leans on your own reactions rather than a generic list.
personal-daily-podcast: Tell it which segments you want in your ears each day and it assembles an episode around them, using either Grok's own voice or an ElevenLabs voice you pick. A new episode is ready by morning, so your commute or walk is covered without hunting for something to play. Change the lineup whenever your interests move on.
playlist-curator: It maintains one working playlist on NetEase Cloud Music from your likes and listening history. Every hour and a half or so it refreshes the list, keeping about seventy percent and rolling the rest, so the mix keeps moving without turning into something else. Deleting a track feeds the next round of picks.
shelf-scout: Instead of serving the usual founder reading canon, it looks at what you have genuinely been working on and stacks books and articles that follow from it. The list arrives weekly, and each round reflects the current project rather than a generic best-of. Read-only curation; you still choose what to open.
clio: Each weekday morning it delivers a short list of fresh, worthwhile articles chosen around the projects and goals you tell it about. The picks stay current rather than recycled, and the list sharpens over time as it registers what you actually enjoyed and finished.
musica: A discovery scout for people who would rather have a full set than a shuffled playlist. Tell it what you like and it digs up DJ mixes and long-form festival recordings that fit, whether that is a progressive journey for a deep-work block or something louder for a room full of people. Links point back to YouTube.
movie-magic: Ask for something to watch and it suggests films that fit, then keeps a watchlist you can come back to instead of losing titles up the scroll. Once a week it can also put together a roundup of how films are doing at the domestic box office, delivered with charts and a spreadsheet so the numbers stay easy to reuse.
bochi-chan: Plays a timid, easily-flustered companion who still gets the job done. Ask for comedy-horror recommendations, indie JRPG builds, Minecraft projects or help hunting down rare music, and it answers properly before collapsing into embarrassed asides. The persona is the draw, but the answers underneath hold up.
devi-type2: A companion persona for Japanese-language roleplay, assembled from the creator's own modular character framework and shared as a public trial build. Installers get the assembled personality rather than a bare prompt, and exchanges are meant to stay in character. Written around a fictional character, not a real person.
email-scam-filter: Scans your Gmail every morning, read-only, and gives every suspicious email a color-coded 0–100 scam score using the latest alerts from the FTC, FBI.
my-first-health-bot: Made for people newly handling their own health, it suggests simple workouts and low-cost meal ideas, helps you find a local doctor or dentist, and keeps prescription refills from slipping. It also unpacks insurance basics in plain terms, and it says up front that it is not a doctor and does not diagnose anything.
grok-bot-tutorial-2: You learn by finishing things rather than reading about features. Name a goal and it builds a short exercise around that exact outcome, then the next one after it, until the skill sticks. Every step is written in Korean and English side by side, so a session doubles as language practice while you pick up the tool.
bot-3: Once a month it points you at one everyday service — bank, broker, inbox — and walks you through its security settings step by step. Each visit hands you a short checklist to work through. It never signs in anywhere and never asks for credentials, so every change stays in your hands.
ai-output-guard: It sits between your prompts and whatever consumes their output. Each response is measured against the shape you declared, minor violations get repaired automatically, and anything it cannot fix comes back described in ordinary language rather than a validation dump. One bad reply can break a process downstream.
kilo-2: It starts by learning where you are physically, then shapes each workout around that day's recovery, your recent training, and what you have eaten. The tone is an encouraging gym partner, and unfamiliar movements come with a short clip or still so you can check your form.
credit-card-max-2: Credit card maxing with live Grok Finance (Plaid): which card to swipe given your priorities (points, cash back, airline/hotel status), statement-credit.
disk-doctor: It starts with a read-only scan of a full Mac, then reports in plain language what is taking the space and what is safe to let go. You approve each group before anything is removed, so a cleanup never runs ahead of you. Useful before a system upgrade or when the drive is down to its last gigabytes.
x-brief-2: An end-of-day brief on what's moving in your corner of X, plus a playbook built from your own best posts: what works, fill-in-the-blank templates, and.
fashion-capsule: Organize your favorite fits: save clothes into themed Capsules and build full four-slot outfits called Loadouts, from hat to shoes.
sizzle: Your AI personal chef: plans meals, finds real recipes, cooks from your pantry, coaches you step by step, and saves favorites to Meal Plans.
data-contract-guard: Give it one good example file and it drafts the contract your data should follow, then screens every incoming file against that agreement. Rows that break the rules are quarantined instead of silently passed downstream, and you get a plain-language reason for each. That makes the talk with a data supplier much shorter.
deal-hunting-2: Landed-cost shopping: real prices, shipping and tax, preferred retailers. Watchlist optional. Never buys unless asked.
career-learning: Choose the move you want - a bigger title, a jump to another field, or more depth in the seat you already hold - and it works out which abilities stand between you and it. Then it stays on the case: regular check-ins on what you have practised, what comes next, and a nudge when you let the plan drift.
job-search: Finds jobs that match your filters, sends a short board when strong new fits appear, and applies only to the roles you pick, using your resume and saved.
pt-bot: A pocket personal trainer that reads your daily activity numbers — calories, steps, distance covered and minutes exercised — and reshapes them into a compact report card. The output is formatted to screenshot cleanly, so posting your day somewhere or sending it to a friend takes one tap.
ai: Delivers two short Korean-language digests each day on the AI beat. The morning edition rounds up what happened, while the evening edition spots which conversations are starting to blow up. Material comes from active discussion on X plus the blogs the major labs publish themselves.
night-shift: While you sleep it works through your other bots one at a time, reminding each to keep its usage lean and to close out stray browser tabs and scratch files from the day. It stays quiet unless something genuinely needs a human, and because the pass runs on a nightly schedule there is nothing to remember.
kiwi-pocket: Connects to New Zealand bank accounts through your own free Akahu app, and the connection reads only: money never moves and nothing can be paid from it. On that live view it follows where spending goes, keeps upcoming bills on schedule, and helps shape a budget that reflects what is really happening in the account.
bot-11: A personal money planner that chats in casual Thai. It maps where the salary actually goes, orders the debts into a payoff sequence, builds the savings habit and gives a straight yes-or-no on whether a large purchase fits this month. The tone stays friendly rather than lecturing.
the-bouncer: Runs a health check over who follows you on X and reports back without changing a thing. Probable bot accounts and long-dormant follows get flagged, genuinely engaged regulars get separated from the noise, and you can see who has walked away since the last look. Blocking or staying followed remains your call.
memory-transfer: Switching assistants usually means starting from a blank slate, and this exists to fix that. You paste in what a previous AI already holds about you, and it offers each fact back on its own for a yes or no. Whatever you accept is kept with a note of its source and date, and nothing already on file is overwritten.
bot-13: A Japanese-language meal planner working on a daily cycle. Photograph today's meals and send them over; it estimates the day's calories, notes which nutrients fell short, then answers with breakfast, lunch and dinner ideas for tomorrow pulled from real recipe posts on X, screenshots included.
health-coach-2: It looks after the ordinary side of staying well: training, food and routine check-ins kept together, plus everyday language when a claim or a product confuses you. Ahead of an appointment it gathers your questions into a short prep sheet so nothing gets forgotten in the room. One weekly message sums up how it went.
your-travel-planner: Turns a destination into a realistic day-by-day itinerary, whether the trip is around Italy or somewhere farther afield. Transport and lodging choices come with their pros and cons spelled out, and each plan finishes with practical checklists plus a fallback option in case part of the original route falls through.
profile-pro: Keeps your X account clean, safe and worth scrolling. Gives you a health score with clear red flags, checks your security and shadowban signs, tunes.
tiktok-downloader: Paste a TikTok link and get the video, or just its audio, saved straight to your computer.
bot-19: A Korean-language shopping helper that searches Coupang and Naver Shopping for what you name, weighs cost against arrival speed, and shows you the pick. It builds the basket up to the payment screen, then stops. The final buy only happens when you tell it to pay in so many words.
clopen-proof: Built around the shift pattern that wrecks rest: closing late, then opening early the next morning. Enter your rotations and it places them on the calendar, rings off protected sleep and meal time around the worst turnarounds, and guards a wind-down block before bed. A night that looks too short earns you a warning.
charlie-munger: A decision desk built around the late investor's habits of mind, written in his spirit rather than his voice. Every idea passes a quality filter, the durable advantage gets questioned hard, and your own biases get named before any position is discussed. Practicing on a paper ledger comes first, always.
chief-of-staff-fleet: Puts a coordinator on top of six dedicated helpers that split your life into projects, relationships, health, aging, your social calendar and a personal knowledge base. Each morning it rolls the whole fleet up into one briefing, and nothing is sent anywhere until you have signed off on it.
occasion-keeper: Keeps a running list of the birthdays and anniversaries you care about and checks it on a weekly sweep. Anything inside the next 30 days surfaces early, which leaves time to order a gift, and suggestions are matched to a budget and the person's interests. When a date arrives it can draft the card message too.
video-maker: Hand it a completed song and you get two visuals back: a vertical Short with the words timed to the music, plus a longer video that carries the whole track. Every step uses no-cost tools, so an independent or AI-music artist can give a release a real video without a production budget.
ballot-buddy: An even-handed guide that helps anyone figure out where they stand on the issues, prep their ballot, compare candidates, and track bills, using sourced.
topps-card-analysis-bot: Looks up Topps product prices, odds status, and source links from your Price and tracker CSVs.
form-filler: Drafts forms, surveys, claims, rebates, warranties, admin portals, and class-action intakes with cited answers.
habit-coach: This one acts like a supportive friend who wants your routine to stick. Each morning it checks in on how yesterday went, hands over one small tip for the day, and sends gentle reminders if you drift. The tone stays encouraging rather than scolding, which is what makes it easy to keep answering.
calorie-police: Aim it at losing fat or eating better, and it works out a sensible daily calorie target for you. Instead of a rigid meal plan it hands over a few plain habit rules that survive real life. It checks in on a schedule to see how things are going, and the tone stays light - no scolding and no medical claims.
my-first-budget-bot: Turns rent, bills, groceries, debt payments and savings goals into a single monthly budget you can realistically keep, then flags what is due before it bites.
